java/interview.html:
What this is
A complete, 9-part Java core interview reference — 690 questions with answers, code, tables, traps, and self-tests.
Built for Obsidian: collapsible callouts, wiki links, tags, and checklists.

The 9 Parts

# Part Topics Questions
1 Part 1 — Basics JVM/JDK/JRE, data types, operators, Strings, wrappers, static/final, constructors, arrays, access modifiers Q1–Q70
2 Part 2 — OOP Four pillars, inheritance, polymorphism, abstract vs interface, equals/hashCode, immutability, inner classes, enum/record/sealed Q71–Q154
3 Part 3 — Collections Hierarchy, List family, HashMap internals, Maps, Sets, Queues, CME, Big-O cheat sheet Q155–Q240
4 Part 4 — Exceptions & Generics Throwable hierarchy, try-with-resources, custom exceptions, type erasure, wildcards, PECS Q241–Q316
5 Part 5 — Concurrency Threads, synchronized, JMM, volatile, deadlock, thread pools, CompletableFuture, virtual threads Q317–Q400
6 Part 6 — JVM JVM architecture, heap generations, GC algorithms, class loading, memory leaks, tuning tools Q401–Q468
7 Part 7 — Java 8 & Modern Java Lambdas, functional interfaces, Streams, Collectors, Optional, java.time, Java 9–21 Q469–Q556
8 Part 8 — IO & Reflection I/O and NIO, serialization, reflection, dynamic proxies, annotations Q557–Q620
9 Part 9 — Patterns & Puzzles Design patterns, 28 output puzzles, coding round list, behavioural prep, final review sheet Q621–Q690

A 3-Week Study Plan

Do not read all nine parts in one week. Depth beats coverage.

Week 1 — Foundations

Day Task
1–2 Part 1 + write every code sample yourself
3–4 Part 2, focus on equals/hashCode and immutability
5–7 Part 3 — spend 2 full days on HashMap internals alone

Week 2 — Depth

Day Task
8–9 Part 4 (PECS and erasure need slow reading)
10–12 Part 5 — the hardest part; do the concurrency coding exercises
13–14 Part 6 — GC and class loading

Week 3 — Modern Java + polish

Day Task
15–16 Part 7 — write 20 stream one-liners from memory
17 Part 8
18 Part 9 patterns
19 All 28 output puzzles, twice
20 Coding round list — 10 problems on paper
21 Final review sheet + prepare your 3 stories

The Highest-Value Questions

If you only have one evening, learn these:

  1. HashMap internals — Part 3, Q179–Q185
  2. equals/hashCode contract — Part 2, Q118–Q123
  3. sleep vs wait, volatile vs synchronized — Part 5, Q323, Q350
  4. ThreadPoolExecutor parameters — Part 5, Q369
  5. Heap generations + memory leaks — Part 6, Q413, Q421
  6. map vs flatMap + stream laziness — Part 7, Q496, Q498
  7. Type erasure + PECS — Part 4, Q299, Q308
  8. Immutable class design — Part 2, Q128
  9. Composition over inheritance — Part 2, Q75
  10. The 28 output puzzles — Part 9

How to Actually Use This

Reading is not studying
Memorizing 690 answers does not create confidence. Doing these three things does:
  1. Type every code sample. The Integer cache trap sticks forever after you print it once; it never sticks from reading.
  2. Answer out loud. Interviews are spoken. Silent recognition ≠ spoken explanation.
  3. Prepare stories, not just facts. For each question, have one line from your own experience: "I hit this when…". That single sentence is what separates a memorizer from an engineer.

Obsidian tips:

  • Blocks written as > [!question]- ... are collapsed by default — perfect for self-testing. Guess, then click to reveal.
  • Use the tag #java in the graph view to see the whole map.
  • The checklists at the end of each part are real checkboxes — tick them as you go.

Recommended Next Steps

After this series, the natural extensions are:

  • Spring / Spring Boot (DI, AOP, transactions, Spring MVC lifecycle)
  • SQL & JPA/Hibernate (N+1 problem, lazy loading, transaction isolation)
  • System design (caching, load balancing, database scaling)
  • Testing (JUnit 5, Mockito, test doubles)
  • Books: Effective Java (Bloch) and Java Concurrency in Practice (Goetz) — most of the deeper answers here trace back to these two.
690 questions · 9 parts · 1 goal
Walk in knowing five topics cold rather than ninety topics vaguely. Good luck.

About this note
Part 1 of 9 — Java Basics & Language Fundamentals
Format: Question ➜ Short answer ➜ Deep answer ➜ Code ➜ Interview trap

Series Map

Part Topic Status
1 Language Basics & Fundamentals You are here
2 OOP Deep Dive
3 Collections Framework
4 Exceptions & Generics
5 Multithreading & Concurrency
6 JVM Memory, GC & Class Loading
7 Java 8+ (Lambda, Stream, Optional)
8 I/O, Serialization, Reflection, Annotations
9 Design Patterns + Tricky Output Puzzles

Table of Contents

  • Section 1 — Java Platform (Q1–Q8)
  • Section 2 — Data Types & Variables (Q9–Q18)
  • Section 3 — Operators & Control Flow (Q19–Q26)
  • Section 4 — Strings (Q27–Q36)
  • Section 5 — Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing (Q37–Q42)
  • Section 6 — Keywords: static, final, this, super (Q43–Q52)
  • Section 7 — Constructors & Initialization Order (Q53–Q58)
  • Section 8 — Arrays & Varargs (Q59–Q65)
  • Section 9 — Packages & Access Modifiers (Q66–Q70)
  • Section 10 — Quick Fire Round

Section 1 — Java Platform (Q1–Q8)

Q1. What is Java and what are its main features?

Short answer: Java is an object-oriented, class-based, platform-independent programming language that runs on the JVM.

Key features:

Feature Meaning
Platform Independent Write once, run anywhere (WORA) via bytecode
Object Oriented Everything lives inside classes (except primitives)
Secure No pointers, bytecode verifier, security manager
Robust Strong typing, exception handling, automatic memory management
Multithreaded Threads are built into the language
Automatic GC You never call free()
Portable Fixed sizes for primitives on every platform
Interview tip
Do not just list words. Say why: "Java is portable because int is always 32-bit on every OS, unlike C where it changes."

Q2. Difference between JDK, JRE and JVM? (asked 90% of the time)

Short answer: JVM runs the code, JRE = JVM + libraries, JDK = JRE + developer tools.

JVM JRE JDK
Full name Java Virtual Machine Java Runtime Environment Java Development Kit
Purpose Executes bytecode Runs Java apps Develops Java apps
Contains compiler? javac
Platform dependent? Yes Yes Yes
Trap
"Java is platform independent" — but the JVM itself is platform dependent. You download a different JVM for Windows and Linux. That is exactly what makes your .class file portable.

Q3. How does Java achieve platform independence?

Answer: Compilation happens in two steps.

Bytecode is an intermediate language understood by every JVM. The JVM translates it to native instructions for that specific OS/CPU.

Q4. What is JIT compiler?

Short answer: Just-In-Time compiler is part of the JVM that compiles hot bytecode into native machine code at runtime, so it does not need to be interpreted again and again.

How it works:

  1. JVM starts by interpreting bytecode (fast startup, slow execution).
  2. JVM counts how many times a method runs.
  3. When a method becomes "hot" (many calls / loops), JIT compiles it to native code.
  4. Next calls run at near-C speed.
Extra point that impresses
The JIT also does optimizations the compiler cannot: inlining, dead code elimination, escape analysis, loop unrolling — because it knows real runtime behaviour.

Q5. Why is Java not a 100% object-oriented language?

Answer: Because of primitive data types (int, char, boolean, double, ...). They are not objects and do not inherit from Object.

Also arguable: static members belong to a class, not to an object.

Good closing line
"Languages like Smalltalk or Ruby are 100% OO. Java kept primitives for performance — an int on the stack is much cheaper than an object on the heap."

Q6. Explain the main method signature.

Part Why it is needed
public JVM is outside your class, so it must be visible everywhere
static JVM must call it without creating an object
void JVM does not use any return value
main Fixed name that JVM searches for
String[] args Command line arguments

Valid variations:

Invalid:

Trap question
"Can we overload main?" ➜ Yes, compiler allows it, but JVM only calls main(String[]). Other versions must be called manually.

Q7. Can we run a Java program without a main method?

Answer: In modern Java (7+): No for normal execution.

Before Java 7 you could use a static block to print something before JVM complained. Since Java 7 the JVM checks for main first, so you get:

Java 21+ update
Java 21 introduced a preview of unnamed classes and instance main methods — you can write just void main() { }. Mentioning this shows you follow modern Java.

Q8. What is bytecode? How to see it?

Answer: Bytecode is the platform-neutral instruction set inside .class files.

Sample output:

Section 2 — Data Types & Variables (Q9–Q18)

Q9. List all primitive data types with size and range.

Type Size Default Range Wrapper
byte 8 bit 0 −128 … 127 Byte
short 16 bit 0 −32,768 … 32,767 Short
int 32 bit 0 −2³¹ … 2³¹−1 Integer
long 64 bit 0L −2⁶³ … 2⁶³−1 Long
float 32 bit 0.0f ~7 decimal digits Float
double 64 bit 0.0d ~15 decimal digits Double
char 16 bit '\u0000' 0 … 65,535 (unsigned!) Character
boolean JVM-dependent (~1 bit logical) false true / false Boolean
Trap
char is the only unsigned primitive in Java. And boolean size is not defined by the spec — do not say "1 bit" confidently, say "not precisely specified, usually 1 byte in arrays".

Q10. What are default values? Do local variables get them?

Answer: Instance and static fields get default values. Local variables do NOT.

Why? Fields live on the heap and the JVM zeroes memory. Local variables live on the stack frame, which is reused — so Java forces you to assign explicitly. This is a safety feature.

Q11. Difference between instance variable, static variable and local variable?

Instance Static (class) Local
Declared inside class, outside method with static keyword inside method/block
Memory Heap (inside object) Method Area / Metaspace Stack
Copies one per object one per class one per method call
Default value yes yes no
Lifetime as long as object lives as long as class is loaded until method ends

Q12. What is type casting? Widening vs Narrowing.

Widening (implicit / automatic) — no data loss:

Narrowing (explicit) — possible data loss:

Classic trap

Because a + b is promoted to int. Fix: byte c = (byte)(a + b);
But byte c = 10 + 20; compiles fine — compile-time constants are checked at compile time.

Q13. int vs Integer?

int Integer
Type primitive object (wrapper)
Memory stack (as local) heap
Default 0 null
Can be null?
Usable in collections? List<Integer>
Size 4 bytes ~16 bytes header + 4

Q14. Why does 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in Java?

Reason: float/double follow IEEE 754 binary floating point. Numbers like 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary (same as 1/3 cannot be written exactly in decimal).

Solution — use BigDecimal with String constructor:

Never do this
new BigDecimal(0.1) — passing a double copies the error into BigDecimal. Always use the String constructor for money.

Q15. float vs double — which to choose?

  • float: 32 bit, ~7 digits precision, needs f suffix → float f = 1.5f;
  • double: 64 bit, ~15 digits, default for decimal literals
  • For money use neither → use BigDecimal or store cents in long.

Q16. What is integer overflow? Does Java throw an error?

Answer: No exception. It silently wraps around.

Safe way (Java 8+):

Q17. What is var? (Java 10)

Answer: Local variable type inference. The compiler figures out the type — Java stays statically typed, this is not JavaScript.

Where var is NOT allowed:

Q18. Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? (favourite trap)

Answer: Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value of the reference is copied.

Mental picture:

One-line answer to memorize
"Java passes references by value. You can change the object's state, but you cannot make the caller's variable point somewhere else."

Section 3 — Operators & Control Flow (Q19–Q26)

Q19. i++ vs ++i?

  • i++ (post): use the old value, then increment.
  • ++i (pre): increment, then use the new value.

Famous puzzle:

Because i++ returns 0, then that 0 is assigned back over the incremented value.

Q20. >> vs >>>?

Operator Name Behaviour
<< Left shift multiply by 2ⁿ
>> Signed right shift keeps sign bit (fills with sign)
>>> Unsigned right shift always fills with 0
There is no <<< operator in Java.

Q21. & vs && (and | vs ||)?

& / | && / ||
Type bitwise or logical logical only
Short-circuit? evaluates both sides stops early

Q22. == vs .equals()?

  • == compares references (memory address) for objects, values for primitives.
  • .equals() compares content — if the class overrides it.
Object.equals() default implementation is just this == obj. If your class does not override it, equals behaves like ==.

Q23. What is a switch statement? What types are allowed?

Allowed: byte, short, char, int, their wrappers, enum, String (Java 7+), and sealed types/patterns (Java 21).
Not allowed: long, float, double, boolean.

Classic switch — fall-through danger:

Enhanced switch (Java 14+) — no fall-through:

Q24. while vs do-while?

  • while: checks condition first → may run 0 times.
  • do-while: runs body first → runs at least 1 time.

Q25. What is a labeled break/continue?

Used to exit outer loops directly.

Java has no goto — goto is a reserved keyword but unused. Labels are the safe replacement.

Q26. Ternary operator and its traps.

Trap — auto unboxing NPE:

Section 4 — Strings (Q27–Q36)

Q27. Why is String immutable in Java?

Answer: Once created, the character content of a String never changes.

Reasons:

Reason Explanation
String Pool Many references share one object. If one could change it, all would break.
Security Usernames, URLs, file paths, DB connections are Strings. Immutability blocks change-after-check attacks.
Thread safety Immutable = automatically thread-safe, no synchronization needed.
#️⃣ HashCode caching String caches its hashCode → fast HashMap keys.
Class loading Class names are Strings; mutability would allow loading a wrong class.

How is it implemented?

  • String class is final (cannot be subclassed).
  • Internal private final byte[] value (was char[] before Java 9 Compact Strings).
  • No method modifies the array; every "modifying" method returns a new String.

Q28. What is the String Constant Pool (SCP)?

Answer: A special area in the heap (since Java 7; before that in PermGen) where string literals are stored and reused.

Diagram:

Q29. new String("abc") — how many objects are created?

Answer: 1 or 2.

  • 1 object in the pool (only if "abc" is not already there).
  • 1 object in the heap (always, because of new).

If the literal already existed in the pool → only 1 new object.

Q30. What does intern() do?

Answer: Puts the string into the pool (or returns the existing pooled one).

Q31. String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?

String StringBuilder StringBuffer
Mutable
Thread safe (immutable) (synchronized)
Speed slow for concat fastest slower (lock overhead)
Since 1.0 1.5 1.0
Use when fixed text, keys single-thread building multi-thread building (rare)
Real answer for "which one to use?"
"StringBuilder in 99% of cases. StringBuffer is legacy — if I need thread safety I usually keep the builder local to one thread anyway, which is cheaper than locking."

Q32. Why is concatenation in a loop bad?

Nuance that scores points
A single "a" + b + "c" expression is fine — the compiler converts it to StringBuilder (or invokedynamic StringConcatFactory in Java 9+). The problem is only inside loops, where a new builder is created every iteration.

Q33. Important String methods to know

Q34. String.equals() vs == in real interview code

Rule: concatenation with a non-final variable happens at runtime → new object, not pooled. If part were final String part = "ja"; then s1 == s4 would be true.

Q35. What is a String's hashCode() formula?

Why 31? It is an odd prime, gives good distribution, and 31 * i can be optimized by the JVM to (i << 5) - i.

Q36. Text Blocks (Java 15)

No more \n and \" everywhere.

Section 5 — Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing (Q37–Q42)

Q37. What are wrapper classes and why do we need them?

Answer: Object versions of primitives (int → Integer).

Needed for:

  • Collections & generics: List<Integer> (generics do not accept primitives)
  • null to represent "no value"
  • Utility methods: Integer.parseInt(), Integer.MAX_VALUE, Integer.toBinaryString()
  • Reflection / frameworks that work with Object

Q38. Autoboxing and unboxing?

Q39. The Integer cache trap (very common)

Why? Integer.valueOf() caches objects from −128 to 127. Inside that range the same object is reused; outside it, a new object is created.

Cached by default: Boolean, Byte, Character(0–127), Short, Integer, Long (−128..127).
Not cached: Float, Double.

Lesson: always compare wrappers with .equals(), never ==.

Q40. How can unboxing cause NullPointerException?

Fix:

Q41. parseInt() vs valueOf()?

Both throw NumberFormatException for bad input.

Q42. Are wrapper classes immutable?

Yes — all wrapper classes are final and immutable. That is why they are safe as HashMap keys.

Section 6 — Keywords: static, final, this, super (Q43–Q52)

Q43. Explain the static keyword completely.

static = belongs to the class, not the object.

1️⃣ Static variable — one copy shared by all objects

2️⃣ Static method — called without an object

3️⃣ Static block — runs once when the class is loaded

4️⃣ Static nested class — does not need an outer instance

Q44. Why can't a static method access instance variables?

Because static methods run without any object, so there is no this to read the instance data from.

Q45. Can we override a static method?

No. Static methods are hidden, not overridden. Binding happens at compile time based on the reference type, not the object type.

This is a favourite trap. Say the words: "method hiding".

Q46. Explain final in all its usages.

Applied to Meaning
variable value cannot be reassigned (constant)
method cannot be overridden
class cannot be extended (e.g. String, Integer)
parameter cannot be reassigned inside the method
Huge trap
final on an object reference means the reference cannot change, not the object's content.

Q47. final vs finally vs finalize()?

final finally finalize()
Type keyword block method of Object
Purpose restrict change/inherit/override always execute cleanup code called by GC before object destroy
Status used used deprecated since Java 9, removed in Java 18+

Use try-with-resources instead of finalize().

Q48. What is a blank final variable?

A final field with no initial value — it must be assigned in the constructor (or instance block).

Q49. What does this do?

  • refers to the current object
  • this.field = field; resolves name shadowing
  • this(...) calls another constructor of the same class (must be the first statement)
  • can be passed as an argument or returned (used for method chaining)

Q50. What does super do?

  • super.field / super.method() accesses the parent version
  • super(...) calls a parent constructor (must be the first statement)

Q51. Can a class be both abstract and final?

No. abstract means "must be extended", final means "cannot be extended". They contradict.
Similarly invalid: abstract static, abstract final methods, abstract private methods.

Q52. What is the transient and volatile keyword? (preview)

  • transient: field is skipped during serialization. → detail in Part 8
  • volatile: value is always read from main memory, not the CPU cache → detail in Part 5

Section 7 — Constructors & Initialization Order (Q53–Q58)

Q53. What is a constructor? Rules?

Rules:

  • Same name as the class
  • No return type (not even void)
  • Called automatically on new
  • Can be overloaded
  • Cannot be final, static, abstract, or synchronized
  • Can be private (Singleton pattern!)

Q54. Default constructor vs no-arg constructor?

  • Default constructor: created by the compiler when you write no constructor at all.
  • No-arg constructor: written by you with empty parameters.
If you write any constructor, the compiler stops adding the default one. So this breaks:

Q55. What is constructor chaining?

this() and super() cannot both appear in the same constructor, and each must be the first statement.

Q56. What is the exact initialization order? (killer question)

When the class is first loaded (once):

  1. Static variables & static blocks — in the order they appear in the code

Every time you create an object:
2. Parent's instance blocks → parent constructor body
3. Instance variables & instance initializer blocks (in code order)
4. Constructor body

Memory hook: statics first (parent → child), then for the object: parent all the way, then child.

Q57. Can a constructor call a static method? Can a static method create an object?

Both yes. Statics do not need an object, and constructors can use anything visible.

Q58. Can a constructor be private? Why would we do that?

Yes. Used for:

  • Singleton pattern
  • Static factory methods (Integer.valueOf(), List.of())
  • Utility classes (Math, Collections) to prevent instantiation
  • Builder pattern

Section 8 — Arrays & Varargs (Q59–Q65)

Q59. How do you declare and initialize arrays?

Q60. Is array size fixed? What is length vs length() vs size()?

  • Array size is fixed at creation.
  • array.length → field, no parentheses
  • string.length() → method
  • collection.size() → method

Q61. Array vs ArrayList?

Array ArrayList
Size fixed dynamic (grows ~1.5×)
Types primitives + objects objects only
Performance faster, less memory small overhead
Type safety runtime (ArrayStoreException) compile-time via generics
Methods almost none add, remove, contains, ...
Length .length .size()

Q62. What is array covariance and why is it dangerous?

Generics are invariant to prevent exactly this: List<Object> l = new ArrayList<String>(); does not compile.

Q63. Useful array utilities

arr1 == arr2 and arr1.equals(arr2) both compare references for arrays. Use Arrays.equals().

Q64. What are varargs?

Rules: only one varargs parameter, and it must be the last one.

Q65. Shallow copy vs deep copy of an array?

Section 9 — Packages & Access Modifiers (Q66–Q70)

Q66. Explain all access modifiers.

Modifier Same class Same package Subclass (other pkg) Everywhere
private
default (no keyword)
protected
public
A top-level class can only be public or default — never private or protected.

Q67. Can a Java file have multiple classes?

Yes, but only one can be public, and the file name must match that public class.

Q68. What is a package? Why use it?

Namespace for grouping related classes. Benefits: avoid name conflicts, control access (default/protected), better organization.

java.lang is imported automatically.

Q69. Does import make the program slower or bigger?

No. import is only a compile-time convenience so you can write short names. It does not load or copy anything at runtime.

Q70. What is java.lang and what is inside it?

Auto-imported core package: Object, String, StringBuilder, wrappers, Math, System, Thread, Runnable, Exception, Throwable, Enum, Class.

Section 10 — Quick Fire Round

Is Java 100% platform independent?
No. Bytecode is portable, but the JVM is platform specific.
What is the difference between path and classpath?
PATH = where the OS finds executables (java, javac). CLASSPATH = where the JVM finds .class files and JARs.
Why is String[] args and not String args?
Because a program can receive many command-line arguments.
What happens if main throws an exception?
The JVM prints the stack trace and terminates that thread with a non-zero exit code.
Can we have an empty .java file?
Yes, it compiles fine and produces no .class file.
Is null a keyword?
No — null is a literal (like true/false). goto and const are reserved but unused keywords.
What is the output of System.out.println('a' + 1);
98 — char is promoted to int. To print "a1" write "" + 'a' + 1.
What is the output of System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);
3345 — left to right: 1+2=3, then everything becomes concatenation.
Can we declare a class inside a method?
Yes — a local class (or anonymous class, or lambda).
Difference between System.out, System.err, System.in?
out = standard output stream, err = error stream (unbuffered, usually red), in = standard input.
What is Integer.MIN_VALUE absolute value trap?
Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) returns a negative number, because +2147483648 does not fit in an int.
What does n & 1 tell you?
0 = even, 1 = odd. Faster than % and works on negatives too.

Self-Test Checklist for Part 1

  • I can explain JDK/JRE/JVM in 30 seconds with the diagram
  • I can explain why Java is pass-by-value with the Dog example
  • I can explain String immutability with 4 reasons
  • I know the Integer cache −128..127 trap
  • I can write the initialization order 1→6 from memory
  • I know why byte c = a + b; fails to compile
  • I can explain method hiding vs overriding
  • I know the access modifier table by heart
Part 1 complete — 70 questions
Next up ➜ Part 2: OOP Deep Dive — inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, encapsulation, interface vs abstract class, equals/hashCode contract, Object class methods, inner classes, Comparable vs Comparator, immutable class design, cloning, records, sealed classes.

Type: "give me part 2"

Section 1 — The Four Pillars (Q71–Q78)

Q71. What are the four pillars of OOP?

Pillar One line Java tool
Encapsulation Hide data, expose behaviour private fields + getters/setters
Abstraction Show what, hide how abstract class, interface
Inheritance Reuse and specialize extends, implements
Polymorphism One interface, many forms overriding + overloading
How to answer well
Do not recite definitions. Give one real example each:
"Encapsulation = my BankAccount keeps balance private so nobody can set it to −500 directly; withdraw() validates first."

Q72. Encapsulation vs Abstraction — what is the real difference?

They are often confused. The clean separation:

Encapsulation Abstraction
Question it answers How do I protect data? What should the user see?
Level implementation level design level
Achieved by access modifiers abstract classes / interfaces
Focus data hiding complexity hiding

Analogy : Abstraction = you press the brake pedal and the car stops (you don't need to know about hydraulics). Encapsulation = the brake fluid is sealed inside the system so you cannot touch it.

Q73. What is a class and what is an object?

  • Class = blueprint / template. No memory for instance data until instantiated.
  • Object = an instance of a class. Lives on the heap, has state (fields) + behaviour (methods) + identity (address).

Q74. What exactly happens when you write new Car()?

  1. JVM checks whether class Car is loaded → if not, load, link, initialize (statics run once)
  2. Allocate memory on the heap for instance fields
  3. Set all fields to default values (0 / null / false)
  4. Run instance initializer blocks and field initializers, top to bottom
  5. Run the constructor body (after super() finishes first)
  6. Return the reference to the variable

Q75. What is composition? Composition vs Inheritance?

  • Inheritance = "IS-A" → Dog extends Animal
  • Composition = "HAS-A" → Car has an Engine

Why composition is usually better:

Inheritance Composition
Tight coupling to parent Loose coupling
Fixed at compile time Can swap at runtime
Breaks encapsulation (subclass sees parent internals) Parent internals stay hidden
Only one parent class Combine many components
Parent change breaks children (fragile base class) Isolated
Golden sentence
"Favour composition over inheritance." — Effective Java, Item 18. Use inheritance only when there is a true IS-A relationship and the parent was designed for extension (documented + non-final).

Q76. Give an example where inheritance is the WRONG choice.

Classic: class Stack extends ArrayList.
Now someone can call stack.add(0, x) and insert into the middle — the LIFO guarantee is destroyed. Stack is not an ArrayList; it uses one.

Real JDK mistake: java.util.Stack extends Vector and Properties extends Hashtable — both are considered design errors today.

Q77. What is coupling and cohesion?

  • Coupling = how much one class depends on another → we want low - Cohesion = how focused one class is on a single job → we want high
    A class named UserManagerHelperUtils that sends emails, saves to DB and formats PDFs has low cohesion. Split it.

Q78. What are the SOLID principles? (short version)

Letter Name Meaning
S Single Responsibility One class, one reason to change
O Open/Closed Open for extension, closed for modification
L Liskov Substitution A subclass must work anywhere the parent works
I Interface Segregation Many small interfaces > one fat interface
D Dependency Inversion Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes

Liskov violation example: Square extends Rectangle — setting width on a Square also changes height, so code written for Rectangle breaks.

Section 2 — Inheritance (Q79–Q90)

Q79. What is inheritance and what are its types in Java?

Type Supported? Note
Single (B extends A)
Multilevel (C extends B extends A)
Hierarchical (B, C both extend A)
Multiple (C extends A, B) classes via interfaces
Hybrid classes via interfaces

Q80. Why does Java NOT support multiple inheritance of classes?

The Diamond Problem

Also: constructor chaining and state duplication become ambiguous. Java's designers chose simplicity.

Interfaces solve it because (before Java 8) they had no implementation and no state — nothing to conflict.

Q81. But Java 8 added default methods — is the diamond problem back?

Yes, partially — and Java forces you to resolve it manually.

Without the override → compile error. Java refuses to guess.

Resolution rules when conflicts happen:

  1. Class wins over interface (concrete method beats default method)
  2. More specific sub-interface wins over super-interface
  3. Otherwise → you must override explicitly

Q82. What is inherited and what is NOT inherited?

Inherited Not inherited
public / protected members private members
default members (same package only) constructors
static members (accessible, but hidden not overridden) initializer blocks
Trap: a private field is not accessible, but it does exist in memory inside the child object. The child just cannot see it directly — only via parent's public methods.

Q83. Can a subclass access a private member of the parent?

No, not directly. Only through inherited public/protected methods (getters).

Q84. What is the parent of every class?

java.lang.Object. If you write class A {}, the compiler makes it class A extends Object.

Q85. Does the constructor get inherited?

No. But the child constructor must call a parent constructor — implicitly super() is inserted as the first line if you do not write one.

Q86. What is the super() call rule?

  • Must be the first statement in the constructor
  • Cannot use this() and super() together
  • If absent, the compiler inserts super() automatically
  • Cannot be used inside a static context

Q87. What is the fragile base class problem?

If a parent class changes its internal implementation, subclasses that depended on that behaviour break — even though the public API did not change.

Famous example: overriding addAll() in a subclass of HashSet to count elements → breaks because HashSet.addAll() internally calls add(), so counting happens twice. Self-use is an invisible contract.

Q88. How do you prevent inheritance?

  1. Make the class final → public final class String
  2. Make all constructors private (then only static factories create it)
  3. Java 17: use sealed to allow only specific subclasses

Q89. What is protected really for?

It exists only for inheritance: a subclass in a different package can access it. Same-package classes get access too (like default).

protected members are part of your public API for extenders — once released, you can never change them safely.

Q90. Can we inherit a class with a private constructor?

No (from outside). The child cannot call super(). That is exactly how Math and Collections prevent both instantiation and subclassing.

Exception: an inner class of the same class can, because private members are visible inside the same top-level class.

Section 3 — Polymorphism, Overloading & Overriding (Q91–Q104)

Q91. What is polymorphism? Types?

Poly = many, morph = form. One reference, many possible behaviours.

Type Also called When resolved Java feature
Compile-time static / early binding compile time overloading
Runtime dynamic / late binding runtime overriding

Q92. Overloading vs Overriding — the full table

Overloading Overriding
Where same class (or subclass) parent child
Parameters must differ must be identical
Return type can differ freely same or covariant (subtype)
Access modifier any cannot be more restrictive
Exceptions any cannot throw broader checked exceptions
Binding compile time runtime
static methods can overload hidden, not overridden
private/final can overload cannot override

Q93. Can we overload a method by changing ONLY the return type?

No. The compiler picks methods by the signature (name + parameter types). Return type is not part of the signature.

Q94. Can we overload the main method?

Yes, but the JVM always starts with main(String[]).

Q95. How does the compiler choose which overload to call?

Order of preference (first match wins):

  1. Exact match
  2. Widening (int → long → float → double)
  3. Autoboxing (int → Integer)
  4. Varargs (last resort)

Famous trap:

If you add void m(Integer i) too → m(null) becomes ambiguous → compile error.

Q96. What are the rules for method overriding?

Must have:

  • same method name
  • same parameter list
  • same or covariant return type
  • same or wider access modifier
  • same or narrower checked exceptions

Cannot override: static, final, private methods, and constructors.

Q97. Can an overriding method throw a different exception?

  • Unchecked (RuntimeException, Error) → any, no restriction
  • Checked → only the same or a subclass; or fewer; or none

Q98. What is covariant return type?

Since Java 5, an overriding method may return a subtype of the parent's return type.

This removes the need for casting by the caller. Widely used in builder patterns and clone().

Q99. What is dynamic method dispatch? How does the JVM do it?

Answer: The mechanism that picks the overridden method at runtime based on the actual object.

Under the hood [Likely]: every class has a vtable (virtual method table) in method area. The reference points to the object → the object header points to its class → the class holds the pointer to the correct method implementation. The JIT often optimizes this to a direct call when only one implementation exists (monomorphic inline caching).

Q100. Fields are NOT polymorphic — the variable hiding trap

Memorize: methods are overridden (runtime), fields are hidden (compile time). Same for static methods.

Q101. What is upcasting and downcasting?

Safe way:

Q102. What does instanceof return for null?

Always false — never throws NPE.

Q103. What is the @Override annotation? Is it required?

Not required, but always use it. It makes the compiler verify that you really are overriding. Without it, a typo like hashcode() instead of hashCode() silently creates a new method and your HashMap breaks.

Q104. Can you override a method and make it synchronized / final / static?

  • synchronized → yes, it is not part of the signature
  • final → yes (it just stops further overriding)
  • static → an instance method cannot become static and vice versa → compile error

Section 4 — Abstract Class vs Interface (Q105–Q116)

Q105. What is an abstract class?

A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract (unimplemented) methods.

Rules:

  • If a class has any abstract method → the class must be abstract
  • An abstract class may have zero abstract methods (still not instantiable)
  • Abstract methods cannot be private, static, or final

Q106. Can an abstract class have a constructor? Why?

Yes. It is never called by new Shape(), but it is called via super() when a concrete subclass is created — to initialize the inherited state.

Q107. Abstract class vs Interface — full comparison

Abstract Class Interface
Keyword abstract class interface
Inheritance single (extends) multiple (implements)
State / fields any instance fields only public static final constants
Constructor yes no
Method types abstract, concrete, static, final, private abstract, default, static, private (J9)
Access modifiers any members are implicitly public
Relationship IS-A, shares code CAN-DO, defines capability
Use when related classes share code + state unrelated classes share a contract

Rule of thumb : Bird, Plane, Superman are unrelated but all implements Flyable. Dog and Cat both extends Animal because they share fields and code.

Q108. What can an interface contain in modern Java?

Q109. Why were default methods added in Java 8?

Backward compatibility. They wanted to add stream() to Collection. Adding an abstract method would break every existing implementation in the world. A default method lets the interface evolve without breaking anyone.

Q110. Can an interface extend another interface? Can it extend a class?

  • Interface extends interface → and it can extend multiple interfaces
  • Interface extends class → never

Q111. Can an abstract class implement an interface without providing the methods?

Yes — it can leave them abstract for its subclasses. This is the Adapter idea.

Q112. What is a marker interface? Give examples.

An interface with no members, used only to tag a class with metadata for the JVM or a framework.

Examples: Serializable, Cloneable, RandomAccess, Remote.

Today annotations are usually preferred (@FunctionalInterface, @Deprecated), but marker interfaces still win when you need a type for compile-time checks and for instanceof.

Q113. What is a functional interface?

An interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM). Can be implemented by a lambda.

default, static, and Object's public methods (equals, hashCode, toString) do not count toward the one-abstract-method rule. More in Part 7 — Java 8 & Modern Java.

Q114. Can we create an object of an interface or abstract class?

Not directly — but you can use an anonymous class, which creates a hidden subclass:

Q115. What happens if a class implements two interfaces with the same abstract method?

Nothing bad — one implementation satisfies both. Conflict only occurs with two default methods (see Q81).

Q116. When would you choose abstract class over interface in real design?

Choose abstract class when:

  • you need shared state (fields) or a constructor
  • you want to provide a template (AbstractList, AbstractMap)
  • subclasses are truly the same kind of thing

Choose interface when:

  • multiple unrelated classes need the capability
  • you want to allow multiple inheritance of type
  • you are defining a public API contract (better for testing / mocking / DI)

Section 5 — The Object Class & equals/hashCode (Q117–Q126)

Q117. What methods does Object have?

Method Purpose
equals(Object) logical equality (default: ==)
hashCode() integer hash for hash-based collections
toString() text representation (default: ClassName@hexHash)
getClass() runtime class — final
clone() shallow copy — protected
finalize() deprecated / removed
wait(), notify(), notifyAll() thread coordination — final

Which can be overridden? equals, hashCode, toString, clone, (finalize). The rest are final.

Q118. What is the equals() contract?

For non-null references:

  1. Reflexive — x.equals(x) is true
  2. Symmetric — x.equals(y) ⇔ y.equals(x)
  3. Transitive — if x=y and y=z then x=z
  4. Consistent — repeated calls return the same result
  5. Null — x.equals(null) is always false

Q119. What is the hashCode() contract?

  1. If a.equals(b) is true → a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must be true
  2. If hash codes are equal → objects may or may not be equal (collision allowed)
  3. Hash code must stay consistent during one execution while the object does not change
The #1 interview answer
"If you override equals(), you MUST override hashCode()."
Otherwise HashMap/HashSet will "lose" your object: it is stored in bucket A (old hash) and searched in bucket B.

Q120. Show a correct equals() and hashCode() implementation.

Q121. getClass() != o.getClass() vs instanceof in equals — which is correct?

Both are used, and they trade off differently:

getClass() instanceof
Subclass equals parent? never possible
Symmetry safe? always can break with subclasses
Liskov friendly? strict flexible

Effective Java recommendation: use getClass() unless you deliberately design a value class where subclasses should be comparable — or better, prefer composition over inheritance for value classes.

Q122. What happens if hashCode() always returns the same constant?

The code still works correctly, but every object lands in the same bucket → HashMap degenerates from O(1) to O(n) (or O(log n) after treeification in Java 8).

Q123. What happens if you mutate a field used in hashCode() after inserting into a HashSet?

The object becomes unreachable:

Lesson: make hash-key classes immutable.

Q124. Why override toString()?

Default output is com.app.Person@1b6d3586 — useless in logs. A good toString() saves hours of debugging.

Q125. Do two equal objects always have the same reference? Do two objects with the same hash code have to be equal?

  • Equal objects → not necessarily the same reference (new String("a").equals("a") is true, == is false)
  • Same hash code → not necessarily equal (that is a collision, perfectly legal)

Q126. == vs equals() vs Objects.equals() vs compareTo() == 0?

BigDecimal trap: new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is false (scale differs), but compareTo returns 0. For money comparisons use compareTo.

Section 6 — Encapsulation & Immutable Classes (Q127–Q132)

Q127. How do you achieve encapsulation?

  1. Make all fields private
  2. Expose controlled public getters/setters
  3. Validate inside setters
Better answer: "Encapsulation is not about writing getters and setters for every field — that is just public fields with extra steps. It is about exposing behaviour (deposit) instead of data (setBalance)."

Q128. How do you create an immutable class? (very common)

The 5 rules:

  1. Make the class final (no subclass can break it)
  2. Make all fields private final
  3. No setters — only getters
  4. Initialize everything in the constructor
  5. Defensive copy mutable fields in both the constructor and the getters

Q129. Why is immutability good?

  • Thread-safe with zero synchronization
  • Safe as Map keys and Set elements
  • Fewer bugs — no unexpected state change
  • Can be cached and shared freely (String pool, Integer cache)

Cost: creates more objects. Usually cheap because modern GC handles short-lived objects very well.

Q130. Is final class = immutable class?

No. final only stops inheritance. A final class with a setter is fully mutable.

Q131. What is a defensive copy and why do we need it?

Without it, the caller keeps a reference to your internal object:

Q132. Are getters/setters always necessary?

No. For a pure data carrier, use a record (Java 16) — it generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString for you. See Q151.

Section 7 — Inner & Nested Classes (Q133–Q138)

Q133. What are the four types of nested classes?

Type Declared Needs outer instance? Typical use
Static nested static class inside a class Builder, Node in LinkedList
Inner (non-static) class inside a class Iterator that needs outer state
Local inside a method one method's helper
Anonymous on the fly with new depends listeners, one-off Runnable

Q134. Static nested vs Inner class?

Memory leak risk > A non-static inner class holds a hidden reference to the outer instance. If the inner object lives long (a listener, a static map, a thread), the outer object can never be garbage collected. Prefer static nested classes unless you truly need the outer state.

Q135. What is an anonymous class?

A class with no name, declared and instantiated at once. It can extend a class or implement an interface — but only one, and it cannot have a constructor.

Q136. Anonymous class vs Lambda?

Anonymous class Lambda
Target any interface / abstract class functional interface only
this refers to the anonymous object the enclosing object
Can hold state fields allowed
Compiled to separate Outer$1.class file invokedynamic, no extra class
Readability verbose concise

Q137. Why must a local variable used inside an inner class be final or effectively final?

Because the inner class copies the value (the local variable dies when the method returns, but the object may live longer). If the original could change, the two copies would disagree. Java forbids it to keep them consistent.

Java 8+: you no longer need to write final — "effectively final" (never reassigned) is enough.

Q138. Can an inner class have static members?

  • Before Java 16: only static final constants
  • Java 16+: inner classes can declare static members freely

Section 8 — Comparable vs Comparator (Q139–Q142)

Q139. Comparable vs Comparator?

Comparable Comparator
Package java.lang java.util
Method compareTo(T o) compare(T a, T b)
Where inside the class outside, separate object
How many orders one (natural order) unlimited
Modify original class? required not needed
Used by Collections.sort(list), TreeMap Collections.sort(list, cmp)

Q140. Show both in code.

Q141. What must compareTo() return?

  • negative → this comes before
  • zero → equal in order
  • positive → this comes after
Never write return this.age - o.age; — it overflows for large/negative values. Use Integer.compare(a, b).

Q142. Should compareTo() be consistent with equals()?

Strongly recommended. TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo, not equals. If they disagree, a TreeSet will silently drop an element that equals says is different.

Section 9 — Cloning & Object Copy (Q143–Q146)

Q143. What is clone() and the Cloneable interface?

Object.clone() is protected and creates a field-by-field shallow copy. To use it, the class must implement the marker interface Cloneable, otherwise you get CloneNotSupportedException.

Q144. Shallow copy vs Deep copy?

Q145. Why is clone() considered broken?

  • Cloneable does not declare clone() — a broken marker design
  • super.clone() bypasses the constructor → final fields cannot be reassigned
  • Checked exception in a place nobody wants it
  • Shallow by default → surprising bugs

Better alternatives: a copy constructor, a static factory, a builder, or serialization.

Q146. How do you deep copy with serialization?

Serialize to bytes and read back — everything in the graph becomes new. Simple but slow and requires all classes to be Serializable. More in Part 8 — IO & Reflection.

Section 10 — Enum, Record, Sealed Class (Q147–Q154)

Q147. What is an enum? Can it have fields and methods?

A special class with a fixed set of instances. Yes, it can have fields, constructors (implicitly private), and methods.

Q148. Can an enum extend a class? Implement an interface?

  • Extend a class → (it already extends java.lang.Enum)
  • Implement an interface →

Each constant can even have its own body:

Q149. Useful enum methods

Q150. Why is enum the best Singleton?

The JVM guarantees a single instance, it is thread-safe by construction, and it is safe against reflection and serialization attacks — which the classic private static final singleton is not. (Effective Java, Item 3)

Q151. What is a record? (Java 16)

An immutable, transparent data carrier.

The compiler generates: private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors x() / y(), equals, hashCode, toString.

Validation via compact constructor:

Restrictions: implicitly final, cannot extend another class, no extra instance fields, but can implement interfaces and have static members.

Q152. Record vs Class vs Lombok @Data?

Use a record when the type is a transparent carrier of data with no hidden state and no mutability. Use a normal class when you need mutability, inheritance, or hidden internal representation. A record is a language feature, not code generation at build time like Lombok.

Q153. What is a sealed class/interface? (Java 17)

Restricts who may extend it — controlled inheritance.

Every permitted subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.

Why? It makes the hierarchy exhaustive, so switch pattern matching does not need a default:

Q154. What is the "algebraic data type" combo everyone mentions in modern Java?

sealed interface + record + switch pattern matching = model your domain exactly and let the compiler check completeness. This is the modern alternative to the classic Visitor pattern.

Section 11 — Quick Fire Round

Can an abstract class be final?
No — direct contradiction.
Can an interface have a main method?
Yes, as a static method. It runs fine.
Can we declare a constructor as abstract?
No. Constructors are never inherited, so overriding them is meaningless.
What is the output? Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod();
The Parent's static method — resolved by reference type (method hiding).
Can a class implement two interfaces that both declare int getX() with different return types?
No — incompatible return types → compile error.
Does overriding equals require overriding hashCode even if I never use HashMap?
Yes — you cannot control what future code does with your object. Always keep the contract.
What is a POJO vs a Java Bean?
POJO = plain object with no framework rules. JavaBean = POJO + no-arg public constructor + private fields + getters/setters + Serializable.
Can you override a private method?
No. The child simply defines a new, unrelated method — no polymorphism.
What is the diamond problem and how do interfaces avoid it before Java 8?
Ambiguity from two parents with the same method. Old interfaces had no bodies, so nothing to be ambiguous about.
IS-A vs HAS-A?
IS-A = inheritance (Dog extends Animal). HAS-A = composition (Car has Engine).
Can you cast Object o = "hello" to Integer?
It compiles (both are Objects) but throws ClassCastException at runtime.
Is an empty interface useless?
No — see marker interfaces (Serializable).
Can a record be abstract or extend a class?
No. Records are implicitly final and already extend java.lang.Record.

Self-Test Checklist for Part 2

  • I can explain the diamond problem and how Java 8 default methods resolve it
  • I can recite the overloading vs overriding table
  • I know why fields are hidden but methods are overridden
  • I can write correct equals/hashCode from memory
  • I can state the 5 rules of an immutable class and explain defensive copy
  • I can explain why inner classes cause memory leaks
  • I know when Comparable beats Comparator and vice versa
  • I can explain composition over inheritance with the Stack extends Vector example
  • I can describe record, sealed, and pattern-matching switch
Part 2 complete — 84 questions (Q71–Q154)
Next up ➜ Part 3: Collections Framework — the hierarchy, ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap internals (buckets, load factor, treeification, resize), ConcurrentModificationException, fail-fast vs fail-safe, TreeMap, LinkedHashMap LRU, Set family, Queue/Deque, Iterator, and the Collections utility class.

Type: "give me part 3"

Table of Contents

  • Section 1 — Hierarchy & Fundamentals (Q155–Q164)
  • Section 2 — List Family (Q165–Q178)

Section 1 — Hierarchy & Fundamentals (Q155–Q164)

Q155. Draw the Collections Framework hierarchy.

The #1 fact people forget
Map does not extend Collection. A Collection holds single elements; a Map holds key→value pairs. They are separate hierarchies, connected only through map.entrySet(), keySet(), values().

Q156. What is the Collections Framework and why does it exist?

A unified architecture of interfaces + implementations + algorithms for storing groups of objects.

Benefits: less code to write, tested/optimized data structures, interoperability (any List works everywhere a List is expected), and reusable algorithms (sort, binarySearch, reverse).

Q157. Collection vs Collections?

  • Collection = root interface (java.util.Collection)
  • Collections = utility class with static methods (sort, unmodifiableList, synchronizedList, emptyList, reverse, shuffle)

Similarly: Array (no such class for utilities) vs Arrays (utility class).

Q158. Main differences: List vs Set vs Map vs Queue?

List Set Map Queue
Duplicates allowed unique keys , values allowed
Order insertion order, indexed depends on impl depends on impl FIFO / priority
Null multiple nulls one null (HashSet) 1 null key (HashMap) usually not
Access by index no index by key head only

Q159. Which collections allow null?

Collection Null allowed?
ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector many
HashSet, LinkedHashSet one
TreeSet NullPointerException (needs comparison)
HashMap one null key, many null values
LinkedHashMap same as HashMap
TreeMap null key, null values
Hashtable neither key nor value
ConcurrentHashMap neither
ArrayDeque, PriorityQueue
List.of(...), Map.of(...)
Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null? Because map.get(k) == null would be ambiguous: "absent" or "mapped to null"? In a single-threaded HashMap you can call containsKey() to disambiguate; in a concurrent map that check is racy.

Q160. Which classes are synchronized (legacy thread-safe)?

Vector, Stack, Hashtable, Properties. They synchronize every method, which is slow and still not safe for compound operations.

Modern replacements → ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue. Details in Part 5 — Concurrency.

Q161. How do you make a collection thread-safe?

Better: use java.util.concurrent classes designed for it.

Q162. Iterable vs Iterator?

  • Iterable — "I can be looped over". One method: iterator(). Enables the for-each loop.
  • Iterator — the cursor itself: hasNext(), next(), remove().

Q163. What is the initial capacity and load factor?

  • Capacity = number of buckets/slots allocated
  • Load factor = how full before resizing (default 0.75)
  • Threshold = capacity × load factor → resize when exceeded

ArrayList default capacity 10 (lazily created), HashMap default 16.

Q164. Why is 0.75 the default load factor?

It is a time–space trade-off:

  • Lower (e.g. 0.5) → fewer collisions, faster lookups, but wasted memory
  • Higher (e.g. 1.0) → less memory, more collisions, slower lookups

0.75 is empirically balanced; with a good hash the number of entries per bucket follows a Poisson distribution where collisions stay rare. [Likely] This exact reasoning is documented in the HashMap source comments.

Section 2 — List Family (Q165–Q178)

Q165. ArrayList vs LinkedList? (asked constantly)

Operation ArrayList LinkedList
Internal dynamic array doubly linked list
get(i) O(1) O(n)
add() at end O(1) amortized O(1)
add/remove at start O(n) O(1)
add/remove in middle O(n) shift O(n) search + O(1) unlink
Memory compact +2 pointers per node (~24 bytes overhead)
Cache locality excellent poor (scattered nodes)
Implements List, RandomAccess List, Deque
The honest real-world answer that impresses seniors
"In practice I almost always use ArrayList. LinkedList wins on paper for head insertion, but its poor CPU cache locality makes it slower in real benchmarks for most workloads. The only common case for LinkedList is when I need a Deque — and even then ArrayDeque is faster."

Q166. How does ArrayList grow internally?

  1. Default capacity 10 (created lazily on first add)
  2. When size == capacity → grow() is called
  3. New capacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1) = 1.5×
  4. Arrays.copyOf() copies the old array into the new one

Cost: each resize is O(n), but it happens rarely → amortized O(1) for add().

Optimization: if you know the size, pre-allocate: new ArrayList<>(10000) — avoids many copies.

Q167. ArrayList vs Vector?

ArrayList Vector
Sync not synchronized every method synchronized
Speed fast slow (lock overhead)
Growth 1.5× 2× (doubles)
Since 1.2 1.0 (legacy)
Iterator fail-fast fail-fast (Enumeration is not)

Use Vector? Never in new code.

Q168. What is CopyOnWriteArrayList?

A thread-safe list where every write creates a fresh copy of the internal array.

  • Reads are lock-free and very fast
  • Iterators never throw ConcurrentModificationException (they see a snapshot)
  • Writes are O(n) and expensive

Use when: many reads, very few writes — e.g. a listener/observer registry.

Q169. How do you remove elements while iterating?

Q170. remove(int) vs remove(Object) — the overload trap

For a List<Integer> this bites everyone. The int overload wins because exact match beats boxing.

Q171. What does Arrays.asList() return? What are its traps?

It returns a fixed-size list backed by the original array — not an ArrayList.

Primitive trap:

To get a real modifiable list: new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("a","b"))

Q172. List.of() vs Arrays.asList() vs new ArrayList<>()?

List.of() (J9) Arrays.asList() new ArrayList<>()
Mutable fully immutable fixed-size, set allowed fully
Nulls NPE allowed
Backed by array copy the original array own array

Q173. How do you convert between arrays and lists?

Q174. What is RandomAccess?

A marker interface implemented by ArrayList and Vector saying "index access is fast". Algorithms in Collections check it and choose an index loop vs an iterator loop accordingly.

Q175. How does Collections.sort() / List.sort() work internally?

It uses TimSort (a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort) for objects — stable, adaptive, O(n log n) worst case, O(n) on already-sorted data.

For primitives, Arrays.sort() uses dual-pivot QuickSort — faster but not stable (stability does not matter for primitives).

Why the difference? Stability matters for objects (you may sort by name, then by age, and want the first order preserved). Merge sort needs extra memory but is stable.

Q176. What is a stable sort?

Equal elements keep their original relative order. TimSort , QuickSort .

Q177. What is subList() and its danger?

list.subList(1, 3) returns a view, not a copy. Changing the view changes the original — and structurally modifying the original invalidates the view (ConcurrentModificationException).

Q178. What is Stack and what should we use instead?

Stack extends Vector — a design mistake (see Part 2, Q76): it exposes add(index, e) and is synchronized.

Use ArrayDeque instead:

Section 3 — HashMap Internals THE BIG ONE (Q179–Q196)

If you learn only one section in this whole series, make it this one.

Q179. How does HashMap work internally? (the classic)

The 60-second answer:

HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets (Node<K,V>[] table). Each Node holds hash, key, value, next.

On put(key, value):

  1. Compute key.hashCode()
  2. Spread it: h = hash ^ (hash >>> 16) (mixes high bits into low bits)
  3. Find the bucket: index = (n - 1) & hash (works because n is a power of 2 — equal to hash % n but much faster)
  4. If the bucket is empty → place the new Node
  5. If occupied (collision) → walk the chain:
    • if a node has the same hash AND (== or equals) → replace the value
    • else append to the end of the linked list
  6. If the chain length reaches 8 and table size ≥ 64 → convert the list into a red-black tree 7. If size > capacity × 0.75 → resize (double the table and rehash)

On get(key): same hash → same bucket → compare with equals() → return the value or null.

Q180. Why is capacity always a power of 2?

Because then index = (n - 1) & hash is equivalent to hash % n but uses a single AND instruction instead of an expensive modulo. n-1 gives a mask of all 1 bits (e.g. 16-1 = 1111).

If you pass a non-power-of-2 to the constructor, HashMap rounds up to the next power of 2 (tableSizeFor).

Q181. What is the hash spreading function and why is it needed?

Because the index uses only the low bits of the hash, two keys differing only in high bits would collide. XOR-ing the top 16 bits down mixes them in — cheap but effective.

Q182. What happens on a hash collision?

Two keys land in the same bucket. They are stored in a linked list (Java 7: at the head; Java 8: at the tail) and compared one by one using hashCode then equals.

Java 8 upgrade: if one bucket's chain grows to 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the chain becomes a red-black tree → worst case improves from O(n) to O(log n).
If the tree shrinks back to 6 nodes, it un-treeifies into a list.

Q183. Why 8 for treeify and 6 for untreeify? Why not 7 and 7?

The gap prevents thrashing — constant conversion back and forth when the size oscillates around the threshold. 8 was chosen because with a good hash, the probability of a bucket reaching 8 elements is around 0.00000006 (Poisson) — so trees should be extremely rare in healthy maps. [Certain] These numbers are documented in the JDK source.

Q184. What happens during HashMap resize?

  1. New table with double the capacity
  2. Every entry is redistributed

Java 8 clever trick: since capacity doubles, an entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity — determined by a single bit check (hash & oldCap) == 0. No rehashing needed, and the split preserves relative order (which is why Java 8 fixed the infinite loop bug).

Cost: O(n). Pre-size your map to avoid it: new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75 + 1).

Q185. What was the infinite loop bug in Java 7 HashMap?

In Java 7, resizing under concurrent access could create a circular linked list in a bucket, because entries were re-inserted at the head (order reversed). A later get() would loop forever → 100% CPU on a production server.
Java 8 appends at the tail and preserves order during split → the infinite loop is gone. But HashMap is still not thread-safe — you can still lose updates and get corrupted state. Use ConcurrentHashMap.

Q186. Can HashMap have a null key? How is it stored?

Yes, exactly one. Its hash is defined as 0, so it always lands in bucket 0. Null values are unlimited.

Q187. What happens if two keys have the same hashCode but are not equals?

Both are stored in the same bucket as separate entries in the chain. Lookups still work correctly — just slower.

Q188. What if you use a mutable object as a key?

The entry becomes unreachable:

Rule: keys must be immutable (or at least their hashCode must never change). That is why String is the perfect key.

Q189. What if a key's class does not override hashCode()?

It uses Object.hashCode() = identity hash. Two logically equal objects get different hashes → you can never look up with a new instance:

Q190. Time complexity of HashMap operations?

Case get/put/remove
Average O(1)
Worst (all collide, list) O(n)
Worst (Java 8 tree) O(log n)

Q191. HashMap vs Hashtable?

HashMap Hashtable
Sync every method
Null key/value 1 key, many values NPE
Performance fast slow
Iteration Iterator (fail-fast) Enumeration (not fail-fast) + Iterator
Since 1.2 1.0 (legacy)
Extends AbstractMap Dictionary
Initial capacity / growth 16 / ×2 11 / ×2+1

Q192. HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap?

HashMap ConcurrentHashMap
Thread safe
Locking none per-bucket (synchronized on the head node) + CAS
Null allowed NPE
Iterator fail-fast (CME) weakly consistent, no CME
Read performance fastest almost as fast (reads are lock-free via volatile)

Java 7 vs 8: Java 7 used segment locking (16 segments = 16 concurrent writers max). Java 8 dropped segments for CAS + synchronized on the first node of each bucket → concurrency level = number of buckets.

Q193. What are the useful Java 8 Map methods?

Word count in one line:

Q194. How do you iterate over a Map? Which way is fastest?

Q195. How would you design a good hashCode() for a key class?

Use all fields that participate in equals, combine with the 31-multiplier pattern (or just Objects.hash):

Objects.hash(...) creates a varargs array — in ultra-hot code, write the manual 31 * result + field version to avoid allocation.

Q196. How do you sort a HashMap by value?

Section 4 — Other Map Implementations (Q197–Q208)

Q197. HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap?

HashMap LinkedHashMap TreeMap
Order none insertion (or access) sorted by key
Internal array + list/tree HashMap + doubly linked list Red-Black Tree
get/put O(1) O(1) O(log n)
Null key 1 1
Extra memory low +2 pointers per entry tree nodes
Implements Map Map NavigableMap, SortedMap

Q198. How do you build an LRU cache with LinkedHashMap?

This is a classic interview coding question — knowing the 3-argument constructor is the trick.

Q199. What extra methods does TreeMap give you?

Very useful for range queries, "find the nearest value", scheduling, and leaderboard problems.

Q200. How does TreeMap sort? What if the key is not Comparable?

By natural order (compareTo) or by a Comparator passed to the constructor. If neither exists → ClassCastException at runtime on the first put that needs comparison.

Q201. What is WeakHashMap?

Keys are held by weak references — if no other strong reference points to a key, the GC removes that entry automatically.

Use: caches and metadata that must not prevent objects from being collected.

Q202. What is IdentityHashMap?

Uses == instead of equals() for key comparison. Used in serialization frameworks and graph traversal to track "have I seen this exact object?"

Q203. What is EnumMap and why is it fast?

A Map whose keys are enum constants. Internally it is just an array indexed by ordinal() — no hashing, no collisions, extremely compact and fast. Always prefer it over HashMap<SomeEnum, V>.

Q204. What is Properties?

Hashtable<Object,Object> subclass for configuration strings, with load()/store() for .properties files. Legacy but still common.

Q205. What is Map.Entry? Can you modify it?

An interface representing one key→value pair. entry.setValue(v) writes through to the map , but setKey does not exist (that would break the bucket placement).

Java 9 added immutable Map.entry(k, v).

Q206. How do you create immutable maps?

unmodifiableMap is only a view — if someone still holds the original map, they can change it and your "immutable" view changes too.

Q207. ConcurrentHashMap vs Collections.synchronizedMap()?

ConcurrentHashMap synchronizedMap
Lock fine-grained (per bucket) one lock for the whole map
Concurrent reads lock-free blocked
Iteration weakly consistent, safe must be manually synchronized
Performance under load much better

Q208. Is ConcurrentHashMap fully atomic?

Individual operations are atomic, but compound ones are not unless you use the atomic APIs:

Section 5 — Set Family (Q209–Q216)

Q209. HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet?

HashSet LinkedHashSet TreeSet
Backed by HashMap LinkedHashMap TreeMap
Order none insertion sorted
add/contains O(1) O(1) O(log n)
Null 1 1

Q210. How does HashSet work internally?

It is a HashMap in disguise. Each element becomes a key, and all values point to one shared dummy object:

That is why HashSet gives O(1) contains() and why elements need correct equals/hashCode.

Q211. How does HashSet detect duplicates?

Same rule as HashMap keys: same bucket (hash) and equals() returns true → duplicate → add returns false and nothing is stored.

Q212. What happens if you add an object twice with a bad equals?

Both copies are stored — your Set now contains logical duplicates. This is the practical consequence of skipping equals/hashCode.

Q213. What extra methods does TreeSet provide?

first(), last(), floor(), ceiling(), higher(), lower(), headSet(), tailSet(), subSet(), descendingSet(), pollFirst(), pollLast().

Q214. What is EnumSet?

A high-performance Set for enum constants, implemented as a bit vector (a single long for ≤64 constants). Operations are pure bitwise math — dramatically faster and smaller than HashSet.

Q215. How do you perform set operations (union, intersection, difference)?

Q216. Why is there no ConcurrentHashSet?

Because you can build one:

Also CopyOnWriteArraySet exists for read-heavy cases.

Section 6 — Queue, Deque & PriorityQueue (Q217–Q224)

Q217. What is a Queue? What are its two method families?

FIFO — first in, first out.

Action Throws exception Returns special value
Insert add(e) offer(e) → false
Remove remove() poll() → null
Examine element() peek() → null
In bounded queues, always prefer offer/poll/peek — exceptions for a full queue are not an error condition.

Q218. What is a Deque?

Double Ended Queue — insert and remove from both ends. Can act as both a queue (FIFO) and a stack (LIFO).

Q219. ArrayDeque vs LinkedList as a Deque?

ArrayDeque uses a circular array → better cache locality, less memory, faster in almost all cases. LinkedList only wins if you need List index operations too.

ArrayDeque does not allow null — because null is the "empty" signal for poll()/peek().

Q220. What is a PriorityQueue?

A queue where poll() always returns the smallest element (by natural order or a Comparator), backed by a binary min-heap stored in an array.

Operation Time
offer / poll O(log n)
peek O(1)
contains / remove(Object) O(n)
Biggest trap
Iterating a PriorityQueue does NOT give sorted order! Only poll() does. The array is a heap, not a sorted list. Printing it directly shows heap order.

Q221. What is BlockingQueue?

A queue that blocks the thread when it is empty (on take) or full (on put) — the backbone of the producer-consumer pattern.

Behaviour
put(e) blocks until space is free
take() blocks until an element exists
offer(e, timeout, unit) waits up to a timeout

Implementations: ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded), LinkedBlockingQueue, PriorityBlockingQueue, SynchronousQueue, DelayQueue. Details in Part 5 — Concurrency.

Q222. How do you implement a stack and a queue in modern Java?

Skip java.util.Stack (legacy, synchronized, extends Vector).

Q223. Real use cases for PriorityQueue?

Task schedulers, Dijkstra's shortest path, A* search, "top K elements" problems, merging K sorted lists, event simulation.

Q224. How do you find the top K largest elements efficiently?

Keep a min-heap of size K — O(n log k) time, O(k) memory:

Section 7 — Iterator, Fail-Fast & CME (Q225–Q232)

Q225. What is ConcurrentModificationException?

Thrown when a collection is structurally modified while being iterated (outside the iterator's own remove()).

It is NOT only about threads — a single-threaded for-each loop with list.remove() throws it too.

Q226. How does the fail-fast mechanism work internally?

Each collection has an internal counter modCount that increments on every structural change. When the iterator is created, it copies it into expectedModCount. On every next():

It is a best-effort bug detector, not a guarantee. The JDK explicitly says you must not rely on it for program correctness.

Q227. Fail-fast vs Fail-safe?

Fail-fast Fail-safe (weakly consistent)
On modification throws CME continues silently
Works on the actual collection a snapshot / a tolerant view
Memory low may copy (CopyOnWrite)
Sees new changes? n/a may or may not
Examples ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList

Q228. Iterator vs ListIterator?

Iterator ListIterator
Direction forward only both directions
Available on any Collection List only
Can add? add()
Can replace? set()
Index access nextIndex(), previousIndex()

Q229. Iterator vs Enumeration?

Enumeration is the legacy version (hasMoreElements, nextElement), has no remove(), and is not fail-fast. Only in Vector, Hashtable, StringTokenizer.

Q230. Can you modify a collection during a for-each loop at all?

You can change an element's internal state (non-structural). You cannot add or remove elements. Also list.set(i, v) is allowed since it does not change modCount.

Q231. Why does removing the second-to-last element sometimes NOT throw CME?

A famous quirk: hasNext() is implemented as cursor != size. After removing the second-to-last element, cursor accidentally equals the new size, so the loop exits early without checking modCount — silently skipping an element instead of throwing.

This is exactly why you must never rely on fail-fast for correctness.

Q232. What is a "weakly consistent" iterator?

It reflects the state of the collection at some point at or since creation, never throws CME, and may or may not show later modifications. Used by all java.util.concurrent collections.

Section 8 — Collections Utility & Immutable Collections (Q233–Q240)

Q233. Most useful Collections methods

Q234. Collections.emptyList() vs new ArrayList<>()?

emptyList() returns a shared immutable singleton — zero allocation. Use it for return values when there is nothing to return (never return null from a method that returns a collection ).

Q235. unmodifiableList() vs List.copyOf() vs List.of()?

Immutable? Copies data?
Collections.unmodifiableList(x) view — original can still change
List.copyOf(x) truly
List.of(a, b) truly n/a

Q236. Are immutable collections deeply immutable?

No. The list cannot be structurally changed, but the objects inside can still be mutated if they are mutable. Immutability is only one level deep.

Q237. How does Collections.binarySearch() behave when the element is missing?

Returns -(insertionPoint) - 1 — a negative number telling you where it would go:

Q238. What is Collections.synchronizedList really doing?

It wraps every method with synchronized (mutex) { ... } on a single lock object. Compound operations and iteration still need your own synchronized block.

Q239. How do you remove duplicates from a List, preserving order?

Q240. How do you choose the right collection in an interview design question?

Ask yourself in this order:

  1. Key→value? → Map. Sorted keys? TreeMap. Insertion order? LinkedHashMap. Concurrent? ConcurrentHashMap. Enum key? EnumMap.
  2. Unique elements? → Set (same sub-questions).
  3. Ordered with duplicates + index access? → ArrayList.
  4. Both ends / stack / queue? → ArrayDeque.
  5. Always need the min/max first? → PriorityQueue.
  6. Producer-consumer across threads? → BlockingQueue.
Saying this decision tree out loud is more impressive than reciting definitions.

Section 9 — Big-O Performance Cheat Sheet

Collection get/contains add remove Ordered? Null? Thread-safe
ArrayList O(1) idx / O(n) search O(1)* O(n) insertion
LinkedList O(n) O(1) ends O(1) via iterator insertion
CopyOnWriteArrayList O(1) O(n) O(n) insertion
HashSet O(1) O(1) O(1) 1
LinkedHashSet O(1) O(1) O(1) insertion 1
TreeSet O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) sorted
HashMap O(1) O(1) O(1)
LinkedHashMap O(1) O(1) O(1) insert/access
TreeMap O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) sorted key
ConcurrentHashMap O(1) O(1) O(1)
ArrayDeque O(n) O(1) ends O(1) ends insertion
PriorityQueue O(n) O(log n) O(log n) poll heap

* amortized

Section 10 — Quick Fire Round

Is Map part of the Collection interface?
No. Map is a separate hierarchy.
Which is faster for contains(): ArrayList or HashSet?
HashSet — O(1) vs O(n). Converting a list to a set before many lookups is a classic optimization.
What happens if you put the same key twice in a HashMap?
The value is replaced, size stays the same, and put() returns the old value.
Why is String the most common HashMap key?
Immutable, hashCode is cached, and equals/hashCode are correctly implemented.
Can we store primitives in collections?
No — only objects. Autoboxing hides this, but List<int> does not compile.
Difference between poll() and remove() on an empty queue?
poll() returns null, remove() throws NoSuchElementException.
Difference between peek() and element()?
Same rule: peek() returns null, element() throws.
What is the difference between Set.add() returning true/false?
true = added, false = duplicate already present.
Does HashSet preserve insertion order?
No. If output looks ordered for small integers, that is a coincidence of hashing, not a guarantee.
What is the default size of a HashMap and when does it resize?
16 buckets; resizes at 12 entries (16 × 0.75).
Can two threads safely read a HashMap with no writes?
Yes — a read-only HashMap is safe, provided it is safely published (e.g. final field or made immutable before sharing).
What is Collections.unmodifiableList NOT protecting against?
Changes to the underlying original list, and mutation of the contained objects.
Which collection would you use for a browser back button?
A Deque used as a stack (ArrayDeque).
Which collection for an autocomplete prefix search?
TreeMap with subMap(prefix, prefix + '\uffff'), or a Trie for large scale.

Self-Test Checklist for Part 3

  • I can draw the collections hierarchy and say why Map is separate
  • I can explain HashMap.put() step by step including hash spreading and (n-1) & hash
  • I know the treeify (8) / untreeify (6) / min-table (64) numbers and why
  • I can explain the Java 7 infinite loop bug and the Java 8 fix
  • I can explain the CME modCount mechanism and 3 safe ways to remove
  • I can write an LRU cache with LinkedHashMap from memory
  • I know the null rules for every major collection
  • I can recite the Big-O table for the top 6 collections
  • I can walk through the "which collection should I use" decision tree
Part 3 complete — 86 questions (Q155–Q240)
