Q241. Draw the exception hierarchy.

Q242. Error vs Exception?

Error Exception
Cause JVM / system level application level
Recoverable? usually not usually yes
Should you catch it? no yes
Examples OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError IOException, NullPointerException
You can technically catch an Error, but you should not — the JVM is already in a broken state. The one legitimate case is logging before shutdown.

Q243. Checked vs Unchecked exceptions?

Checked Unchecked
Compiler forces handling yes no
Extends Exception (not Runtime) RuntimeException or Error
Meaning expected external problem programming bug
Examples IOException, SQLException NPE, IllegalArgumentException
Handle by try-catch or throws fix the code

Memory rule : Checked = the world can fail (file missing, network down). Unchecked = your code is wrong.

Q244. Is ClassNotFoundException checked or unchecked?

Checked. But NoClassDefFoundError is an Error — the class was present at compile time and missing at runtime. Different problems:

  • ClassNotFoundException → you called Class.forName("...") and it was not found
  • NoClassDefFoundError → the JVM tried to link a class it saw at compile time, or the class's static initializer previously failed

Q245. Why do many people dislike checked exceptions?

  • They force try-catch boilerplate everywhere
  • They break lambdas and streams (you cannot throw checked exceptions from most functional interfaces)
  • They leak implementation details up the call stack
  • People "swallow" them with an empty catch block, which is worse than nothing

Modern frameworks (Spring, Hibernate) wrap checked exceptions into unchecked ones on purpose.

Q246. What are the most common runtime exceptions?

Exception Typical cause
NullPointerException calling a method on null
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException bad array index
StringIndexOutOfBoundsException bad substring/charAt
ClassCastException invalid downcast
NumberFormatException Integer.parseInt("abc")
ArithmeticException integer / 0
IllegalArgumentException invalid method argument
IllegalStateException object in the wrong state
UnsupportedOperationException modifying an immutable collection
ConcurrentModificationException modifying while iterating

Q247. Does 1.0 / 0 throw ArithmeticException?

No! Floating-point division by zero gives Infinity, -Infinity, or NaN. Only integer division by zero throws.

Q248. What are Helpful NullPointerExceptions? (Java 14+)

The JVM now tells you exactly which part was null:

Enabled by default since Java 15. Mention this — it shows you use modern Java.

Q249. What is StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError?

  • StackOverflowError → too deep recursion; the thread stack is exhausted
  • OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space → the heap is full and GC cannot free anything
  • OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace → too many loaded classes (classloader leak)
  • OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread → OS thread limit hit

Q250. What is Throwable and its key methods?

Section 2 — try / catch / finally (Q251–Q264)

Q251. What is the order of catch blocks?

Most specific first. Catching a parent before a child is a compile error.

Q252. What is multi-catch? (Java 7)

The types must not be in a parent-child relationship with each other.

Q253. Is finally ALWAYS executed?

Almost always. It runs even if try or catch returns or throws.

It does NOT run when:

  1. System.exit() is called
  2. The JVM crashes or is killed (kill -9)
  3. The thread is killed / an infinite loop or deadlock in try
  4. A power failure (yes, interviewers accept this)

Q254. What happens if both try and finally return?

finally wins — it overwrites the return value.

Never return inside finally — it silently swallows exceptions too. Most linters flag it as an error.

Q255. The classic puzzle: does finally change a returned primitive?

For a mutable object, mutation in finally is visible, because the reference was copied, not the object.

Q256. What is try-with-resources? (Java 7)

Automatically calls close() on anything implementing AutoCloseable.

Java 9 improvement — use an existing effectively-final variable:

Q257. What is a suppressed exception?

If try throws and close() also throws, the primary exception is kept and the close exception is attached as suppressed — nothing is lost.

Before try-with-resources, the finally exception would replace and hide the real one — a classic debugging nightmare.

Q258. AutoCloseable vs Closeable?

  • Closeable (Java 5, java.io) → close() throws IOException, idempotent
  • AutoCloseable (Java 7, java.lang) → close() throws Exception, the parent interface

Closeable extends AutoCloseable.

Q259. Can we have try without catch?

Yes:

  • try + finally
  • try with resources (no catch needed)

But try alone → compile error.

Q260. Can we have nested try blocks?

Yes. The inner block is checked first; if it has no matching catch, the exception propagates outward.

Q261. What is exception propagation?

An uncaught exception moves up the call stack until a matching handler is found. If none exists, the thread dies and the default handler prints the stack trace.

  • Unchecked exceptions propagate freely
  • Checked exceptions must be declared with throws at each level

Q262. What happens if an exception is thrown inside catch?

The new exception propagates up; finally still runs first. The original exception is lost unless you chain it as a cause.

Q263. What is exception chaining?

Preserving the original cause when re-throwing:

Losing the cause (throw new MyException("failed") with no e) destroys the stack trace and makes production bugs unfixable. This is one of the most common real code review comments.

Q264. What is rethrow with more precise type analysis? (Java 7)

Section 3 — throw, throws & Custom Exceptions (Q265–Q276)

Q265. throw vs throws?

throw throws
statement inside a method clause in the method signature
throws one object declares many types
throw new IOException(); void m() throws IOException, SQLException

Q266. Can we throw an exception without throws in the signature?

Yes for unchecked exceptions. Checked exceptions must be caught or declared.

Q267. How do you create a custom exception?

Checked or unchecked?

  • Caller can realistically recover → checked
  • It is a bug or unrecoverable → unchecked (most modern code prefers this)

Q268. Overriding rules for exceptions?

An overriding method:

  • can throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions
  • can throw any unchecked exception
  • cannot throw broader or new checked exceptions

Q269. Can a constructor throw an exception?

Yes. The object is then never fully created and becomes eligible for GC. This is the standard way to enforce invariants:

Q270. IllegalArgumentException vs IllegalStateException?

  • IllegalArgumentException → the argument is wrong (setAge(-5))
  • IllegalStateException → the object is in the wrong state for this call (iterator.remove() before next())

Q271. What is Objects.requireNonNull()?

Fail fast with a clear message, at the boundary instead of deep inside:

Q272. What is the finally + try-with-resources execution order?

Q273. How do you handle exceptions in a Thread?

A thread's exception does not propagate to the main thread.

With ExecutorService.submit(), the exception is captured in the Future and only appears when you call future.get() (wrapped in ExecutionException). This is why exceptions silently disappear in thread pools.

Q274. Can main declare throws?

Yes. The JVM then prints the stack trace and exits with a non-zero status.

Q275. What happens to an exception thrown in a static block?

It is wrapped in an ExceptionInInitializerError and the class becomes permanently unusable — every later use throws NoClassDefFoundError.

Q276. How do you throw a checked exception from a lambda?

You cannot directly — most functional interfaces do not declare throws. Options: wrap in an unchecked exception, write your own throwing functional interface, or handle it inside the lambda.

Section 4 — Best Practices & Real Traps (Q277–Q286)

Q277. What are exception handling best practices?

  1. Catch specific exceptions, not Exception
  2. Never swallow: catch (Exception e) { } is a crime 3. Always preserve the cause when wrapping
  3. Use try-with-resources instead of manual finally close
  4. Fail fast — validate inputs early
  5. Do not use exceptions for control flow (they are expensive: stack trace capture)
  6. Log or rethrow — never both (double logging noise)
  7. Throw the most specific meaningful exception
  8. Never catch (Throwable) unless you are a framework
  9. Document with @throws in Javadoc

Q278. Why are exceptions expensive?

fillInStackTrace() walks the entire call stack when the exception object is created. In a hot loop this dominates the runtime. If you truly need a cheap signal exception (rare), override fillInStackTrace() to return this.

Q279. What is the anti-pattern of using exceptions for flow control?

Q280. Should you catch NullPointerException?

Almost never. An NPE means a bug — fix the bug, do not hide it. Use Optional, null checks, or Objects.requireNonNull.

Q281. What is the difference between printStackTrace() and a logger?

printStackTrace() writes to System.err — unstructured, no timestamp, no log level, not captured by log aggregation. Always use log.error("context", e).

Q282. How do you test that a method throws an exception?

Q283. What is a global exception handler in a web app?

Spring: @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler translate exceptions into HTTP responses centrally, so controllers stay clean.

Q284. What happens when an exception is thrown inside finally while an exception is already propagating?

The finally exception replaces the original — the first one is lost forever. This is exactly the problem try-with-resources solved with suppressed exceptions.

Q285. Can you catch multiple exception types and rethrow as one?

Yes — that is exception wrapping/translation. Common in layered architecture: DAO exceptions → service exceptions → API errors.

Q286. What is the difference between "handle" and "declare"?

Handle = try-catch here. Declare = throws, pushing responsibility to the caller. Declare when the caller has more context to decide what to do.

Section 5 — Generics Basics (Q287–Q298)

Q287. What are generics and why do we need them?

Type parameters that give compile-time type safety and remove casting.

Benefits: type safety, no casts, reusable algorithms, clearer APIs.

Q288. What are the naming conventions for type parameters?

Letter Meaning
T Type
E Element (collections)
K, V Key, Value
N Number
R Return type
S, U 2nd, 3rd types

Q289. How do you write a generic class and a generic method?

Q290. What is a bounded type parameter?

Multiple bounds — class first, then interfaces:

Q291. Why can't you use primitives as type arguments?

Because of type erasure — generics compile down to Object, and primitives are not objects. Use wrappers (List<Integer>). Project Valhalla may change this someday.

Q292. What is the diamond operator?

Q293. What is a raw type and why avoid it?

List without a type parameter. It exists only for backward compatibility. It disables all generic checks and produces "unchecked" warnings.

Q294. Is List<Object> the same as List<?> or raw List?

No, all three differ:

Can add anything? Type safe?
List (raw) yes no checks
List<Object> yes checked
List<?> only null checked

Q295. Is List<String> a subtype of List<Object>?

No — generics are invariant. This is intentional:

Arrays are covariant, which is why they fail at runtime with ArrayStoreException instead.

Q296. Can a generic class extend another generic class?

Q297. Can you have static generic members?

  • Static methods with their own type parameter →
  • Static fields of the class's type parameter → (there is only one class, but many T's)

Q298. What is a recursive generic bound?

Used for self-referential builders and enums. It looks strange but it means "the type parameter must be the same as the implementing type".

Section 6 — Type Erasure (Q299–Q306)

Q299. What is type erasure?

The compiler removes all generic type information after checking it. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List.

Why? Backward compatibility — Java 5 generics had to run on existing bytecode and existing libraries (migration compatibility).

What the compiler does:

  1. Replaces T with Object (or the first bound)
  2. Inserts casts where needed
  3. Generates bridge methods to preserve polymorphism

Q300. What are the consequences of erasure?

Q301. Why can't you create a generic array?

Arrays are covariant and reified (they know their type at runtime), generics are invariant and erased. Mixing them would break the array store check.

The standard workaround:

Or pass the type: T[] arr = (T[]) Array.newInstance(clazz, size);

Q302. What is a bridge method?

A synthetic method the compiler generates so that overriding still works after erasure.

You can see them with javap -c.

Q303. How can you get generic type info at runtime then?

Erasure removes type arguments of variables, but class and field declarations keep their signature in the class file metadata.

This is the trick behind Jackson's TypeReference and Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference — the anonymous subclass preserves the type.

Q304. What is heap pollution?

When a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object of a different type — usually via raw types or varargs. It causes a ClassCastException far away from the real bug.

Q305. What is @SafeVarargs?

Generic varargs create an array of a generic type internally (T... args → T[]), which triggers an unchecked warning. @SafeVarargs says "I only read from it, I never store the wrong type".

Allowed only on static, final, or private methods.

Q306. Does erasure hurt performance?

No — generics are purely a compile-time feature; the bytecode is the same as hand-written casts. The cost is expressiveness, not speed. (Boxing primitives does cost, but that is separate.)

Section 7 — Wildcards & PECS (Q307–Q316)

Q307. What is a wildcard ??

An unknown type. Three forms:

Form Name Meaning
List<?> unbounded some unknown type
List<? extends Number> upper bounded Number or a subtype
List<? super Integer> lower bounded Integer or a supertype

Q308. What is PECS? (very common)

Producer Extends, Consumer Super

  • If the collection produces values you read → use ? extends T
  • If the collection consumes values you write → use ? super T
  • If you do both → use plain T

Q309. Why can't you add to a List<? extends Number>?

Because ? could be Integer, Double, or Float — the compiler cannot know which, so no add is safe.

Q310. Why CAN you add to a List<? super Integer>?

Because whatever ? is (Integer, Number, or Object), an Integer always fits.

Q311. <T> vs <?> — when to use which?

  • Use a type parameter T when you need to refer to the type (as a return value, in multiple places, or to relate two arguments)
  • Use a wildcard ? when the type appears only once and you do not care what it is

Q312. Real JDK examples of PECS

Q313. What is capture conversion / the "capture of ?" error?

The compiler assigns a temporary name (CAP#1) to the unknown type. When you need to work with it, use a private helper method that captures it into a real type parameter:

Q314. Can you use wildcards in a class declaration?

No — class Box<?> is illegal. Wildcards are only for variable types, parameters, and return types.

Q315. What does Class<?> mean?

"A Class object of some unknown type." Using raw Class loses type checking, so Class<?> is the safe way to say "any class".

Q316. How do generics interact with inheritance in method overriding?

Return types may be covariant, and generic signatures must match after erasure. Overriding List<String> get() with ArrayList<String> get() is fine; with List<Object> get() is not.

Section 8 — Quick Fire Round

Can finally be used without catch?
Yes — try-finally is valid.
What is the parent of all exceptions?
java.lang.Throwable.
Is NullPointerException checked?
No — unchecked (RuntimeException).
Can you catch Exception to also catch Error?
No. Error is a sibling of Exception, not a subclass. Only catch (Throwable) gets both.
What happens if a catch block itself throws?
The new exception propagates; finally still runs; the original is lost unless chained.
Difference between throw new Exception() and throw e?
Rethrowing e preserves the original stack trace; creating a new one starts a fresh trace at that line.
Can an interface method declare throws?
Yes, and implementations may declare fewer/narrower checked exceptions.
What is UncheckedIOException?
Java 8 wrapper that turns IOException into a runtime exception — designed for lambdas and streams.
What generic type does List.of() infer from List.of() with no arguments?
Object, unless the target type says otherwise (List<String> l = List.of();).
What is Collections.emptyList() returning generically?
A List<T> inferred from context — a nice example of a generic method.
Can you overload void m(List<String>) and void m(List<Integer>)?
No — same erasure, compile error.
Which is correct: Consumer<? super T> or Consumer<? extends T>?
super — a Consumer consumes (PECS).

Self-Test Checklist for Part 4

  • I can draw the Throwable hierarchy and mark the checked/unchecked boundary
  • I know the 4 cases where finally does not run
  • I can explain try-with-resources + suppressed exceptions
  • I always pass the cause when wrapping an exception
  • I can explain type erasure and its 6 consequences
  • I can state PECS and apply it to copy(dest, src)
  • I can explain why generics are invariant but arrays are covariant
  • I know why you cannot create new T[]
Part 4 complete — Q241–Q316
Next: Part 5 — Concurrency

java/interview/concurrency.html:
Part 5 of 9 — Threads, synchronization, the Java Memory Model, executors
Previous: Part 4 — Exceptions & Generics | Hub: Interview Hub
This is the hardest part of the series — and the one that decides senior interviews. Read it slowly.

Table of Contents

  • Section 1 — Thread Basics (Q317–Q330)
  • Section 2 — Synchronization & Locks (Q331–Q346)
  • Section 3 — Java Memory Model & volatile (Q347–Q358)
  • Section 4 — Deadlock, Livelock & Starvation (Q359–Q366)
  • Section 5 — Executors & Thread Pools (Q367–Q380)
  • Section 6 — Concurrency Utilities (Q381–Q392)
  • Section 7 — CompletableFuture & Virtual Threads (Q393–Q400)
  • Section 8 — Quick Fire Round

Section 1 — Thread Basics (Q317–Q330)

Q317. Process vs Thread?

Process Thread
Memory own address space shares heap with other threads
Creation cost heavy light
Communication IPC (slow) shared memory (fast, but risky)
Crash impact isolated can corrupt the whole process
Owns resources a stack + program counter

Each thread has its own stack and own PC, but shares the heap, metaspace, and static fields. That sharing is the source of every concurrency bug.

Q318. How do you create a thread? Which way is better?

Why Runnable over Thread? Separates the task from the execution mechanism, keeps inheritance free, and lets you reuse the task in a thread pool.

Q319. start() vs run()? (classic trap)

  • start() → asks the JVM to create a new OS thread and call run() there
  • run() → just a normal method call on the current thread. No concurrency at all.

Q320. What happens if you call start() twice?

IllegalThreadStateException. A thread's lifecycle is one-way — a dead thread can never be restarted.

Q321. Runnable vs Callable?

Runnable Callable<V>
Method void run() V call() throws Exception
Returns value
Throws checked exceptions
Since 1.0 1.5
Used with Thread, execute() submit(), returns a Future

Q322. What are the thread states?

State Meaning
NEW created, not started
RUNNABLE running or ready to run (Java does not distinguish "ready" and "running")
BLOCKED waiting for a monitor lock (synchronized)
WAITING wait(), join(), park() with no timeout
TIMED_WAITING sleep(n), wait(n), join(n)
TERMINATED finished

Q323. sleep() vs wait()? (asked everywhere)

sleep() wait()
Class Thread (static) Object
Releases the lock? NO YES
Needs synchronized block (else IllegalMonitorStateException)
Wakes up by time expiry / interrupt notify(), notifyAll(), timeout, interrupt
Purpose pause inter-thread communication
The single sentence that gets you the point: sleep() keeps the lock, wait() releases it.

Q324. wait(), notify(), notifyAll() — how are they used?

Why while not if? Because of spurious wakeups (the JVM may wake a thread without notify) and because another thread may have consumed the condition before you re-acquired the lock. Re-checking is mandatory.

Q325. notify() vs notifyAll()?

  • notify() wakes one arbitrary waiting thread — risk of waking the "wrong" one and causing a hang
  • notifyAll() wakes all — safer, slightly more overhead

Default to notifyAll() unless you can prove all waiters are interchangeable.

Q326. Why are wait/notify defined on Object, not Thread?

Because the lock (monitor) belongs to an object, not to a thread. Every object in Java has a monitor, so wait/notify must live on Object.

Q327. What does join() do?

Makes the current thread wait for another thread to finish.

Q328. What is yield()?

A hint to the scheduler that this thread is willing to give up the CPU. Platform dependent and mostly useless in production. It does not release locks.

Q329. What is a daemon thread?

A background thread that does not prevent the JVM from exiting.

When only daemon threads remain, the JVM exits immediately — finally blocks may not run. Examples: the GC thread, timers, monitoring.

Q330. What is thread priority?

Thread.MIN_PRIORITY(1) … NORM_PRIORITY(5) … MAX_PRIORITY(10). It is only a hint to the OS scheduler — behaviour differs per platform. Never build logic on priorities.

Section 2 — Synchronization & Locks (Q331–Q346)

Q331. What is a race condition?

Two threads access shared mutable data and at least one writes; the result depends on timing.

Two threads can both read 5, both write 6 → one increment is lost.

Q332. What is synchronized and how does it work?

It acquires the monitor of an object. Only one thread can hold a given monitor at a time.

Instance and static synchronized methods use different locks — they do not block each other.

Under the hood: monitorenter / monitorexit bytecode instructions, backed by an object header mark word that can be biased, thin (CAS), or inflated to an OS mutex.

Q333. What does synchronized guarantee besides mutual exclusion?

Visibility — entering a synchronized block gives you everything written before the previous thread exited it (happens-before). Mutual exclusion alone would not be enough without this memory guarantee.

Q334. Why is synchronized(this) risky in library code?

Any external code holding a reference to your object can also lock on it and cause a deadlock you cannot see. Use a private final lock object:

Q335. Can you synchronize a constructor?

No — a constructor is not accessible to multiple threads before the object exists. You may use a synchronized block inside it, but that usually signals a design problem.

Q336. What is the double-checked locking singleton and why does it need volatile?

Why volatile? new Singleton() is three steps: allocate memory, run the constructor, assign the reference. The JVM may reorder steps 2 and 3. Without volatile, another thread could see a non-null but not-yet-constructed object.

Better singletons: an enum (Part 2, Q150) or the holder idiom:

Lazy, thread-safe, and lock-free — the JVM guarantees class initialization is atomic.

Q337. synchronized vs ReentrantLock?

synchronized ReentrantLock
Syntax keyword, automatic release explicit lock() / unlock()
Try without blocking tryLock()
Timeout tryLock(1, SECONDS)
Interruptible lockInterruptibly()
Fairness optional new ReentrantLock(true)
Multiple conditions one wait set many Condition objects
Release on exception automatic you must use finally

Q338. What does "reentrant" mean?

A thread that already holds a lock can acquire it again without deadlocking. Both synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant — essential for recursion and for calling one synchronized method from another.

Q339. What is ReadWriteLock?

Many readers or one writer.

Great for read-heavy caches. StampedLock (Java 8) adds an even faster optimistic read mode.

Q340. What is lock striping?

Splitting one lock into many so different keys can be updated in parallel — exactly what ConcurrentHashMap does per bucket.

Q341. What is an atomic operation? What is CAS?

CAS = Compare-And-Swap, a single CPU instruction: "if the value is still X, set it to Y; otherwise fail and let me retry."

Advantage: no blocking, no context switch. Disadvantage: under very high contention, threads spin and burn CPU.

Q342. What is the ABA problem?

A value changes A → B → A. CAS sees "still A" and succeeds, but the world changed in between (common with pointers/stacks). Fix: AtomicStampedReference adds a version counter.

Q343. What atomic classes exist?

AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference, AtomicIntegerArray, AtomicStampedReference, and the Java 8 high-contention counters LongAdder / DoubleAdder.

LongAdder beats AtomicLong under heavy contention because it spreads updates across multiple cells and only sums them on sum().

Q344. Is i++ atomic on a volatile int?

No. volatile gives visibility, not atomicity. i++ is still read-modify-write. Use AtomicInteger or synchronized.

Q345. What is thread confinement?

Avoiding sharing entirely — the safest concurrency strategy. ThreadLocal is the explicit tool:

ThreadLocal + thread pools = memory leak. Pooled threads live forever, so the value is never released. Always remove() in a finally.

Q346. Which common classes are NOT thread-safe?

SimpleDateFormat (famous!), ArrayList, HashMap, StringBuilder, Calendar. Use DateTimeFormatter (immutable, Java 8) instead of SimpleDateFormat.

Section 3 — Java Memory Model & volatile (Q347–Q358)

Q347. What is the Java Memory Model (JMM)?

The specification that defines when a write by one thread becomes visible to another, and which reorderings the compiler/CPU may perform.

Without it, each CPU core could keep values in its own cache forever and other threads would never see updates.

Q348. What is the visibility problem?

The JIT may hoist running into a register and never re-read it. Adding volatile fixes it.

Q349. What does volatile do?

  1. Visibility — every read goes to main memory, every write is flushed to it
  2. Ordering — prevents reordering across the volatile access (memory barriers)
  3. Atomicity for 64-bit — makes long/double reads and writes atomic

What it does NOT do: make compound operations (i++, check-then-act) atomic.

Q350. volatile vs synchronized?

volatile synchronized
Mutual exclusion
Visibility
Blocking never can block
Applies to variables only methods & blocks
Performance cheap more expensive
Use case status flags, DCL compound state updates

Q351. What is the happens-before relationship?

If A happens-before B, then everything A wrote is visible to B. The main rules:

  1. Program order — within one thread, statements happen in order
  2. Monitor lock — unlocking happens-before a later locking of the same monitor
  3. volatile — a write happens-before every later read of that field
  4. Thread start — t.start() happens-before everything in t
  5. Thread join — everything in t happens-before t.join() returns
  6. Transitivity — if A→B and B→C then A→C
  7. Final fields — properly constructed final fields are visible without synchronization

Q352. What is instruction reordering?

The compiler, JIT, and CPU may reorder instructions for speed as long as the single-threaded result is unchanged. Other threads can observe the reordered order — the cause of many concurrency bugs. volatile, synchronized, and final insert barriers that limit it.

Q353. What is safe publication?

Making an object visible to other threads such that they see it fully constructed. Safe ways:

  • Initialize it in a static initializer
  • Store it in a volatile or final field
  • Store it in an AtomicReference
  • Guard it with a lock
  • Put it into a thread-safe collection

Q354. Why does final help concurrency?

The JMM guarantees that correctly constructed final fields are visible to all threads without synchronization — as long as this did not escape during the constructor.

Q355. What is "this escaping" in a constructor?

Publishing this before the constructor finishes (registering a listener, starting a thread inside the constructor) lets other threads see a half-built object. Use a static factory that constructs first and registers after.

Q356. Are long and double writes atomic?

Not guaranteed without volatile on 32-bit JVMs — a thread could see the high 32 bits of one value and the low 32 bits of another (word tearing). All other primitives and references are atomic.

Q357. What is false sharing?

Two independent variables sit in the same CPU cache line; updating one invalidates the cache for the other core. It kills performance silently. @Contended (JDK internal) or padding fixes it.

Q358. Is an immutable object automatically thread-safe?

Yes, provided it is properly constructed (all fields final, no this escape, defensive copies). This is why immutability is the strongest concurrency tool.

Section 4 — Deadlock, Livelock & Starvation (Q359–Q366)

Q359. What is deadlock?

Two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs, so nobody can proceed.

Q360. What are the four Coffman conditions?

Deadlock requires all four at once:

  1. Mutual exclusion — resources are exclusive
  2. Hold and wait — hold one while waiting for another
  3. No preemption — locks cannot be forcibly taken
  4. Circular wait — a cycle of dependencies

Break any one and deadlock becomes impossible.

Q361. How do you prevent deadlock?

  1. Lock ordering — always acquire locks in a global, consistent order (breaks circular wait)
  2. tryLock with timeout — back off and retry (breaks hold-and-wait)
  3. Hold locks for the shortest time possible
  4. Avoid nested locks entirely
  5. Use higher-level constructs (ConcurrentHashMap, executors, immutable objects) instead of raw locks

Q362. How do you detect a deadlock in production?

  • jstack <pid> → it explicitly prints "Found one Java-level deadlock"
  • JConsole / VisualVM → "Detect Deadlock" button
  • ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() programmatically
  • A thread dump shows threads BLOCKED on monitors owned by each other

Q363. Deadlock vs Livelock vs Starvation?

Deadlock Livelock Starvation
Threads are blocked, doing nothing busy, but making no progress waiting forever for CPU/lock
Analogy two cars stuck at a junction two people repeatedly stepping aside for each other a low-priority thread never scheduled
Fix lock ordering randomized backoff fair locks

Q364. What is a fair lock and what does it cost?

new ReentrantLock(true) serves threads in FIFO arrival order — no starvation, but significantly slower because it prevents barging and causes more context switches.

Q365. What is thread interruption?

A cooperative request to stop — not a forced kill.

Catching InterruptedException clears the flag. If you swallow it, the shutdown signal is lost and your service will not stop cleanly.

Q366. Why are stop(), suspend(), and resume() deprecated?

stop() kills a thread mid-operation, releasing all its locks and leaving shared data corrupted. suspend() keeps the locks while frozen → guaranteed deadlock. Use interruption + a volatile flag instead.

Section 5 — Executors & Thread Pools (Q367–Q380)

Q367. Why use a thread pool instead of new Thread()?

  • Thread creation is expensive (~1 MB stack each + OS call)
  • Unbounded thread creation → OutOfMemoryError under load
  • Pools give reuse, bounded concurrency, queueing, and lifecycle management

Q368. What are the built-in Executors factories?

Factory Behaviour
newFixedThreadPool(n) n threads, unbounded queue
newCachedThreadPool() grows without limit, 60s idle timeout
newSingleThreadExecutor() 1 thread, sequential, unbounded queue
newScheduledThreadPool(n) delayed and periodic tasks
newWorkStealingPool() ForkJoinPool with parallelism = cores
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() Java 21 — a virtual thread per task
Why senior engineers avoid these factories
newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue → under overload, tasks pile up until OutOfMemoryError. newCachedThreadPool creates unlimited threads. In production, build a ThreadPoolExecutor manually with a bounded queue and an explicit rejection policy.

Q369. Explain the ThreadPoolExecutor parameters.

Task arrival logic (the order matters!):

  1. Threads < core → create a new thread
  2. Else → put in the queue
  3. Queue full → create threads up to max
  4. Max reached and queue full → reject
Counter-intuitive: with an unbounded queue, maximumPoolSize is never reached — step 3 never happens.

Q370. What are the rejection policies?

Policy Behaviour
AbortPolicy (default) throws RejectedExecutionException
CallerRunsPolicy the submitting thread runs it → natural backpressure
DiscardPolicy silently drops it
DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task

Q371. How do you size a thread pool?

  • CPU-bound: threads ≈ number of cores (or cores + 1)
  • I/O-bound: cores × (1 + waitTime / computeTime) — can be much larger
  • Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() gives the core count

Always measure; the formula is a starting point, not a law.

Q372. execute() vs submit()?

execute() submit()
Accepts Runnable Runnable or Callable
Returns void Future
Exceptions go to the uncaught handler / printed captured in the Future — silent until get()

Q373. How do you shut down an executor properly?

shutdown() vs shutdownNow(): the first is graceful, the second interrupts and returns the queued tasks that never ran.

Non-daemon pool threads keep the JVM alive forever if you never shut down.

Q374. What is a Future? What are its limits?

Limits: get() blocks, no callbacks, no chaining, no combining. CompletableFuture solves all of these.

Q375. What is invokeAll() / invokeAny()?

  • invokeAll(tasks) → runs all, blocks until all complete, returns a list of Futures
  • invokeAny(tasks) → returns the result of the first to succeed, cancels the rest

Q376. What is ScheduledExecutorService?

AtFixedRate can bunch up tasks if one run is slow; WithFixedDelay never overlaps.

Q377. What is the ForkJoinPool and work stealing?

Designed for divide and conquer. Each worker has its own deque; an idle worker steals tasks from the tail of a busy worker's deque, which minimizes contention.

parallelStream() uses the common ForkJoinPool by default. Never run blocking I/O in a parallel stream — you starve the shared pool for the whole JVM.

Q378. RecursiveTask vs RecursiveAction?

RecursiveTask<V> returns a value; RecursiveAction returns nothing.

Q379. How do you name threads in a pool and why does it matter?

Because a production thread dump full of pool-1-thread-7 tells you nothing. Naming threads is a small habit that marks an experienced engineer.

Q380. What happens if a task throws inside a pool thread?

  • With execute() → the thread dies, the pool creates a replacement, and the uncaught handler fires
  • With submit() → the exception is stored in the Future and is invisible until get(). This is why bugs silently vanish in pools. Always log inside the task or check the Future.

Section 6 — Concurrency Utilities (Q381–Q392)

Q381. What is CountDownLatch?

A one-shot gate: wait until N events happen.

Cannot be reset. Use case: wait for all services to boot before accepting traffic.

Q382. What is CyclicBarrier? How is it different from CountDownLatch?

CountDownLatch CyclicBarrier
Reusable one-shot resets automatically
Who waits usually one waiter, many counters all parties wait for each other
Barrier action runs a task when the barrier trips

Q383. What is Semaphore?

A permit counter that limits concurrent access.

Use: connection pools, rate limiting, bounding parallelism.

Q384. What is Exchanger?

Two threads swap objects at a rendezvous point. Rare, used in pipeline/buffer-swapping designs.

Q385. What is Phaser?

A more flexible CyclicBarrier — the number of parties can change dynamically, and it supports multiple phases.

Q386. How do you implement producer-consumer?

The blocking queue handles all the waiting and signalling — no wait/notify needed. This is the answer interviewers want.

Manual version (if they ask for wait/notify):

Q387. What BlockingQueue implementations exist?

Class Note
ArrayBlockingQueue bounded, one lock
LinkedBlockingQueue optionally bounded, separate put/take locks (better throughput)
PriorityBlockingQueue unbounded, ordered
SynchronousQueue zero capacity — a direct handoff
DelayQueue elements become available after a delay
LinkedTransferQueue most flexible/fastest

Q388. What concurrent collections exist?

ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentSkipListMap (sorted), CopyOnWriteArrayList, CopyOnWriteArraySet, ConcurrentLinkedQueue/Deque (non-blocking, CAS-based), ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().

Q389. What is ThreadLocalRandom?

A per-thread random generator. Math.random() and a shared Random have a single internal seed updated by CAS → contention. ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(10) avoids it entirely.

Q390. What is AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS)?

The framework behind ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch, and ReadWriteLock. It maintains an int state plus a FIFO queue of waiting threads, using CAS on the state. Knowing this name signals depth.

Q391. What is LockSupport.park()/unpark()?

Low-level thread blocking primitives used by AQS. Unlike wait/notify, unpark can be called before park and the permit is remembered — no lost-wakeup problem.

Q392. What is StampedLock?

Java 8 lock with three modes: write, read, and optimistic read (no lock at all — you read, then validate(stamp) and retry if a write happened). Very fast for read-dominated data. Not reentrant.

Section 7 — CompletableFuture & Virtual Threads (Q393–Q400)

Q393. What is CompletableFuture?

A Future you can compose, chain, and combine — non-blocking async programming.

Q394. thenApply vs thenCompose vs thenCombine?

Method Analogy Signature
thenApply map T → U
thenCompose flatMap T → CompletableFuture<U> (avoids nesting)
thenCombine zip combines two independent futures

Q395. What is the difference between the Async variants?

thenApply may run on the thread that completed the previous stage; thenApplyAsync always submits to the pool (ForkJoinPool.commonPool by default, or one you pass). Use the Async variant with your own executor for blocking work.

Q396. How do you wait for many futures?

Q397. How do you handle exceptions in CompletableFuture?

Q398. What are virtual threads? (Java 21)

Lightweight threads managed by the JVM, not the OS. You can run millions of them.

Key idea: when a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it from its carrier (platform) thread instead of blocking the OS thread. So blocking code becomes cheap again — you write simple synchronous code and get async scalability.

Q399. What changes with virtual threads?

  • Thread pools become unnecessary for I/O tasks — create a thread per task
  • synchronized can "pin" a virtual thread to its carrier (improved in later JDKs); prefer ReentrantLock in hot paths
  • ThreadLocal is still supported but costly at millions of threads
  • Ideal for I/O-bound servers; no benefit for CPU-bound work

Q400. Platform thread vs virtual thread?

Platform Virtual
Backed by one OS thread a JVM continuation on a carrier thread
Cost ~1 MB stack a few hundred bytes, growable heap stack
Practical count thousands millions
Best for CPU-bound I/O-bound
Pooling needed anti-pattern

Section 8 — Quick Fire Round

Can two threads execute two different synchronized methods of the SAME object at the same time?
No — both need the same object monitor.
Can a thread execute a synchronized method while another executes a non-synchronized one?
Yes. Non-synchronized methods do not check the lock at all.
Does sleep() release the lock?
No. Only wait() does.
What happens if you call wait() outside a synchronized block?
IllegalMonitorStateException.
Is Vector enough to be thread-safe in real use?
No — individual methods are safe, but if (!v.contains(x)) v.add(x) is still a race.
Is ConcurrentHashMap's size() exact?
It is an estimate under concurrent modification — weakly consistent by design.
What is a memory barrier / fence?
A CPU instruction that prevents reordering across it; inserted by volatile and lock operations.
What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
Concurrency = dealing with many things at once (structure). Parallelism = doing many things at once (execution).
What is an immutable object's biggest concurrency advantage?
Zero synchronization needed — it can be shared freely.
Can finally fail to run in a killed thread?
Yes — daemon threads at JVM exit, or Thread.stop().
Should you use Timer for scheduled tasks?
No — one thread, and one exception kills all future tasks. Use ScheduledExecutorService.
What is the "common pool" and why is it dangerous?
The shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool() used by parallel streams — blocking in it starves the entire JVM.

Self-Test Checklist for Part 5

  • I can explain start() vs run() and sleep() vs wait() instantly
  • I know all 6 thread states and what moves between them
  • I can write double-checked locking and explain why volatile is required
  • I can list the happens-before rules
  • I can explain the 4 Coffman conditions and 3 ways to prevent deadlock
  • I can explain every ThreadPoolExecutor parameter and the task-arrival order
  • I know why Executors.newFixedThreadPool is dangerous in production
  • I can implement producer-consumer with BlockingQueue from memory
  • I can explain virtual threads and when they help
Part 5 complete — Q317–Q400
Next: Part 6 — JVM

java/interview/jvm.html:
Part 6 of 9 — JVM architecture, memory areas, GC, class loading, performance
Previous: Part 5 — Concurrency | Hub: Interview Hub

Table of Contents

  • Section 1 — JVM Architecture (Q401–Q410)
  • Section 2 — Memory Areas (Q411–Q426)
  • Section 3 — Garbage Collection (Q427–Q444)
  • Section 4 — Class Loading (Q445–Q456)
  • Section 5 — Tuning & Troubleshooting (Q457–Q468)
  • Section 6 — Quick Fire Round

Section 1 — JVM Architecture (Q401–Q410)

Q401. Draw the JVM architecture.

Q402. Which memory areas are shared and which are per-thread?

Area Shared? Contents
Heap shared all objects, arrays, instance fields
Metaspace (Method Area) shared class metadata, static fields, constant pool
JVM Stack per thread frames: local variables, operand stack
PC Register per thread address of the current instruction
Native Method Stack per thread native (C/C++) call frames
One-line memory rule: objects on the heap, references on the stack.

Q403. What is inside a stack frame?

One frame per method call, containing:

  1. Local variable array (including this for instance methods)
  2. Operand stack (where bytecode does its arithmetic)
  3. Frame data (constant pool reference, return address, exception table)

The frame is destroyed when the method returns — which is why locals need no GC.

Q404. Stack vs Heap?

Stack Heap
Stores primitives (locals), references, frames objects, arrays, instance fields
Scope per thread thread-safe shared across threads
Allocation LIFO, automatic dynamic, managed by GC
Speed very fast (pointer bump) slower
Size small (~512 KB–1 MB, -Xss) large (-Xmx)
Error StackOverflowError OutOfMemoryError
Lifetime until method returns until unreachable + GC

Q405. Where are static variables stored?

The metadata lives in Metaspace, but since Java 8 the actual static field values are stored in the java.lang.Class object — which lives on the heap. [Certain] So static objects are collectible when their classloader is.

Q406. Where do String literals live?

The String Constant Pool, which since Java 7 is part of the heap (before that, PermGen). This move was made specifically so that pooled strings can be garbage collected.

Q407. What is the Execution Engine?

Three parts:

  1. Interpreter — executes bytecode line by line; fast startup, slow repeated execution
  2. JIT compiler — compiles hot methods to native code (C1 = fast compile, C2 = deep optimization; tiered compilation uses both)
  3. Garbage Collector — reclaims unreachable objects

Q408. What optimizations does the JIT perform?

  • Method inlining (the most valuable one)
  • Escape analysis → scalar replacement (an object that never escapes may never be allocated at all!)
  • Dead code elimination, constant folding, loop unrolling
  • Lock elision / biased locking
  • Devirtualization of monomorphic calls

Q409. What is -XX:+PrintCompilation / JITWatch used for?

Observing which methods get compiled, inlined, or deoptimized. Mentioning deoptimization (when the JIT's assumption is invalidated and it falls back to the interpreter) shows real depth.

Q410. What is AOT and GraalVM native image?

Ahead-Of-Time compilation produces a native binary with near-instant startup and low memory — at the cost of losing runtime reflection flexibility (needs configuration) and peak JIT throughput. Popular for serverless and CLI tools.

Section 2 — Memory Areas (Q411–Q426)

Q411. What is the structure of the heap?

Default ratios: Young:Old ≈ 1:2, Eden:S0:S1 = 8:1:1.

Q412. What is the generational hypothesis?

"Most objects die young." Empirically, the vast majority of objects become garbage almost immediately. So the JVM collects the young generation frequently and cheaply, and touches the old generation rarely. This single observation drives the entire GC design.

Q413. Walk me through an object's life in the heap.

  1. Allocated in Eden (via a fast pointer bump in a thread-local allocation buffer, TLAB)
  2. Eden fills → Minor GC: live objects are copied to Survivor S0, everything else is freed
  3. Next Minor GC: live objects from Eden and S0 move to S1; the age counter increments
  4. Survivors ping-pong between S0 and S1, aging each time
  5. Age reaches the tenuring threshold (default 15) → promoted to Old Gen
  6. Old Gen fills → Major/Full GC (slower, longer pause)

Also promoted early if: the object is too big for Eden (humongous), or the survivor space overflows.

Q414. Minor GC vs Major GC vs Full GC?

Minor (Young) GC Major (Old) GC Full GC
Collects Young gen Old gen Young + Old + Metaspace
Frequency often rare rarest
Pause short (ms) long longest
Trigger Eden full Old gen threshold promotion failure, System.gc(), metaspace full

Q415. What is a "stop-the-world" pause?

All application threads are paused so the GC can work on a consistent object graph. Every GC has some STW; modern collectors just make it shorter and more predictable. Threads stop at safepoints — well-defined bytecode positions where the thread state is known.

Q416. What is a TLAB?

Thread-Local Allocation Buffer — each thread gets a private chunk of Eden so allocation needs no synchronization: just bump a pointer. That is why Java object allocation is often faster than C's malloc.

Q417. What is Metaspace and how does it differ from PermGen?

PermGen (≤ Java 7) Metaspace (Java 8+)
Location inside the heap native memory (off-heap)
Size fixed (-XX:MaxPermSize) grows automatically by default
Common error OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
String pool inside it (≤ Java 6) moved to the heap in Java 7

The change removed the most common tuning headache but did not remove classloader leaks — Metaspace can still grow until the machine dies. Bound it with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.

Q418. What is the runtime constant pool?

Per-class table of literals and symbolic references (class names, method names, field names) built from the .class file's constant pool. It lives in Metaspace.

Q419. What causes StackOverflowError?

Deep or infinite recursion; each call adds a frame. Increase with -Xss2m, but the real fix is usually converting recursion to iteration or making it tail-friendly (note: Java has no tail-call optimization).

Q420. What are the different OutOfMemoryError messages?

Message Cause
Java heap space genuine leak or heap too small
GC overhead limit exceeded >98% time in GC, <2% memory recovered
Metaspace too many classes (classloader leak)
Direct buffer memory leaked ByteBuffer.allocateDirect
unable to create new native thread OS thread/memory limit
Requested array size exceeds VM limit array larger than ~Integer.MAX_VALUE

Q421. Can you have a memory leak in Java?

Yes — GC only frees unreachable objects. A leak is an object you no longer need but still reference.

Classic sources:

  1. Static collections that only ever grow (a cache with no eviction) 2. Unclosed resources (streams, connections)
  2. Listeners/callbacks never unregistered
  3. ThreadLocal in a thread pool without remove()
  4. Inner class holding an outer reference (Part 2, Q134)
  5. Mutated keys in a HashSet/HashMap (Part 2, Q123)
  6. ClassLoader leaks in app servers on redeploy
  7. substring() in Java 6 (shared the parent char array — fixed in Java 7)

Q422. What is -Xms and -Xmx?

Initial and maximum heap size. Setting them equal in production avoids resize pauses and makes behaviour predictable: -Xms4g -Xmx4g.

Q423. What is off-heap memory?

Memory outside GC control: ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(), memory-mapped files, Unsafe. Used for zero-copy I/O and huge caches (Netty, Chronicle). It avoids GC pressure but you manage the lifetime yourself.

Q424. What is the object memory layout / how big is an object?

Roughly: 12-byte header (mark word + class pointer with compressed oops) + fields + padding to a multiple of 8 bytes. An empty object is 16 bytes; an Integer is 16 bytes to hold a 4-byte value — which is why primitive collections libraries exist.

Q425. What are compressed oops?

On 64-bit JVMs with a heap under ~32 GB, references are stored as 32-bit offsets instead of 64-bit pointers — saving significant memory. This is why going from a 31 GB heap to a 33 GB heap can reduce effective capacity.

Q426. Where do arrays live?

Always on the heap, even int[]. The reference to the array lives on the stack (if it's a local).

Section 3 — Garbage Collection (Q427–Q444)

Q427. What is garbage collection and when does an object become eligible?

An object is eligible when it is unreachable from any GC root.

Common ways objects become eligible:

Q428. What are GC roots?

The starting points for reachability analysis:

  • Local variables and parameters in active stack frames
  • Static fields of loaded classes
  • Active threads
  • JNI references (native code)
  • Monitor objects held by synchronized blocks

Q429. Reference counting vs reachability analysis? Why does Java use the latter?

Reference counting cannot free circular references (A→B→A) — a well-known leak source in Python and old COM. Java uses reachability from roots, so cycles are collected correctly as long as nothing outside points into them.

Q430. What are the reference types in Java?

Type Collected when Use case
Strong new Object() never while reachable normal code
Soft SoftReference only when memory is low memory-sensitive caches
Weak WeakReference at the next GC WeakHashMap, metadata
Phantom PhantomReference after finalization replacement for finalize() cleanup

Q431. Can you force garbage collection?

No. System.gc() is only a suggestion — the JVM may ignore it. Calling it in production is an anti-pattern: it often triggers an expensive Full GC. (-XX:+DisableExplicitGC disables it entirely.)

Q432. What is finalize() and why is it dead?

A method the GC called before reclaiming an object. Deprecated in Java 9, removed in Java 18. Problems: no guarantee it ever runs, unpredictable timing, it can resurrect the object, it delays collection by a full extra GC cycle, and exceptions in it are swallowed.
Use instead: try-with-resources / AutoCloseable, or java.lang.ref.Cleaner.

Q433. What GC algorithms exist?

Collector Flag Best for Pause
Serial -XX:+UseSerialGC tiny heaps, single core, containers long
Parallel (Throughput) -XX:+UseParallelGC batch jobs, max throughput medium
CMS removed in 14 -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC legacy low-pause short
G1 (default since Java 9) -XX:+UseG1GC general purpose, big heaps predictable target
ZGC -XX:+UseZGC huge heaps (TB), ultra low pause <1 ms
Shenandoah -XX:+UseShenandoahGC low pause, any heap size <10 ms
Epsilon -XX:+UseEpsilonGC no-op, for benchmarking n/a

Q434. What are the basic GC algorithms?

  1. Mark-Sweep — mark reachable, free the rest → causes fragmentation
  2. Mark-Sweep-Compact — plus moving survivors together → no fragmentation, slower
  3. Copying — copy live objects to a new space → fast, wastes half the space (used in the young gen, where few survive)
  4. Generational — different algorithms per age region

Q435. How does G1 work?

G1 splits the heap into ~2048 equal regions, each dynamically labelled Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous.

  • It marks concurrently, then collects the regions with the most garbage first ("Garbage First") - It aims to meet a pause target: -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
  • It compacts incrementally, so no full-heap fragmentation
  • Objects larger than half a region are "humongous" and allocated directly in Old

Q436. How do ZGC and Shenandoah achieve sub-millisecond pauses?

They do marking and relocation concurrently with the application, using load barriers (ZGC) or Brooks pointers (Shenandoah) so threads always find the moved object. Pause time becomes independent of heap size — a 16 TB heap pauses as briefly as a 1 GB one.

Q437. What is a write barrier / card table?

To avoid scanning the whole Old Gen during a Minor GC, the JVM tracks old→young references using a card table updated by a small write barrier on every reference store. Then only "dirty" cards are scanned.

Q438. Does GC cause memory to return to the OS?

Historically no. Modern collectors (G1 with -XX:+ShrinkHeapInSteps, ZGC, Shenandoah) can uncommit unused memory — important in containers where you pay for RAM.

Q439. What is the tenuring threshold?

The number of survived GC cycles before promotion (-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold, default 15). The JVM also adapts it dynamically based on survivor space occupancy.

Q440. What is premature promotion and why is it bad?

When survivor space is too small, objects are promoted to Old Gen before they die → Old Gen fills quickly → frequent expensive Major GCs. Fix: enlarge the young gen or survivor ratio.

Q441. What is a GC pause and how do you measure it?

Enable logging: -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log (Java 9+) or -XX:+PrintGCDetails (Java 8). Analyze with GCViewer, GCEasy, or JFR. Look at pause duration, frequency, and live set after Full GC (that is your real memory need).

Q442. Which GC should you choose?

  • Small container / CLI → Serial
  • Batch processing, throughput matters more than latency → Parallel
  • Typical web service → G1 (the default; usually correct)
  • Latency-critical, large heap → ZGC or Shenandoah
The honest senior answer: "Start with the default G1 and a pause target. Do not change collectors until GC logs prove there is a problem."

Q443. Is GC a stop-the-world for all collectors?

All have some STW phases (at minimum, root scanning). "Concurrent" collectors mean most work overlaps with the application, not that pauses are zero.

Q444. What is escape analysis and stack allocation?

If the JIT proves an object never escapes its method, it can perform scalar replacement — breaking the object into plain local variables so it is never allocated on the heap at all, and never needs GC. This is why "avoid creating objects" advice is often outdated.

Section 4 — Class Loading (Q445–Q456)

Q445. What are the class loading phases?

  1. Loading — find the .class bytes, create the Class object
  2. Verification — check the bytecode is valid and safe (this is a core Java security feature)
  3. Preparation — allocate static fields and set them to default values (0/null) — not your assigned value yet
  4. Resolution — replace symbolic references with direct ones (may be lazy)
  5. Initialization — run static initializers and static field assignments, in code order

Q446. What are the built-in class loaders?

Loader Loads from
Bootstrap core JDK classes (java.lang.*); written in native code, getClassLoader() returns null
Platform (was Extension) JDK platform modules
Application/System your classpath
Custom anything you want (app servers, plugins, hot reload)

Q447. What is the parent delegation model?

A classloader first asks its parent to load the class, and only loads it itself if the parent cannot.

Why?

  1. Security — you cannot replace java.lang.String with your own version
  2. Uniqueness — a class is loaded once, avoiding duplicates

Q448. What defines the identity of a class at runtime?

Fully qualified name + the ClassLoader that loaded it. The same .class file loaded by two different loaders produces two incompatible types — casting between them throws ClassCastException even though the code looks identical. This is the root of most app-server class loading mysteries.

Q449. When is a class initialized (static block run)?

Triggered by:

  • new instance creation
  • Accessing a static method or a non-constant static field
  • Reflection (Class.forName)
  • Initializing a subclass (initializes the parent first)
  • Being the main class

NOT triggered by:

Q450. Class.forName() vs ClassLoader.loadClass()?

  • Class.forName(name) → loads and initializes (runs static blocks) — that is why old JDBC drivers were registered this way
  • loadClass(name) → loads but does not initialize
  • Class.forName(name, false, loader) → load without init

Q451. Why write a custom ClassLoader?

Hot reloading, plugin isolation, loading classes from a database/network, encrypted class files, application servers isolating each deployed app.

Q452. What is a ClassLoader leak?

When an app is redeployed, the old classloader must be collected. If any object from it is still referenced (a thread, a ThreadLocal, a static registry, a JDBC driver in the shared classloader), the entire classloader plus all its classes stays in Metaspace forever → OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after a few redeploys.

Q453. What breaks parent delegation and why?

SPI (Service Provider Interface) — java.sql.DriverManager is loaded by Bootstrap but must load driver implementations from the classpath, which Bootstrap cannot see. The fix is the Thread Context ClassLoader, which deliberately reverses the delegation. OSGi and app servers also break it for isolation.

Q454. What is the JPMS module system? (Java 9)

module-info.java declares requires and exports, giving strong encapsulation (internal packages become truly inaccessible, not just discouraged) and reliable configuration at startup instead of classpath chaos.

Q455. What is static final constant inlining?

Consequence: if you change MAX and recompile only Config, the other class still uses the old value until it is recompiled too. A real production trap.

Q456. What is bytecode verification protecting against?

Malicious or corrupt bytecode: stack overflows/underflows, illegal casts, accessing private members, jumping to invalid instructions. It is one of the pillars of the Java sandbox.

Section 5 — Tuning & Troubleshooting (Q457–Q468)

Q457. What JVM tools do you know?

Tool Purpose
jps list running JVMs
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1s live GC statistics
jstack <pid> thread dump (deadlocks, stuck threads)
jmap -histo <pid> object histogram
jmap -dump:live,file=heap.hprof <pid> heap dump
jcmd <pid> ... the modern all-in-one tool
JFR (Java Flight Recorder) low-overhead production profiling
VisualVM / JMC / Eclipse MAT GUI analysis of dumps
async-profiler flame graphs, very low overhead

Q458. How do you diagnose a memory leak?

  1. Confirm it: GC logs show the live set after Full GC growing over time 2. Take two heap dumps hours apart: jmap -dump:live,file=h1.hprof <pid>
  2. Open in Eclipse MAT → "Leak Suspects" report
  3. Compare histograms — which class keeps growing?
  4. Use "Path to GC Roots" (exclude weak/soft) on a sample instance to see who is still holding it
  5. Fix the retaining reference
Say the phrase "path to GC roots" — it instantly shows you have done this for real.

Q459. How do you diagnose high CPU usage?

  1. top -H -p <pid> → find the hottest thread ID
  2. Convert to hex: printf '%x\n' <tid>
  3. jstack <pid> → find the matching nid=0x... and read its stack
  4. Or just use async-profiler for a flame graph

Common causes: an infinite loop, GC thrashing, or a hash collision hot spot.

Q460. What are the most useful JVM flags?

Q461. Why does the JVM ignore container memory limits (and how was it fixed)?

Old JVMs read the host CPU/memory, not the cgroup limit → they sized the heap for 64 GB inside a 512 MB container and got OOM-killed. Java 10+ is container aware by default (-XX:+UseContainerSupport).

Use ratios instead of absolutes in containers:

Q462. What is JMX?

Java Management Extensions — exposes MBeans for runtime monitoring and management (memory, threads, GC, custom metrics). Used by JConsole, Prometheus exporters, and APM tools.

Q463. How do you reduce GC pressure in code?

  • Avoid allocating in hot loops (reuse buffers)
  • Pre-size collections
  • Prefer primitives and primitive arrays over boxed collections
  • Use StringBuilder in loops
  • Stream carefully — boxing in Stream<Integer> vs IntStream matters
  • Do not fear short-lived objects; the young gen handles them cheaply

Q464. What is a heap dump vs a thread dump?

  • Heap dump = snapshot of all objects and their references → for memory problems
  • Thread dump = snapshot of all thread stacks and lock states → for hangs, deadlocks, CPU problems

Q465. What does "live set" mean and why does it matter?

The bytes still reachable after a Full GC. It is your application's true memory requirement — the number you size -Xmx around (typically live set × 2–3).

Q466. What are safepoints and safepoint pauses?

Points where all threads can be paused with a known state. Some operations (biased lock revocation, deoptimization, huge counted loops without a safepoint poll) cause time-to-safepoint delays that look like GC pauses but are not. -Xlog:safepoint reveals them.

Q467. What is JFR and why prefer it in production?

Java Flight Recorder collects detailed events (allocation, GC, locks, I/O, exceptions) at roughly 1% overhead, so it can run continuously in production.

Q468. What happens when the JVM starts, in order?

  1. Parse the command line and create the JVM
  2. Load core classes with the Bootstrap loader
  3. Initialize the heap, GC, and JIT
  4. Load the main class via the Application loader
  5. Verify + prepare + initialize (run static blocks)
  6. Invoke main(String[])
  7. On exit: run shutdown hooks, then terminate (daemon threads are killed abruptly)

Section 6 — Quick Fire Round

Is memory allocated for a class or for an object?
Class metadata → Metaspace at load time. Instance fields → heap at new.
Can the GC be forced?
No. System.gc() is only a hint.
Does setting a reference to null guarantee immediate collection?
No — it only makes the object eligible. Timing is the GC's choice.
Where is the String pool since Java 7?
On the heap, so it can be garbage collected.
What is an "island of isolation"?
A group of objects referencing each other but unreachable from any GC root — correctly collected by Java.
Which is the default GC in modern Java?
G1 (since Java 9).
What replaced PermGen?
Metaspace, in native memory, since Java 8.
Do local primitives get garbage collected?
No — they live in the stack frame and disappear when the method returns.
What is the difference between -Xmx and -XX:MaxRAMPercentage?
Absolute size vs a percentage of available RAM — the latter is container friendly.
Can Metaspace cause OOM?
Yes — usually a classloader leak, or too many dynamically generated classes/proxies.
Does the JVM ever return memory to the OS?
Modern collectors can uncommit unused heap; older ones generally do not.
What is deoptimization?
The JIT discarding compiled code when an assumption (like a monomorphic call site) is invalidated, falling back to the interpreter.

Self-Test Checklist for Part 6

  • I can draw the JVM architecture and the heap generations
  • I can trace an object from Eden to Old Gen with the ages
  • I can name 6 causes of memory leaks in Java
  • I can explain GC roots and why reference cycles are not a problem
  • I can compare Serial / Parallel / G1 / ZGC and choose one with reasons
  • I can explain the 5 class loading phases and parent delegation
  • I know that class identity = name + classloader
  • I can describe a real memory-leak investigation using heap dumps and MAT
  • I know the 5 JVM flags I would always set in production
Part 6 complete — Q401–Q468
Next: Part 7 — Java 8 & Modern Java
