java/interview/java-8-and-modern-java.html:
Part 7 of 9 — Lambdas, functional interfaces, Streams, Optional, Date/Time, and what came after Java 8
Previous: Part 6 — JVM | Hub: Interview Hub

Table of Contents

  • λ Section 1 — Lambdas (Q469–Q480)
  • Section 2 — Functional Interfaces (Q481–Q492)
  • Section 3 — Streams (Q493–Q516)
  • Section 4 — Collectors (Q517–Q526)
  • Section 5 — Optional (Q527–Q536)
  • Time API (Q537–Q544)
  • Section 7 — Java 9 to 21 Features (Q545–Q556)
  • Section 8 — Quick Fire Round

λ Section 1 — Lambdas (Q469–Q480)

Q469. What is a lambda expression?

An anonymous function — a block of behaviour you can pass around like data.

Syntax forms:

Q470. What problems do lambdas solve?

  • Removes anonymous class boilerplate
  • Enables behaviour parameterization (pass logic, not just data)
  • Makes the Streams API possible
  • Encourages a declarative style — say what, not how

Q471. What can a lambda capture?

Local variables that are final or effectively final, plus instance/static fields (no restriction on those).

Why? The value is copied into the lambda; allowing reassignment would create two inconsistent copies. Fields are fine because they are accessed through a reference. See Part 2, Q137.

Q472. What does this mean inside a lambda?

The enclosing instance — unlike an anonymous class, where this is the anonymous object. Lambdas do not introduce a new scope; they are lexically scoped.

Q473. How are lambdas compiled? Are they anonymous classes?

No. The compiler emits an invokedynamic instruction plus a private synthetic method. At first execution, LambdaMetafactory builds the implementation. Benefits: no extra .class file per lambda, and stateless lambdas can be cached and reused instead of allocated each time.

Q474. What is a method reference?

Shorthand for a lambda that just calls one method.

Kind Syntax Equivalent lambda
Static Integer::parseInt s -> Integer.parseInt(s)
Instance of a particular object System.out::println x -> System.out.println(x)
Instance of an arbitrary object String::toUpperCase s -> s.toUpperCase()
Constructor ArrayList::new () -> new ArrayList<>()

Q475. What is the difference between String::length and str::length?

String::length is unbound — the receiver becomes the first argument (Function<String,Integer>). str::length is bound to that specific object (Supplier<Integer>).

Q476. Can a lambda throw a checked exception?

Only if the functional interface declares it. Function, Consumer, etc. do not — so you must handle it inside or wrap it (see Part 4, Q276).

Q477. Can a lambda be recursive?

Not directly (it cannot reference itself during its own initialization). Workaround: assign to a field, or use a named method reference.

Q478. Are lambdas slower than anonymous classes?

No. After JIT warmup they are typically equal or faster, partly due to caching of stateless lambdas and better inlining. Capturing lambdas allocate; non-capturing ones usually do not.

Q479. What is behaviour parameterization? Give an example.

Q480. When should you NOT use a lambda?

When the logic is long (extract a method), when you need state, when you need this to mean the function itself, or when a named method makes the intent clearer. A lambda longer than 3 lines is usually a mistake.

Section 2 — Functional Interfaces (Q481–Q492)

Q481. What are the built-in functional interfaces?

Interface Method Meaning
Predicate<T> boolean test(T) condition
Function<T,R> R apply(T) transform
Consumer<T> void accept(T) side effect
Supplier<T> T get() factory
UnaryOperator<T> T apply(T) Function<T,T>
BinaryOperator<T> T apply(T,T) reduce/combine
BiFunction<T,U,R> R apply(T,U) two inputs
BiPredicate, BiConsumer two-argument versions
Runnable void run() no input, no output
Callable<V> V call() throws like Supplier but can throw

Q482. What are the primitive specializations and why do they exist?

IntPredicate, IntFunction, ToIntFunction, IntUnaryOperator, IntSupplier, IntConsumer, and the Long/Double versions.

Why: to avoid boxing. Stream<Integer> allocates an Integer per element; IntStream does not. On large data this is a big difference.

Q483. What default methods do these interfaces provide?

Q484. andThen vs compose?

Q485. What does @FunctionalInterface do?

It is optional documentation plus a compile-time check: if you later add a second abstract method, the code fails to compile instead of silently breaking every lambda that used it. Always add it to your own functional interfaces.

Q486. Do default and static methods break the SAM rule?

No. Only abstract methods count. Also, public methods of Object (equals, hashCode, toString) declared in an interface do not count.

Q487. Write your own functional interface.

Q488. Is Comparator a functional interface?

Yes — compare() is its single abstract method (equals does not count). That is why Comparator.comparing(Person::getName) works.

Q489. What is Function.identity() and when do you use it?

x -> x. Common in Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), ...) when the element itself is the key.

Q490. What is currying in Java?

Returning a function from a function:

Rarely used in practice but a good conceptual question.

Q491. Can a functional interface extend another interface?

Yes, as long as the total number of abstract methods stays one.

Q492. Why is Supplier used for lazy evaluation?

The value is only computed when get() is called:

Section 3 — Streams (Q493–Q516)

Q493. What is a Stream? Is it a data structure?

No, it is not a data structure. It is a pipeline for computing over a source.

Property Detail
No storage it does not hold elements
Lazy intermediate ops do nothing until a terminal op runs
Single use consuming it twice throws IllegalStateException
Does not modify the source it produces new results
Can be infinite with limit() to bound it

Q494. Collection vs Stream?

Collection Stream
Purpose store data process data
Evaluation eager lazy
Traversal many times once
Mutable yes no
External vs internal iteration you write the loop the library iterates

Q495. Intermediate vs Terminal operations?

Intermediate (return a Stream, lazy):
filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, peek, limit, skip, mapToInt, takeWhile, dropWhile

Terminal (produce a result, trigger execution):
forEach, collect, reduce, count, min, max, sum, average, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch, findFirst, findAny, toArray, toList

Without a terminal operation, nothing runs:

Q496. What is lazy evaluation in streams? Show it.

Elements flow through the whole pipeline one at a time, not stage by stage.

This short-circuiting is why streams over large or infinite sources are efficient.

Q497. How do you create a stream?

Q498. map vs flatMap?

  • map → 1 element in, 1 element out (Stream<Stream<T>> if the function returns a stream)
  • flatMap → 1 element in, N elements out, all flattened into one stream

Q499. findFirst() vs findAny()?

Identical in a sequential stream. In a parallel stream, findAny() may return any matching element and is faster because it does not need to determine encounter order.

Q500. anyMatch / allMatch / noneMatch on an empty stream?

  • anyMatch → false
  • allMatch → true (vacuous truth — a classic trap)
  • noneMatch → true

Q501. What is reduce()? Its three forms?

The combiner is only used in parallel streams to merge partial results.

Q502. What is peek() and why is it dangerous?

peek is for debugging — it observes elements as they pass.

Dangers: it is lazy (does nothing without a terminal op), and the JVM may skip it entirely if the pipeline can prove it is unnecessary (e.g. .peek(...).count() on a sized stream). Never put business logic in peek.

Q503. limit() vs skip()?

limit(n) keeps the first n; skip(n) discards the first n. Both are cheap on ordered sequential streams and expensive on parallel ordered streams.

Q504. takeWhile vs dropWhile? (Java 9)

Different from filter, which checks every element.

Q505. How do you sort with streams?

Q506. What are IntStream and friends?

Primitive streams with no boxing and extra numeric methods:

Q507. What are parallel streams and when should you use them?

They split the source using a Spliterator and process chunks in the common ForkJoinPool.

Use when ALL of these hold:

  • Large data set (rule of thumb: >10,000 elements)
  • CPU-bound work per element
  • The source splits well (ArrayList, arrays / LinkedList, Iterator )
  • Operations are stateless and independent
  • No blocking I/O

Avoid when: small data, I/O-bound work, ordered operations like limit/findFirst, or shared mutable state.

Two real dangers
  1. The common pool is shared by the entire JVM — one blocking parallel stream can starve everything else.
  2. Overhead often makes parallel slower than sequential. Always measure with a real benchmark (JMH), never assume.

Q508. How do you control the thread pool for a parallel stream?

Submit the stream inside your own ForkJoinPool:

There is no official API — this is a known workaround.

Q509. What is a Spliterator?

"Splittable iterator" — the engine behind streams. It can tryAdvance() one element and trySplit() itself in two for parallelism. It also reports characteristics (SIZED, SORTED, DISTINCT, ORDERED) that the pipeline uses to optimize.

Q510. Why must stream operations be stateless and side-effect free?

Use collect, not external mutation.

Q511. What happens if you reuse a stream?

IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Create a new stream from the source, or use a Supplier<Stream<T>>.

Q512. Can you modify the source collection during streaming?

No — same ConcurrentModificationException risk as iteration. Streams are also allowed to throw or produce undefined results ("non-interference" requirement).

Q513. forEach vs forEachOrdered?

In a parallel stream, forEach ignores encounter order (fast); forEachOrdered preserves it (slower). In a sequential stream they behave the same.

Q514. stream().toList() vs collect(Collectors.toList())? (Java 16)

toList() is shorter and returns an unmodifiable list. Collectors.toList() returns a mutable ArrayList (though the API does not guarantee the exact type). Prefer toList() unless you need to mutate.

Q515. How do you handle exceptions inside a stream?

There is no built-in mechanism — wrap in an unchecked exception, or map to a result/Optional type:

Q516. Do streams always improve readability?

No. A 6-stage stream with nested lambdas can be far worse than a plain loop. Use streams for declarative transformation pipelines; keep loops when you need index access, early exit with complex state, or mutation. Saying this out loud shows judgment, not just knowledge.

Section 4 — Collectors (Q517–Q526)

Q517. What are the most used collectors?

Q518. groupingBy — show the multi-level version.

Q519. groupingBy vs partitioningBy?

partitioningBy always produces exactly two entries with Boolean keys (true and false) — even if one is empty. groupingBy produces one entry per distinct key.

Q520. What is the toMap duplicate-key trap?

Second trap: toMap throws NPE if a value is null (unlike HashMap.put).

Q521. How do you write a custom collector?

Rarely needed — usually collectingAndThen or reducing is enough.

Q522. reduce vs collect?

  • reduce → immutable reduction; each step produces a new value. Bad for strings (O(n²) concatenation).
  • collect → mutable reduction into a container. This is why Collectors.joining() beats reduce(String::concat).

Q523. What is flatMapping and filtering? (Java 9)

Downstream collectors that let you filter/flatten inside a groupingBy without losing empty groups:

Different from filtering before grouping, which drops the key entirely.

Q524. How do you compute statistics in one pass?

Q525. How do you join strings?

Q526. What are common stream one-liners worth memorizing?

Section 5 — Optional (Q527–Q536)

Q527. What is Optional and what problem does it solve?

A container that may or may not hold a non-null value. It makes "there may be no result" explicit in the type signature instead of a surprise NPE.

Q528. How do you create and use an Optional?

Q529. orElse vs orElseGet? (common trap)

Q530. What are Optional anti-patterns?

Optional's intended use is a RETURN type. That is what it was designed for.

Q531. Is Optional serializable?

No. That is one reason it should not be a field in an entity or DTO.

Q532. map vs flatMap on Optional?

If the function returns a plain value → map. If it already returns an Optional → flatMap (otherwise you get Optional<Optional<T>>).

Q533. What are OptionalInt, OptionalDouble?

Primitive versions returned by IntStream.max(), average(), etc. — they avoid boxing but have no map/filter.

Q534. Does Optional prevent all NPEs?

No — you can still hold Optional itself as null, and get() on empty throws NoSuchElementException. It is a design signal, not a runtime guard.

Q535. How does Optional chain nicely?

This replaces four nested null checks with one readable chain.

Q536. How do you use Optional with streams?

Section 6 — Date/Time API (Q537–Q544)

Q537. What was wrong with Date and Calendar?

  • Mutable → not thread-safe
  • Date months are 0-based, years offset from 1900 - SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe (a classic production bug)
  • Poor time zone handling, no separation of date vs time vs instant

Q538. What are the main java.time classes?

Class Represents
LocalDate date only (2026-08-11)
LocalTime time only (14:30)
LocalDateTime date + time, no zone
ZonedDateTime date + time + zone
OffsetDateTime date + time + UTC offset (best for APIs/DB)
Instant a point on the UTC timeline (machine time)
Duration time-based amount (seconds/nanos)
Period date-based amount (years/months/days)
DateTimeFormatter immutable and thread-safe

Q539. Show common operations.

Q540. Why is java.time immutable?

Every operation returns a new object, making all classes thread-safe and eliminating the aliasing bugs of Calendar.

Q541. Duration vs Period?

Duration = machine time (seconds, nanos) — use with Instant/LocalTime.
Period = human time (years, months, days) — use with LocalDate, and it respects varying month lengths and DST.

Q542. What should you store in a database?

Usually Instant/UTC timestamps for events, and LocalDate for calendar concepts like a birthday. Store the zone separately if the user's local time matters.

Q543. How do you convert between old and new APIs?

Q544. Why is SimpleDateFormat dangerous?

It keeps mutable internal state (Calendar), so sharing one static instance across threads silently produces wrong dates. Either create a new instance per use, use ThreadLocal, or — best — use DateTimeFormatter.

Section 7 — Java 9 to 21 Features (Q545–Q556)

Q545. What are the notable features by version?

Version Highlights
8 (LTS) lambdas, streams, Optional, java.time, default methods
9 modules (JPMS), List.of(), private interface methods, var-free JShell
10 var (local type inference)
11 (LTS) HttpClient, String methods (isBlank, strip, repeat, lines), single-file source launch, var in lambdas
14 switch expressions, helpful NPEs, records (preview)
15 text blocks
16 records, pattern matching for instanceof
17 (LTS) sealed classes, enhanced pseudo-random
21 (LTS) virtual threads, pattern matching for switch, record patterns, sequenced collections

Q546. What are switch expressions? (Java 14)

No fall-through, returns a value, and must be exhaustive for enums.

Q547. What is pattern matching for instanceof? (Java 16)

No cast needed. The scope is flow-sensitive.

Q548. What is pattern matching for switch + record patterns? (Java 21)

Combined with sealed interfaces, the compiler can verify exhaustiveness.

Q549. What are sequenced collections? (Java 21)

New interfaces SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, SequencedMap giving uniform getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), reversed() to List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap, and SortedMap. Finally consistent.

Q550. What is the new HttpClient? (Java 11)

Supports HTTP/2, WebSocket, and async via CompletableFuture.

Q551. What are the useful Java 11 String methods?

Q552. What is JShell?

The official REPL (jshell) for trying snippets without a class or main — great for interview whiteboarding and learning.

Q553. What is the difference between LTS and non-LTS releases?

Java releases every 6 months; LTS versions (8, 11, 17, 21, 25) get years of updates. Most companies run an LTS. Knowing that 21 is the current common LTS target signals you follow the ecosystem.

Q554. What is var in lambda parameters? (Java 11)

(var x, var y) -> x + y — useful only to attach annotations like (@NonNull var x) -> ....

Q555. What are text blocks used for?

Multi-line strings without escaping — SQL, JSON, HTML. Incidental indentation is stripped automatically.

Q556. What is coming next in Java?

[Guessing — this moves fast, verify before an interview] Project Valhalla (value types / primitive classes), Loom follow-ups (structured concurrency), Panama (foreign function & memory API), and Amber (continued language ergonomics). Naming these projects shows genuine ecosystem awareness.

Section 8 — Quick Fire Round

Can you reuse a stream?
No — IllegalStateException.
Does filter run without a terminal operation?
No. Intermediate operations are lazy.
What does allMatch return on an empty stream?
true.
Is parallelStream() always faster?
No — often slower for small data or I/O work.
Which pool do parallel streams use?
The shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
What is the SAM rule?
Single Abstract Method — the requirement for a functional interface.
Difference between Collection.stream() and Collection.parallelStream()?
Sequential vs parallel execution of the same pipeline.
Should Optional be a method parameter?
No — use overloading or accept null with clear documentation.
Which is lazy: orElse or orElseGet?
orElseGet.
Is DateTimeFormatter thread-safe?
Yes — unlike SimpleDateFormat.
What does flatMap(Optional::stream) do?
Removes empty Optionals from a stream (Java 9).
What replaced Date/Calendar?
The java.time package (JSR-310), inspired by Joda-Time.

Self-Test Checklist for Part 7

  • I can explain lambda capture and effectively-final
  • I know the 6 core functional interfaces and their methods by heart
  • I can explain laziness with the findFirst example
  • I can explain map vs flatMap with a concrete case
  • I can list 5 conditions for parallel streams to actually help
  • I can write multi-level groupingBy from memory
  • I know the toMap duplicate-key and null-value traps
  • I can list 5 Optional anti-patterns
  • I know why SimpleDateFormat is dangerous
Part 7 complete — Q469–Q556

Part 8 of 9 — File handling, streams, serialization, reflection, annotations, and String internals
Previous: Part 7 — Java 8 & Modern Java | Hub: Interview Hub

Table of Contents

  • O Fundamentals (Q557–Q570)
  • Section 2 — NIO & Files (Q571–Q580)
  • Section 3 — Serialization (Q581–Q596)
  • Section 4 — Reflection (Q597–Q610)
  • Section 5 — Annotations (Q611–Q620)
  • Section 6 — Quick Fire Round

Section 1 — I/O Fundamentals (Q557–Q570)

Q557. What is a stream in Java I/O?

A sequence of data flowing from a source to a destination. Note: java.io streams are completely unrelated to java.util.stream (Part 7) — same word, different concept.

Q558. Byte streams vs Character streams?

Byte streams Character streams
Base classes InputStream / OutputStream Reader / Writer
Unit 8-bit bytes 16-bit chars
For images, audio, binary, any file text
Encoding aware handles charset

Rule: text → Reader/Writer; everything else → InputStream/OutputStream.

Q559. Draw the I/O class hierarchy.

Q560. What is the Decorator pattern in java.io?

You wrap streams to add capabilities — this is the textbook example of the Decorator pattern.

Q561. Why use buffering?

Without it, every read() is a system call — reading a 1 MB file byte by byte means a million syscalls. A buffer reads a large block at once into memory.

The speed difference is typically 10–100×. Always wrap file streams in a Buffered variant (or use NIO).

Q562. FileReader vs InputStreamReader — which should you use?

FileReader uses the platform default charset (before Java 18), which makes your program behave differently on different machines — a real production bug source.

Java 18 made UTF-8 the default charset (JEP 400), but being explicit is still correct.

Q563. How do you read a file — the modern ways?

Files.lines() returns a stream backed by an open file handle — you must close it with try-with-resources.

Q564. How do you write a file?

Q565. What is PrintWriter vs PrintStream?

PrintStream is byte-based (System.out); PrintWriter is character-based and preferred for text. Both swallow IOException by default — call checkError() if it matters.

Q566. What does flush() do and when do you need it?

Forces buffered data out to the destination. close() flushes automatically, but you need explicit flush() for long-lived streams (sockets, logs) where the receiver waits for data.

Q567. What is System.in, out, err?

Standard input/output/error streams. They can be redirected with System.setOut(...). System.err is unbuffered so errors appear immediately.

Q568. Scanner vs BufferedReader?

Scanner BufferedReader
Parses types nextInt(), nextDouble() strings only
Buffer size small (1 KB) large (8 KB)
Speed slower (regex-based) faster
Thread safe synchronized

For competitive programming and large input, BufferedReader wins.

Classic Scanner trap: nextInt() leaves the newline in the buffer, so the next nextLine() returns an empty string. Call an extra nextLine() to consume it.

Q569. What is the File class and its limits?

Old API for paths and metadata. Weaknesses: poor error messages (methods just return false), no symlink support, no file attributes, no atomic operations. Replaced by java.nio.file.Path + Files.

Q570. What is try-with-resources for I/O?

The correct way to close streams — see Part 4, Q256. Never rely on finally { stream.close(); } written by hand.

Section 2 — NIO & Files (Q571–Q580)

Q571. What is NIO and how does it differ from IO?

IO (java.io) NIO (java.nio)
Model stream oriented buffer oriented
Blocking blocking only non-blocking possible
Core abstractions streams Channels + Buffers + Selectors
Direction one-way channels are bidirectional
Best for simple sequential files high-concurrency servers, large files

Q572. What is a Channel and a Buffer?

  • Channel — a connection to a file, socket, or device; you read into buffers and write from buffers
  • Buffer — a fixed-size memory block with position, limit, capacity; flip() switches from writing to reading

Q573. What is a Selector?

One thread can monitor many channels for readiness (multiplexing) — the foundation of non-blocking servers like Netty. Instead of one thread per connection, one thread handles thousands.

Q574. What is Path vs File?

Q575. What can the Files utility class do?

Q576. What is a memory-mapped file?

The OS maps the file directly into virtual memory — reads/writes bypass the usual copy into JVM heap. Extremely fast for very large files. Used by databases and message brokers.

Q577. What is WatchService?

Native OS file-change notifications — detect create/modify/delete without polling.

Q578. What is a direct ByteBuffer?

ByteBuffer.allocateDirect() allocates off-heap memory that the OS can use for zero-copy I/O. Faster for I/O, but allocation is expensive and it is not managed by the normal GC — leaks are possible.

Q579. What is zero-copy?

FileChannel.transferTo() moves data directly from a file to a socket in the kernel, without copying it into user space. This is how high-performance file servers work.

Q580. Files.walk() vs Files.list()?

list() = one level, walk() = recursive with an optional depth limit. Both return lazy streams holding OS resources → always close them.

Section 3 — Serialization (Q581–Q596)

Q581. What is serialization?

Converting an object into a byte stream so it can be stored or transmitted, and reconstructed later (deserialization).

Q582. What is serialVersionUID and why does it matter?

A version identifier for the class. During deserialization, the JVM compares the stored UID with the current class's UID — if they differ, it throws InvalidClassException.

If you do not declare it, the compiler generates one from the class structure. Then any small change (adding a method!) changes the UID and breaks compatibility with old data. Always declare it explicitly.

Q583. What is transient?

Marks a field to be skipped during serialization. On deserialization it gets the default value (null/0).

Use for: passwords, caches, derived values, non-serializable references, database connections, loggers.

Q584. Are static fields serialized?

No. They belong to the class, not the instance. After deserialization they hold whatever the current JVM has.

Q585. What happens if a field's type is not serializable?

NotSerializableException at runtime — unless the field is transient. Serialization is deep: the whole object graph must be serializable.

Q586. What if the parent class is not serializable but the child is?

Deserialization calls the parent's no-argument constructor to initialize the inherited fields. If the parent has no accessible no-arg constructor → InvalidClassException.

Note the child's own constructor is not called at all during deserialization.

Q587. Does deserialization call the constructor?

No for the serializable class itself — the object is created without running its constructor. That is exactly why serialization can break invariants and singletons.

Q588. How do you protect a singleton from serialization?

Or use an enum singleton, which the JVM handles correctly for free. (Part 2, Q150)

Q589. What are writeObject / readObject?

Private hooks for custom serialization logic:

Q590. Serializable vs Externalizable?

Serializable Externalizable
Control JVM handles it you write writeExternal/readExternal
Constructor on read not called public no-arg constructor IS called
Performance slower, more metadata faster, compact
Effort zero full manual work

Q591. Why is Java serialization considered dangerous?

  • Deserialization of untrusted data is a major security hole — gadget chains can achieve remote code execution. It has caused many real CVEs.
  • Constructors are bypassed → invariants broken
  • Fragile versioning
  • Verbose, slow format
  • Ties your class structure to your wire format

Recommendation (Effective Java, Item 85): avoid Java serialization entirely in new systems. Use JSON (Jackson), Protobuf, or Avro. If you must accept it, use a deserialization filter (ObjectInputFilter, Java 9+).

Q592. How do you deep-copy with serialization?

Serialize to a ByteArrayOutputStream and read back — every object in the graph is recreated. Simple, but slow and requires everything to be serializable. (Part 2, Q146)

Q593. Is the order of fields important in serialization?

No — fields are written by name. But removing a field or changing its type breaks compatibility; adding a field is usually compatible (it deserializes as the default value).

Q594. What is ObjectInputFilter?

A Java 9+ allow/deny list applied before deserializing, limiting classes, depth, and array sizes — the standard mitigation for deserialization attacks.

Q595. Can you serialize a lambda?

Only if the target type is serializable (e.g. cast to (Runnable & Serializable)). It works but is fragile — the synthetic method name can change between compilations. Avoid.

Q596. What alternatives exist to Java serialization?

JSON (Jackson, Gson), Protocol Buffers, Avro, Kryo, MessagePack, and simple record-to-DTO mapping. All are faster, cross-language, and far safer.

Section 4 — Reflection (Q597–Q610)

Q597. What is reflection?

The ability to inspect and manipulate classes, methods, and fields at runtime, without knowing them at compile time.

Q598. How do you get a Class object? Three ways.

Q599. getMethods() vs getDeclaredMethods()?

getMethods() getDeclaredMethods()
Access public only all: private, protected, default, public
Inherited includes inherited this class only

Same distinction for getFields, getConstructors.

Q600. What are the real uses of reflection?

  • Frameworks: Spring (DI, @Autowired), Hibernate (entity mapping), JUnit (finding @Test methods)
  • JSON libraries mapping fields to keys (Jackson, Gson)
  • IDEs, debuggers, code generators
  • Dynamic proxies and AOP
  • Plugin systems and ServiceLoader

You rarely write reflection yourself — but you use frameworks built on it every day.

Q601. What are the disadvantages of reflection?

  • Slower — no JIT inlining, plus access checks (though much better since Java 9)
  • No compile-time safety — typos become runtime NoSuchMethodException
  • Breaks encapsulation — setAccessible(true) defeats private
  • Breaks refactoring (renaming a field silently breaks reflective code)
  • Restricted by the module system and security managers

Q602. How did Java 9 modules affect reflection?

Strong encapsulation: reflective access to non-exported packages fails unless the module opens them. That is why you sometimes see --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED in startup scripts.

Q603. What is a dynamic proxy?

Creating an implementation of an interface at runtime — the mechanism behind Spring AOP, transactions, and mocking libraries.

Limitation: interfaces only. For classes, frameworks use CGLIB or ByteBuddy (subclassing).

Q604. Can reflection break final?

For non-static fields, setAccessible(true) + Field.set historically worked, but the JIT may have already inlined the constant, giving inconsistent results. Java 17+ blocks it for records and hidden classes. Never rely on it.

Q605. How do you get generic type info via reflection?

Type arguments of variables are erased, but declarations keep signatures:

See Part 4, Q303.

Q606. What is MethodHandle / VarHandle?

Modern, faster alternatives to reflection introduced with invokedynamic. MethodHandle is a typed, JIT-friendly reference to a method; VarHandle (Java 9) gives fine-grained memory access with atomic and volatile semantics — replacing sun.misc.Unsafe.

Q607. What is ServiceLoader?

The standard SPI mechanism: implementations declared in META-INF/services (or provides ... with in a module) are discovered at runtime.

Q608. How does Spring use reflection?

Scans classes for annotations, instantiates beans via reflective constructors, injects fields/setters, and wraps beans in dynamic proxies for transactions and AOP. Knowing this connects core Java to framework knowledge — interviewers love that bridge.

Q609. Is reflection thread-safe?

Class objects are thread-safe, but setAccessible mutates shared AccessibleObject state, and your reflective target may not be thread-safe. Cache Method objects (that is what frameworks do for performance), but be careful with accessibility flags.

Q610. How do frameworks make reflection fast?

They cache the reflective lookups (Method/Field objects) at startup, use MethodHandles, or generate bytecode at build/startup time (Micronaut, Quarkus do exactly this to avoid runtime reflection and enable native images).

Section 5 — Annotations (Q611–Q620)

Q611. What is an annotation?

Metadata attached to code. It does not change behaviour by itself — a processor, compiler, or framework reads it and acts.

Q612. What are the built-in annotations?

Annotation Purpose
@Override compile-time check that you really override
@Deprecated marks obsolete API (since, forRemoval in Java 9)
@SuppressWarnings silence specific compiler warnings
@FunctionalInterface enforce a single abstract method
@SafeVarargs suppress generic varargs warnings

Q613. What are meta-annotations?

Annotations that annotate annotations:

Meta-annotation Meaning
@Retention how long it is kept: SOURCE, CLASS, RUNTIME
@Target where it can be applied: TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, ...
@Documented include in Javadoc
@Inherited subclasses inherit it
@Repeatable can appear multiple times (Java 8)

Q614. What are the retention policies?

Policy Kept in .class? Visible via reflection? Example
SOURCE discarded by the compiler @Override, Lombok
CLASS (default) bytecode tools
RUNTIME Spring, JUnit, Jackson

If a framework needs to read it at runtime, it must be RUNTIME. This is a very common interview question.

Q615. How do you create a custom annotation?

Allowed member types: primitives, String, Class, enums, other annotations, and arrays of these. No arbitrary objects, no null defaults.

Q616. How do you read annotations at runtime?

Q617. What is annotation processing (APT)?

Compile-time code generation via javax.annotation.processing — used by Lombok, MapStruct, Dagger, and immutables. It runs during javac, generating source files before compilation completes. Faster than runtime reflection and native-image friendly.

Q618. Can annotations be inherited?

Only class-level annotations marked @Inherited, and only for class inheritance — method annotations are never inherited. That is why Spring checks the whole hierarchy manually.

Q619. What are type annotations? (Java 8)

Annotations on any type use, enabling static analysis tools like the Checker Framework:

Q620. Do annotations affect performance?

SOURCE and CLASS retention: zero runtime cost. RUNTIME retention: only costs when something reflectively reads them — usually at startup, then cached.

Section 6 — Quick Fire Round

Which class should you use to read a text file line by line?
BufferedReader (or Files.lines() / Files.newBufferedReader).
Is Serializable a marker interface?
Yes — no methods.
What happens if serialVersionUID does not match?
InvalidClassException.
Are transient fields restored after deserialization?
No — they get default values (null/0/false).
Does deserialization run the constructor?
Not for the serializable class; the first non-serializable superclass constructor does run.
What is the default charset problem?
Platform-dependent encoding causing different behaviour per machine. Always specify UTF-8 (default since Java 18).
Can reflection access private members?
Yes, with setAccessible(true) — subject to module restrictions.
Which retention policy do Spring and JUnit annotations use?
RUNTIME.
What is the difference between Class.forName() and .class?
forName loads and initializes; .class does not trigger initialization.
Why is Files.lines() risky?
It holds an open file handle — must be closed with try-with-resources.
Which is faster: Scanner or BufferedReader?
BufferedReader.
What replaced sun.misc.Unsafe for atomic field access?
VarHandle (Java 9).

Self-Test Checklist for Part 8

  • I know when to use byte streams vs character streams
  • I can explain why buffering matters and by how much
  • I always specify the charset explicitly
  • I can explain serialVersionUID and transient
  • I can explain why Java serialization is a security risk and what to use instead
  • I can protect a singleton with readResolve()
  • I know the difference between getMethods and getDeclaredMethods
  • I can explain how Spring uses reflection and proxies
  • I know the three retention policies and which frameworks need RUNTIME
Part 8 complete — Q557–Q620
