Part 9 of 9 — Design patterns, tricky output questions, coding round prep, and the final review sheet
Previous: Part 8 — IO & Reflection | Hub: Interview Hub

Table of Contents

  • Section 1 — Creational Patterns (Q621–Q632)
  • Section 2 — Structural Patterns (Q633–Q642)
  • Section 3 — Behavioural Patterns (Q643–Q654)
  • Section 4 — Principles & Anti-Patterns (Q655–Q662)
  • Section 5 — Output Puzzles (Q663–Q690)
  • Section 6 — Coding Round Classics
  • Section 7 — Behavioural & Closing Questions
  • Section 8 — The Final Review Sheet

Section 1 — Creational Patterns (Q621–Q632)

Q621. What are design patterns and the three categories?

Reusable solutions to recurring design problems.

Category Purpose Examples
Creational how objects are created Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype
Structural how objects are composed Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite
Behavioural how objects communicate Strategy, Observer, Template, Command, Iterator

Q622. Singleton — show the correct implementations.

How can a singleton be broken? Reflection (setAccessible on the private constructor), serialization (creates a new object — fix with readResolve), cloning (fix by throwing in clone), and multiple classloaders. The enum version resists all of these.

Q623. Where is Singleton used in the JDK?

Runtime.getRuntime(), Desktop.getDesktop(), System.getSecurityManager(), logger factories.

Q624. Why do many people call Singleton an anti-pattern?

It introduces global mutable state, makes unit testing hard (you cannot inject a fake), hides dependencies, and often causes concurrency problems. In modern code, a DI container manages a single instance for you without the global access point.

Q625. Factory Method pattern?

A method that decides which concrete class to instantiate, so callers depend only on the interface.

JDK examples: Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getInstance(), valueOf() methods, List.of().

Q626. Abstract Factory vs Factory Method?

Factory Method creates one product; Abstract Factory creates a family of related products (e.g. a WindowsUIFactory producing matching buttons, checkboxes, and menus).

Q627. Builder pattern?

For objects with many optional parameters — replaces the "telescoping constructor" problem.

JDK examples: StringBuilder, Stream.Builder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Calendar.Builder.

Q628. When do you need a Builder?

Rule of thumb: 4+ constructor parameters, or several optional ones, or you want immutability with readable construction.

Q629. Prototype pattern?

Create new objects by copying an existing one instead of constructing from scratch (expensive initialization). Java's clone() is its native form — but a copy constructor is usually cleaner (Part 2, Q145).

Q630. What is a static factory method and its advantages over constructors?

Advantages (Effective Java, Item 1):

  1. They have names (newSortedList vs another anonymous constructor)
  2. They can cache/reuse instances (Integer cache!)
  3. They can return a subtype (List.of returns different hidden classes by size)
  4. They can vary the returned class by input

Q631. Object Pool pattern?

Reuse expensive objects instead of recreating them — connection pools (HikariCP), thread pools. Only worth it when creation cost is genuinely high; for ordinary objects modern GC makes pooling slower.

Q632. Dependency Injection — what and why?

Dependencies are passed in rather than created inside.

Benefits: testability, loose coupling, easy swapping of implementations. Constructor injection is preferred over field injection (it makes dependencies explicit and allows final).

Section 2 — Structural Patterns (Q633–Q642)

Q633. Adapter pattern?

Makes an incompatible interface usable — the "power plug converter".

JDK: Arrays.asList(), InputStreamReader (bytes→chars), Collections.list(Enumeration).

Q634. Decorator pattern?

Adds behaviour by wrapping, without subclass explosion.

JDK: all of java.io, Collections.unmodifiableList(), Collections.synchronizedList().

Q635. Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy — how do they differ?

Pattern Changes the interface? Adds behaviour? Intent
Adapter yes make incompatible things work together
Decorator same interface yes add responsibilities dynamically
Proxy same interface control control access (lazy, remote, security)

Q636. Proxy pattern?

A stand-in that controls access to the real object.

Types: virtual (lazy loading — Hibernate lazy entities), protection (security checks), remote (RMI), smart (logging, caching, transactions — Spring AOP).

Q637. Facade pattern?

One simple interface hiding a complicated subsystem. Example: a OrderFacade.placeOrder() that internally calls inventory, payment, shipping, and notification services.

Q638. Composite pattern?

Treat individual objects and groups uniformly through a shared interface — file system trees, UI component hierarchies, menu structures.

Q639. Flyweight pattern?

Share common state between many objects to save memory. JDK: Integer.valueOf() cache, the String pool, Character.valueOf().

Q640. Bridge pattern?

Separate an abstraction from its implementation so both can vary independently — e.g. Shape (abstraction) × Renderer (implementation) instead of SquareVectorShape, SquareRasterShape, ...

JDK: JDBC — Driver is the bridge between the API and each database.

Q641. What is the difference between inheritance and the Decorator for adding features?

Inheritance is static and multiplies classes (BufferedEncryptedFileReader); decorators compose at runtime in any order.

Q642. What patterns appear in Spring?

Singleton (bean scope), Factory (BeanFactory), Proxy (AOP/transactions), Template Method (JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate), Observer (ApplicationEvent), Strategy (pluggable implementations), Builder (RestClient.builder()).

Section 3 — Behavioural Patterns (Q643–Q654)

Q643. Strategy pattern?

Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms and select one at runtime.

In modern Java, a lambda is a strategy: Comparator, Predicate, and Runnable are all strategy objects.

Q644. Observer pattern?

One-to-many notification: when the subject changes, all observers are told.

JDK: listeners in Swing, PropertyChangeListener, Spring events, reactive streams. (java.util.Observer is deprecated — do not use it.)

Q645. Template Method pattern?

The parent defines the skeleton; subclasses fill in steps.

JDK: AbstractList, InputStream.read(), JdbcTemplate, servlet service().

Q646. Strategy vs Template Method?

Strategy uses composition (swap the whole algorithm at runtime); Template Method uses inheritance (fix the skeleton, vary the steps at compile time).

Q647. Command pattern?

Wrap a request as an object → enables queuing, logging, undo/redo. Runnable submitted to an ExecutorService is exactly this. Also used in transaction logs and GUI actions.

Q648. Chain of Responsibility?

Pass a request along a chain until someone handles it — servlet filters, Spring Security filter chain, exception handlers, logging levels.

Q649. Iterator pattern?

Traverse a collection without exposing its internals — java.util.Iterator is the pattern built into the language.

Q650. State pattern?

An object changes behaviour when its internal state changes, replacing large if/switch chains with state classes. Example: an order that is Draft → Paid → Shipped → Delivered, each with different allowed actions.

Q651. Mediator pattern?

Centralizes communication so components do not reference each other directly — reduces N×N coupling to N.

Q652. Memento pattern?

Capture and restore an object's state without exposing its internals — undo functionality, snapshots.

Q653. Visitor pattern?

Add new operations to an object hierarchy without changing the classes. In Java 21, sealed interfaces + switch pattern matching largely replace it with far less code.

Q654. Which patterns does the JDK use most? (a great answer to have ready)

Pattern JDK example
Singleton Runtime.getRuntime()
Factory Calendar.getInstance(), List.of()
Builder StringBuilder, HttpRequest.newBuilder()
Adapter Arrays.asList(), InputStreamReader
Decorator java.io streams, Collections.unmodifiableX
Proxy java.lang.reflect.Proxy, RMI
Strategy Comparator, Predicate
Observer listeners, Spring events
Template Method AbstractList, JdbcTemplate
Iterator Iterator, Iterable
Flyweight Integer.valueOf() cache, String pool

Section 4 — Principles & Anti-Patterns (Q655–Q662)

Q655. What is DRY, KISS, YAGNI?

  • DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself (one source of truth for each piece of knowledge)
  • KISS — Keep It Simple, Stupid
  • YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It (do not build for imagined future requirements)

Q656. What is the Law of Demeter?

"Talk only to your immediate friends." Avoid a.getB().getC().getD().doThing() — it couples you to the whole chain. Also called the train wreck anti-pattern.

Q657. What are common anti-patterns?

  • God object — one class doing everything
  • Spaghetti code — no structure
  • Magic numbers — unexplained literals
  • Premature optimization — complexity with no measurement
  • Anemic domain model — data classes with all logic in "services"
  • Copy-paste programming
  • Exception swallowing — catch (Exception e) { }

Q658. What makes code testable?

Dependency injection, small functions with single responsibility, no hidden global state, no new inside business logic, deterministic behaviour (inject a Clock instead of calling LocalDate.now()).

Q659. What is the difference between cohesion and coupling? (again — but say it well)

High cohesion inside a class, low coupling between classes. It is the single most reliable measure of a good design.

Q660. What is composition over inheritance in one sentence?

Inheritance couples you to a parent's implementation forever; composition lets you swap behaviour and keeps encapsulation intact. (Part 2, Q75)

Q661. What is "program to an interface, not an implementation"?

Q662. When is it acceptable to break a "best practice"?

When you have measured a real problem, understand the trade-off, and document why. Saying this shows engineering judgment rather than rule-following.

Section 5 — Output Puzzles (Q663–Q690)

Cover the answer, guess first, then open. This is the fastest way to find your blind spots.
Q663. System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);
false — IEEE 754 binary floating point.
Q664. System.out.println('a' + 'b');
195 — chars are promoted to int (97 + 98).
Q665. System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b');
ab — string concatenation, not addition.
Q666. System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);
3345 — evaluated left to right.
Q667. Integer a = 127, b = 127; Integer c = 128, d = 128; print(a<mark>b, c</mark>d);
true false — the Integer cache is −128 to 127.
Q668. int i = 0; i = i++; print(i);
0 — post-increment returns the old value, which overwrites the incremented one.
Q669. System.out.println(Math.min(Double.MIN_VALUE, 0.0d));
0.0 — Double.MIN_VALUE is the smallest positive value, not the most negative.
Q670. System.out.println(Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE));
−2147483648 — the positive value does not fit in an int.
Q671. java int m() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }
2 — finally's return wins.
Q672. java int m() { int x=1; try { return x; } finally { x=2; } }
1 — the return value was already captured.
Q673. String a = "ja"+"va"; String b = "java"; print(a==b);
true — compile-time constant folding puts it in the pool.
Q674. String p="ja"; String a=p+"va"; print(a=="java");
false — runtime concatenation creates a new object. (Make p final → true.)
Q675. System.out.println(new String("a") == "a");
false — new always creates a heap object outside the pool.
Q676. List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10,20,30)); l.remove(1); print(l);
[10, 30] — remove(int) removes by index.
Q677. Set<Point> s; s.add(p); p.setX(9); print(s.contains(p));
false — the hash changed, so it looks in the wrong bucket.
Q678. Parent p = new Child(); print(p.name); where both declare name
Parent's name — fields are resolved by the reference type.
Q679. Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod();
Parent's — static methods are hidden, not overridden.
Q680. System.out.println(Stream.of(1,2,3).allMatch(x -> x > 10)); on an empty stream
On an empty stream allMatch returns true (vacuous truth).
Q681. java list.stream().filter(x -> {print(x); return true;});
Nothing prints — no terminal operation, so nothing executes.
Q682. Optional.ofNullable(null).orElse(expensive());
expensive() always runs, even when the Optional has a value. Use orElseGet.
Q683. System.out.println(0.0/0.0 == 0.0/0.0);
false — NaN is never equal to anything, including itself.
Q684. byte a=10, b=20; byte c=a+b;
Compile error — a+b is promoted to int. byte c = 10+20; would compile (constant expression).
Q685. System.out.println(-8 >> 1); System.out.println(-8 >>> 1);
−4 and 2147483644.
Q686. java for (String s : list) if (s.equals(secondLast)) list.remove(s);
No exception, but an element is silently skipped — the hasNext() quirk (Part 3, Q231).
Q687. new HashSet<>(List.of("b","a","c")) printed
Order is unspecified — do not assume insertion or sorted order.
Q688. java class A { static { print("A"); } } class B extends A { static { print("B"); } } new B();
A then B — parent statics initialize first.
Q689. System.out.println("1" + 2 + 3); System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3");
123 and 33.
Q690. java Integer x = null; int y = false ? 1 : x;
NullPointerException — the ternary unboxes x.

Section 6 — Coding Round Classics

These come up as live coding tasks. Practice writing them without an IDE.

String / array

  1. Reverse a string (and in-place with a char array)
  2. Check palindrome (ignore case and non-letters)
  3. Count character frequency → Map<Character,Integer> with merge
  4. Find the first non-repeating character → LinkedHashMap
  5. Check if two strings are anagrams
  6. Reverse the words in a sentence
  7. Find duplicates in an array → Set.add() returns false
  8. Find the missing number in 1..n → sum formula or XOR
  9. Two Sum → HashMap of complement, O(n)
  10. Move all zeros to the end

Collections / logic
11. Sort a Map by value
12. Group a list of objects by a field → groupingBy
13. Find the top K elements → min-heap of size K
14. Remove duplicates preserving order → LinkedHashSet
15. Implement an LRU cache → LinkedHashMap (Part 3, Q198)
16. Merge two sorted lists
17. Find the second largest element in one pass

Classic algorithms
18. Fibonacci — recursion, memoization, and iterative
19. Factorial (watch for overflow → use BigInteger)
20. Prime check + Sieve of Eratosthenes
21. Binary search (and the left + (right-left)/2 overflow fix)
22. FizzBuzz (yes, still asked)
23. Detect a cycle in a linked list → fast/slow pointers
24. Balanced parentheses → Deque as a stack
25. Matrix rotation / spiral traversal

Concurrency
26. Producer-consumer with BlockingQueue
27. Print odd/even numbers with two alternating threads (wait/notify)
28. Thread-safe counter three ways: synchronized, AtomicInteger, LongAdder
29. Run N tasks and wait for all → CountDownLatch or invokeAll

Design
30. Design a thread-safe singleton
31. Design an immutable class
32. Implement equals/hashCode correctly
33. Design a parking lot / elevator / URL shortener (open-ended design)

Section 7 — Behavioural & Closing Questions

These decide more offers than trivia does. Prepare one concrete story for each.
  1. "Tell me about a difficult bug you fixed." → Structure: symptom → how you narrowed it → root cause → fix → what you changed so it cannot recur.
  2. "Describe a performance problem you solved." → Mention measurement (profiler, GC logs) before the fix. Never say "I guessed."
  3. "A time you disagreed with a technical decision." → Show you argued with data and then committed to the team's choice.
  4. "Code you are proud of / code you would rewrite." → The second half shows growth.
  5. "How do you keep up with Java?" → Name a specific source and a recent feature you tried.

Questions to ask THEM (asking nothing looks disengaged ):

  • What does the code review process look like?
  • What is the biggest technical debt in the codebase right now?
  • How do you handle production incidents?
  • What does success look like for this role in 6 months?
  • Which Java version are you on, and what stops you from upgrading?

Section 8 — The Final Review Sheet

The 20 things you must be able to answer instantly
# Question Part
1 JDK vs JRE vs JVM 1
2 Is Java pass-by-value? 1
3 Why is String immutable? 1
4 Integer cache −128..127 1
5 Overloading vs overriding 2
6 equals/hashCode contract 2
7 Abstract class vs interface 2
8 How to make an immutable class 2
9 HashMap internals 3
10 ArrayList vs LinkedList 3
11 fail-fast vs fail-safe / CME 3
12 Checked vs unchecked exceptions 4
13 try-with-resources + suppressed 4
14 Type erasure and PECS 4
15 sleep vs wait 5
16 volatile vs synchronized 5
17 ThreadPoolExecutor parameters 5
18 Heap generations + GC roots 6
19 map vs flatMap, lazy streams 7
20 Optional anti-patterns 7

The 48-hours-before checklist:

  • Re-read only the questions in each part
  • Redo all 28 output puzzles in Section 5
  • Write HashMap put() on paper from memory
  • Write equals/hashCode on paper from memory
  • Prepare 3 stories: a hard bug, a performance fix, a design decision
  • Prepare 4 questions to ask them
  • Sleep. A rested brain beats one more chapter.
Series complete — Q1 through Q690 across 9 parts
Go back to the hub: Interview Hub

Final advice: you will not be asked most of these. You will be asked five, and then asked to go three levels deeper on two of them. Depth beats coverage — pick your five strongest areas and make them unbreakable.

database.title: Database — SQL & PostgreSQL
database.html:
What this track covers
SQL and PostgreSQL in three tiers: what every backend developer must know, what a professional uses daily, and the internals that make you the database person on the team.

Tiers

Level Tier Topics
1 Must Know 11
2 Professional 9
3 Legend 8

Reference

  • PostgreSQL Cheat Sheet
  • SQL Execution Pipeline (PDF)

database/must-know.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW
database/must-know.html:
Items 1–110. Non-negotiable for any backend developer.
Rule for ticking a box: you can write it from memory and you know when it is the wrong choice.

  1. A. What a database actually is0/7
  2. B. Data types & integrity0/14
  3. C. Core SQL — reading data0/10
  4. D. Joins0/9
  5. E. Subqueries & set operations0/7
  6. F. Expressions & functions0/8
  7. G. Writing data0/7
  8. H. Transactions & concurrency0/11
  9. I. Indexes — this belongs in tier 1, not later0/14
  10. J. Data modelling0/13
  11. K. Postgres in practice0/10

Tier 1 exit test

You can call it done when you can, without help:

  1. Model a small domain (users, orders, items) with correct keys and constraints.
  2. Write a report query using joins, grouping and a CASE.
  3. Explain why one of your queries is slow by reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and fix it with the right index.
  4. Explain what happens when two transactions update the same row at the same time under Read Committed.

database/must-know/what-a-database-actua.title: A. What a database actually is

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/what-a-database-actua.html:
Checklist

  • 1. Database vs file storage — concurrency, durability, querying and integrity are the four things a file cannot give you.
  • 2. RDBMS vs NoSQL — relational is the default; NoSQL is a trade you make for a specific reason (scale shape, schema flexibility), not a fashion.
  • 3. Client / server model — your app talks to a separate process over TCP. Every query is a network round trip.
  • 4. Table, row (tuple), column (attribute) — plus the mental model: a table is a set, not a list. There is no natural order.
  • 5. Schema — the namespace inside a database. In Postgres: cluster → database → schema → table.
  • 6. SQL sub-languages — DDL (create/alter), DML (insert/update/delete), DQL (select), TCL (commit/rollback), DCL (grant/revoke).
  • 7. Declarative thinking — you describe what you want; the planner decides how. This is why the same result can be 1ms or 10s.

database/must-know/data-types-and-integr.title: B. Data types & integrity

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

prev.title: A. What a database actually is

database/must-know/data-types-and-integr.html:
Checklist

  • 8. Numeric types — smallint, integer, bigint, numeric/decimal, real/double. Money is numeric, never floating point.
  • 9. Text types — text, varchar(n), char(n). In Postgres text and varchar perform identically; char(n) pads with spaces and is a trap.
  • 10. Boolean, and why a nullable boolean has three states.
  • 11. Date & time types — date, time, timestamp, timestamptz, interval. Use timestamptz and store UTC.
  • 12. UUID type — real UUID column, not a string.
  • 13. json vs jsonb — jsonb is parsed, indexable and reorders keys; json keeps raw text. Use jsonb.
  • 14. Arrays — Postgres can store an array in a column. Convenient, but often a modelling shortcut you regret.
  • 15. Enum types vs lookup tables — enums are fast but painful to change; lookup tables are flexible.
  • 16. NULL and three-valued logic — NULL = NULL is not true, it is unknown. NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing. This single topic causes more silent wrong results than any other.
  • 17. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL / IS DISTINCT FROM.
  • 18. Constraints: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT — push rules into the database. Application-only validation always leaks eventually.
  • 19. Primary key — unique + not null + the row's identity.
  • 20. Foreign key — referential integrity, plus ON DELETE / ON UPDATE actions (CASCADE, RESTRICT, SET NULL).
  • 21. Why unique constraints beat "check first, then insert" — the check-then-act pattern is a race condition. The constraint is the only real guarantee.

database/must-know/core-sql-reading-data.title: C. Core SQL — reading data

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/core-sql-reading-data.html:
Checklist

  • 22. SELECT, column list, * and why * is bad in application code.
  • 23. WHERE and operators — comparison, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE/ILIKE, ~ regex.
  • 24. ORDER BY — ascending/descending, NULLS FIRST/LAST, multiple keys.
  • 25. LIMIT / OFFSET — and the fact that LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary row.
  • 26. DISTINCT.
  • 27. Aliases (AS) and table aliases.
  • 28. Aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, and how each treats NULL. COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) differ.
  • 29. GROUP BY — one output row per group; every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
  • 30. HAVING — filter after grouping, unlike WHERE.
  • 31. Logical order of execution — FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Learn this and half of SQL's "weird rules" become obvious (for example, why you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE).

database/must-know/joins.title: D. Joins

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/joins.html:
Checklist

  • 32. INNER JOIN — only matching rows.
  • 33. LEFT JOIN — keep all left rows, NULL-fill the right.
  • 34. RIGHT JOIN / FULL OUTER JOIN.
  • 35. CROSS JOIN — every combination; usually an accident.
  • 36. The LEFT JOIN + WHERE trap — putting a right-table condition in WHERE silently turns your outer join into an inner join. Put it in ON instead.
  • 37. Self join — a table joined to itself (hierarchies, comparisons).
  • 38. Joining on multiple columns / composite keys.
  • 39. Join and row multiplication — a one-to-many join multiplies rows and quietly corrupts your SUM. Aggregate before joining, or use a subquery.
  • 40. USING and NATURAL JOIN — shortcuts; NATURAL JOIN is dangerous because it depends on column names.

database/must-know/subqueries-and-set-op.title: E. Subqueries & set operations

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/subqueries-and-set-op.html:
Checklist

  • 41. Scalar subquery — one value inside SELECT or WHERE.
  • 42. Subquery in FROM (derived table).
  • 43. Correlated subquery — runs per row; know it because it explains many slow queries.
  • 44. IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN — semantics differ with NULLs and duplicates, not just performance.
  • 45. ANY / ALL.
  • 46. UNION vs UNION ALL — UNION deduplicates and costs a sort. Default to UNION ALL unless you need dedup.
  • 47. INTERSECT / EXCEPT.

database/must-know/expressions-and-funct.title: F. Expressions & functions

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/expressions-and-funct.html:
Checklist

  • 48. CASE WHEN — conditional logic inside a query.
  • 49. COALESCE, NULLIF, GREATEST, LEAST.
  • 50. String functions — concat, ||, substring, trim, upper/lower, replace, split_part, position, format.
  • 51. Pattern matching — LIKE, ILIKE, SIMILAR TO, POSIX regex.
  • 52. Date/time functions — now(), current_date, age(), date_trunc, extract, interval arithmetic.
  • 53. Time zones done right — timestamptz stores an instant; the zone is applied at display. AT TIME ZONE converts.
  • 54. Casting — ::type and CAST(), plus implicit-cast surprises.
  • 55. Math and rounding — round, ceil, floor, integer division (5/2 = 2 — a classic bug).

database/must-know/writing-data.title: G. Writing data

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/writing-data.html:
Checklist

  • 56. INSERT — single row, multi-row, INSERT ... SELECT.
  • 57. RETURNING — get the generated ID or the updated row back in the same statement. Postgres-specific and very useful.
  • 58. UPDATE — with FROM for update-from-another-table.
  • 59. DELETE — and USING.
  • 60. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE / DO NOTHING (upsert) — the correct, race-free insert-or-update.
  • 61. TRUNCATE vs DELETE — speed, transactionality, sequence reset, foreign keys.
  • 62. The safety habit — run SELECT first, then wrap the write in an explicit transaction. [Certain] Everyone deletes a whole table exactly once; make it not be in production.

database/must-know/transactions-and-conc.title: H. Transactions & concurrency

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

next.title: I. Indexes — this belongs in tier 1, not later

database/must-know/transactions-and-conc.html:
Checklist

  • 63. What a transaction is — a unit of work that fully happens or fully does not.
  • 64. BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK / SAVEPOINT.
  • 65. ACID — atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. Know what each one actually promises.
  • 66. Read phenomena — dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update.
  • 67. Isolation levels — Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable, and which phenomena each prevents.
  • 68. Postgres specifics — the default is Read Committed; Postgres has no true Read Uncommitted; Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation.
  • 69. Row locks — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, and SKIP LOCKED for queue patterns.
  • 70. Deadlocks — why they happen, why consistent lock ordering prevents them, why the loser gets an error and must retry.
  • 71. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking — a version column vs an actual lock.
  • 72. Long transactions are poison — they hold locks, block VACUUM, and grow bloat. Never keep a transaction open across a network call or user think-time.
  • 73. Autocommit — every bare statement is its own transaction. Know what your driver does.

database/must-know/indexes-this-belongs-.title: I. Indexes — this belongs in tier 1, not later

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/indexes-this-belongs-.html:
Checklist

  • 74. What an index is — a separate, ordered structure that turns a full scan into a targeted lookup. Default type: B-tree.
  • 75. The trade — faster reads, slower writes, more disk. Indexes are not free.
  • 76. Primary key and unique constraints create indexes automatically.
  • 77. Foreign keys do NOT create an index in Postgres — a very common cause of slow joins and slow deletes. Add it yourself.
  • 78. Composite index and column order — the leftmost-prefix rule decides which queries can use it. (a, b) helps WHERE a, not WHERE b.
  • 79. Selectivity / cardinality — an index on a column with 2 distinct values usually will not be used.
  • 80. When an index is ignored — a function or cast on the column (WHERE lower(email) = ...), leading wildcard LIKE '%x', type mismatch, or the planner deciding a seq scan is cheaper.
  • 81. Index-only scan / covering index — when the index alone answers the query, the table is never touched.
  • 82. EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE Core — the single most valuable database skill. EXPLAIN shows the plan; ANALYZE actually runs it and shows real times and row counts.
  • 83. Reading a plan — read inner nodes first; compare estimated rows with actual rows. A large gap means the planner is misinformed, and that is usually the real problem.
  • 84. Scan types — sequential scan, index scan, index-only scan, bitmap heap scan, and when each is correct. A seq scan is not automatically bad.
  • 85. Join strategies — nested loop, hash join, merge join, and which one fits which data size.
  • 86. Pagination performance — OFFSET 100000 reads and discards 100,000 rows. Use keyset ("seek") pagination: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY ... LIMIT n.
  • 87. COUNT(*) on a big table is slow — and why exact totals in a paginated UI are often not worth the price.

database/must-know/data-modelling.title: J. Data modelling

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

prev.title: I. Indexes — this belongs in tier 1, not later

database/must-know/data-modelling.html:
Checklist

  • 88. Entity–relationship thinking — entities, attributes, relationships, before any SQL.
  • 89. Relationship types — one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many with a junction table.
  • 90. Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF — in practice: no repeating groups, no partial dependency, no transitive dependency. Aim for 3NF by default.
  • 91. Deliberate denormalization — done for a measured read problem, never because normalizing "felt hard".
  • 92. Surrogate vs natural keys — the ID column versus a real-world identifier. Most of the time: surrogate.
  • 93. bigint identity vs UUID — sequential IDs are compact and index-friendly; UUIDs are distributed-friendly but hurt index locality (look at UUIDv7 as the compromise).
  • 94. SERIAL vs GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY — identity is the modern standard.
  • 95. Sequences — how they work, why gaps are normal and harmless.
  • 96. Naming conventions — pick one (snake_case, singular or plural, _id suffixes) and never mix.
  • 97. Audit columns — created_at, updated_at, created_by. Add them from day one.
  • 98. Soft delete — a deleted_at column changes every query and every unique constraint. Understand the cost before choosing it.
  • 99. Storing money, quantities and units — integer minor units or numeric, and store the currency.
  • 100. Choosing what belongs in JSONB vs columns — structured, queried, constrained data goes in columns. JSONB is for genuinely variable shapes.

database/must-know/postgres-in-practice.title: K. Postgres in practice

crumbs.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/must-know/postgres-in-practice.html:
Checklist

  • 101. Running Postgres — Docker for local, managed service for production.
  • 102. psql — connecting, and the meta-commands: \l, \c, \dt, \d table, \di, \df, \x, \timing.
  • 103. Cluster → database → schema → table, plus search_path.
  • 104. Roles and privileges — CREATE ROLE, GRANT, REVOKE, ownership, and least privilege for your app user.
  • 105. Connection strings & SSL — and connection limits, which are lower than you think.
  • 106. A GUI client — DBeaver or pgAdmin, for exploring and for EXPLAIN visualisation.
  • 107. pg_dump / pg_restore / psql < file — logical backup and restore basics.
  • 108. Migrations as code — Flyway or Liquibase; versioned, forward-only, reviewed. Never change schema by hand in production.
  • 109. SQL injection & parameterized queries Core — string concatenation into SQL is the vulnerability. Bind parameters always, including in dynamic ORDER BY (validate against a whitelist).
  • 110. Least privilege for the app user — your API does not need SUPERUSER or DROP TABLE.

database/professional.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 2: PROFESSIONAL

prev.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 1: MUST KNOW

database/professional.html:
Items 111–235. This is the tier that changes your salary. [Likely] most working developers stop somewhere in the middle of it.

  1. L. Advanced query writing0/20
  2. M. Postgres-specific data features0/15
  3. N. Views, functions, triggers0/11
  4. O. Indexing, deeper0/12
  5. P. Performance & tuning0/22
  6. Q. Partitioning & large data0/7
  7. R. Operations you must understand as a developer0/12
  8. S. Schema change without downtime0/9
  9. T. Beyond a single Postgres0/17

Tier 2 exit test

  1. Solve a top-N-per-group problem two ways (window function and LATERAL) and explain which plan is better.
  2. Take a slow endpoint, find the query with pg_stat_statements, read its plan, and cut its time by 10x.
  3. Add a NOT NULL column to a 50-million-row table with no downtime and explain each step's lock level.
  4. Explain MVCC, bloat and autovacuum to a colleague in five minutes without notes.

database/professional/advanced-query-wri.title: L. Advanced query writing
database/professional/advanced-query-wri.html:
Checklist

  • 111. CTEs (WITH) — name a subquery, read the query top-to-bottom. Note: in modern Postgres a CTE is inlined by default, but MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED lets you force it.
  • 112. Recursive CTEs — trees, hierarchies, graph walks, generated sequences.
  • 113. Window functions — the concept — aggregate without collapsing rows. The biggest single jump in SQL power.
  • 114. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE.
  • 115. LAG / LEAD — compare a row with the previous or next one (deltas, gaps, session detection).
  • 116. SUM/AVG/COUNT ... OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) — running totals and moving averages.
  • 117. Window frames — ROWS vs RANGE, UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, CURRENT ROW. The default frame surprises people.
  • 118. FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE.
  • 119. DISTINCT ON — Postgres shortcut for "the latest row per group".
  • 120. FILTER (WHERE ...) — conditional aggregates, cleaner than CASE inside SUM.
  • 121. GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE — several levels of aggregation in one pass.
  • 122. LATERAL joins — a subquery that can reference the row on its left. Top-N-per-group, correlated expansion.
  • 123. Set-returning functions — generate_series, unnest, jsonb_array_elements.
  • 124. VALUES lists as inline tables.
  • 125. Data-modifying CTEs — WITH deleted AS (DELETE ... RETURNING ...) INSERT ... for atomic move/archive.
  • 126. MERGE — the SQL-standard multi-action upsert (Postgres 15+).
  • 127. Anti-joins and semi-joins — NOT EXISTS versus LEFT JOIN ... WHERE ... IS NULL, and their NULL behaviour.
  • 128. Pivot / unpivot patterns — with FILTER, crosstab, or unnest.
  • 129. Gaps-and-islands problems — the classic window-function exercise.
  • 130. Query readability — CTE naming, formatting, and knowing when a 200-line query should become a view.

database/professional/postgres-specific-.title: M. Postgres-specific data features
database/professional/postgres-specific-.html:
Checklist

  • 131. JSONB operators — ->, ->>, #>, @>, ?, jsonb_set, jsonb_build_object.
  • 132. JSONPath (@?, jsonb_path_query).
  • 133. Indexing JSONB — GIN with jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops, and expression indexes on a single key.
  • 134. Array operators and indexing — @>, &&, ANY, GIN indexes.
  • 135. Full-text search — tsvector, tsquery, to_tsvector, ranking, dictionaries, GIN index, generated tsvector columns.
  • 136. Trigram search (pg_trgm) — fuzzy matching and fast LIKE '%x%' with a GIN/GiST index.
  • 137. Range types — int4range, tstzrange, containment operators.
  • 138. Exclusion constraints — "no two bookings for this room may overlap", enforced by the database.
  • 139. Composite types and domains — custom types with constraints.
  • 140. hstore — the older key/value type; know it exists, prefer JSONB.
  • 141. Generated columns — stored computed columns.
  • 142. Identity columns, sequences, and setval recovery.
  • 143. COPY — bulk load, orders of magnitude faster than row-by-row inserts.
  • 144. Foreign data wrappers (postgres_fdw, file_fdw) — query another database or a CSV as if it were a table.
  • 145. Extensions — how to install them, and the ones worth knowing: pg_trgm, pgcrypto, uuid-ossp, postgis, pg_stat_statements, citext.

database/professional/views-functions-tr.title: N. Views, functions, triggers
database/professional/views-functions-tr.html:
Checklist

  • 146. Views — a named query. No storage, no performance gain by itself.
  • 147. Updatable views and INSTEAD OF triggers.
  • 148. Materialized views — the result is stored; REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking readers. Good for expensive dashboards.
  • 149. Functions in PL/pgSQL — variables, control flow, RETURNS TABLE, exceptions.
  • 150. Function volatility — IMMUTABLE, STABLE, VOLATILE, and why it decides whether an expression index is even allowed.
  • 151. Procedures vs functions — procedures can manage transactions.
  • 152. Triggers — BEFORE/AFTER, row vs statement level, NEW/OLD.
  • 153. Good trigger uses — updated_at, audit tables, denormalized counters.
  • 154. Bad trigger uses — business logic hidden from your application code. [Likely] the most common cause of "why did this row change?" mysteries.
  • 155. LISTEN / NOTIFY — lightweight pub/sub from the database.
  • 156. Row-level security (RLS) — per-row access policies; the real tool for multi-tenant isolation.

database/professional/indexing-deeper.title: O. Indexing, deeper
database/professional/indexing-deeper.html:
Checklist

  • 157. Index types overview — B-tree, Hash, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, BRIN, and what data shape each is for.
  • 158. GIN — many values per row: arrays, JSONB, full text.
  • 159. GiST — geometry, ranges, nearest-neighbour.
  • 160. BRIN — tiny index for huge, naturally ordered tables (time-series).
  • 161. Partial indexes — WHERE status = 'active'; smaller and often dramatically faster.
  • 162. Expression indexes — ON (lower(email)), matching the exact expression your query uses.
  • 163. Covering indexes with INCLUDE.
  • 164. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY — build an index without locking writes. Mandatory in production, and it can fail and leave an invalid index.
  • 165. Operator classes and collations — including text_pattern_ops for LIKE 'abc%'.
  • 166. Unique partial indexes — "only one active record per user".
  • 167. Finding unused and duplicate indexes — pg_stat_user_indexes. Unused indexes cost writes forever.
  • 168. Index bloat and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

database/professional/performance-and-tu.title: P. Performance & tuning
database/professional/performance-and-tu.html:
Checklist

  • 169. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, FORMAT TEXT) — buffers show you actual I/O, which timing alone hides.
  • 170. Reading a plan properly — actual vs estimated rows, loops, the most expensive node, and where time is really spent.
  • 171. Plan visualizers — pev2 / explain.depesz. Use them until plans read naturally.
  • 172. Planner statistics and ANALYZE — the planner guesses from samples; stale statistics produce terrible plans.
  • 173. Extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS) — for correlated columns the planner otherwise treats as independent.
  • 174. Key configuration knobs — shared_buffers, work_mem, effective_cache_size, random_page_cost, max_connections. Know what each affects before touching it.
  • 175. work_mem and spilling to disk — a sort or hash that does not fit goes to disk and gets slow.
  • 176. pg_stat_statements — find your actual worst queries by total time, not by feeling.
  • 177. pg_stat_activity — see what is running, what is blocked, and what is waiting.
  • 178. Lock inspection — pg_locks, blocking-tree queries, finding the blocker.
  • 179. auto_explain and slow query logging.
  • 180. MVCC in practice — an UPDATE writes a new row version; old versions stay until vacuumed. This explains bloat, and why "update-heavy table, no vacuum" ends badly.
  • 181. VACUUM and autovacuum — what they reclaim, why they matter, when the defaults are too lazy for your workload.
  • 182. VACUUM FULL — rewrites the table and takes an exclusive lock. Rarely the answer.
  • 183. Table and index bloat — how to measure it, what causes it.
  • 184. TOAST — how Postgres stores large values out-of-line, and why a wide text column can be cheaper than it looks.
  • 185. HOT updates and fillfactor — updating a non-indexed column can avoid touching indexes.
  • 186. Connection pooling — every connection is a process. Use HikariCP in the app, PgBouncer in front for many services; understand transaction vs session pooling modes.
  • 187. Batching writes — multi-row inserts, COPY, and why 10,000 single-row inserts is a network problem, not a database problem.
  • 188. Query rewriting techniques — pushing filters down, avoiding OR across columns (UNION ALL instead), avoiding functions on indexed columns.
  • 189. Caching layers — materialized views, summary tables, Redis; and cache invalidation as the actual hard part.
  • 190. Benchmarking honestly — realistic data volume, warm vs cold cache, repeat runs. Optimizing against 100 dev rows teaches you nothing.

database/professional/partitioning-and-l.title: Q. Partitioning & large data

next.title: R. Operations you must understand as a developer

database/professional/partitioning-and-l.html:
Checklist

  • 191. Declarative partitioning — range, list, hash.
  • 192. Partition pruning — the whole point; it only works if your query filters on the partition key.
  • 193. Partition maintenance — creating future partitions, detaching and archiving old ones, pg_partman.
  • 194. When partitioning does NOT help — under roughly tens of millions of rows, a good index is usually the better answer.
  • 195. Time-series patterns — BRIN plus range partitions, retention policies, TimescaleDB as an option.
  • 196. Archiving and retention — moving cold data out instead of letting the table grow forever.
  • 197. Bulk delete strategies — batched deletes, or partition detach instead of DELETE.

database/professional/operations-you-mus.title: R. Operations you must understand as a developer
database/professional/operations-you-mus.html:
Checklist

  • 198. WAL (write-ahead log) — the concept — changes are written to a log before the data files. This is what makes durability and replication possible.
  • 199. Checkpoints — and the I/O spikes they cause.
  • 200. Logical vs physical backup — pg_dump versus pg_basebackup.
  • 201. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) — base backup plus WAL archive.
  • 202. Restore drills — an untested backup is not a backup. [Certain]
  • 203. Streaming replication — primary/standby, synchronous vs asynchronous, replication lag.
  • 204. Read replicas from the app side — routing reads, and the fact that a replica can be stale (read-your-own-write problems).
  • 205. Logical replication — publications and subscriptions; replicate selected tables, or between versions.
  • 206. Failover and HA — Patroni, virtual IPs, what your application must do when the primary changes.
  • 207. Major version upgrades — pg_upgrade versus logical replication cutover.
  • 208. Monitoring — connections, cache hit ratio, replication lag, longest transaction, deadlocks, bloat, disk. Know the five you would alert on.
  • 209. Security — TLS, pg_hba.conf, role separation, column encryption with pgcrypto, secret management, audit logging.

database/professional/schema-change-with.title: S. Schema change without downtime

prev.title: R. Operations you must understand as a developer

database/professional/schema-change-with.html:
Checklist

  • 210. Lock levels of ALTER TABLE — some are instant, some rewrite the whole table and block everything. Know which is which before you deploy.
  • 211. Adding a column safely — nullable or with a constant default is fast in modern Postgres; a volatile default rewrites the table.
  • 212. Adding NOT NULL safely — add a CHECK ... NOT VALID, validate, then convert.
  • 213. Adding a constraint or foreign key with NOT VALID + VALIDATE.
  • 214. Renaming and dropping columns — the expand/contract (parallel change) pattern across releases.
  • 215. Backfilling large tables — batched updates with sleeps, never one giant transaction.
  • 216. lock_timeout and statement_timeout in migrations — fail fast instead of blocking your whole application.
  • 217. Blue/green and backwards-compatible schema — the app version before and after must both work against the schema.
  • 218. Migration tooling discipline — forward-only, one change per migration, reviewed, tested against a production-sized copy.

database/professional/beyond-a-single-po.title: T. Beyond a single Postgres
database/professional/beyond-a-single-po.html:
Checklist

  • 219. OLTP vs OLAP — different access patterns need different shapes and often different systems.
  • 220. Star schema, facts and dimensions — basic warehouse modelling.
  • 221. Columnar stores — ClickHouse, DuckDB, and why analytics belongs there rather than in your production OLTP database.
  • 222. ETL / ELT basics — extract, load, transform; dbt as the common tool.
  • 223. Change data capture (CDC) — logical decoding and Debezium; streaming database changes into Kafka.
  • 224. Transactional outbox — the correct way to publish an event and commit a row atomically.
  • 225. Job queues in Postgres — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; good enough far longer than people expect.
  • 226. Sharding basics — key choice, rebalancing, cross-shard queries, and why you delay it as long as possible.
  • 227. Multi-tenancy strategies — shared table with tenant_id, schema per tenant, database per tenant; and RLS as the enforcement layer.
  • 228. Caching with Redis in front of Postgres — patterns and invalidation.
  • 229. Search engines — when Postgres full-text stops being enough and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch starts earning its cost.
  • 230. Other engines for comparison — MySQL differences, SQLite for local/tests, MongoDB's model and its trade-offs.
  • 231. Testing against real Postgres — Testcontainers, seeded fixtures, migration tests. H2 lies about SQL.
  • 232. Anonymized production-like data for testing.
  • 233. Query linting and review — catching SELECT *, missing indexes and full scans before merge.
  • 234. Cost awareness on managed services — IOPS, storage growth, connection limits, egress.
  • 235. Capacity planning — growth per month, when your current instance stops being enough.

database/legend.title: Database & SQL & Postgres — Tier 3: LEGEND
database/legend.html:
Items 236–305. Internals, theory, and distributed systems.

Honest warning: [Likely] none of this makes you more useful at work next month. It makes you the person who can explain why Tier 2 behaves the way it does, and it is what you need to work on databases rather than merely with them. Do not start here to feel advanced.

  1. U. Postgres storage internals0/12
  2. V. Durability, recovery, WAL0/8
  3. W. Query planner & optimizer internals0/12
  4. X. Concurrency control theory0/8
  5. Y. Distributed data0/11
  6. Z. Storage engines & systems research0/7
  7. AA. Extending Postgres0/7
  8. AB. Practice that actually earns the title0/5

Honest priority note

If you are a backend developer, the highest-value items in this whole file are 238–241 (tuple headers and MVCC), 256–261 (how the planner estimates), and 271–272 (write skew and SSI). Those three clusters explain real production behaviour you will meet. The rest is craft and curiosity.

database/legend/postgres-storage-interna.title: U. Postgres storage internals
database/legend/postgres-storage-interna.html:
Checklist

  • 236. Physical layout — cluster directory, tablespaces, relation files, 1 GB segments, the pg_class / pg_attribute catalogs.
  • 237. Page structure — the 8 KB page: header, item pointers, tuples, free space, special area.
  • 238. Tuple headers — xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask bits. Once you can read these, MVCC stops being abstract.
  • 239. MVCC visibility rules — how a snapshot decides which row versions you can see.
  • 240. Snapshots and transaction IDs — xid, running-transaction lists, txid_current().
  • 241. Transaction ID wraparound — the 32-bit counter, freezing, aggressive vacuum, and the shutdown that saves your data.
  • 242. Freeze maps and visibility maps — what makes index-only scans and cheap vacuums possible.
  • 243. Dead tuples, bloat mechanics, and free space maps.
  • 244. HOT chains in detail.
  • 245. TOAST internals — compression, out-of-line storage, storage strategies (PLAIN, EXTENDED, EXTERNAL, MAIN).
  • 246. Buffer manager — shared buffers, pinning, the clock-sweep replacement algorithm, and the OS page cache underneath.
  • 247. Background processes — checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher, stats collector.

database/legend/durability-recovery-wal.title: V. Durability, recovery, WAL
database/legend/durability-recovery-wal.html:
Checklist

  • 248. WAL record structure and LSNs.
  • 249. Full-page writes and torn-page protection.
  • 250. Checkpoint mechanics and tuning — max_wal_size, checkpoint_completion_target.
  • 251. Crash recovery / REDO — how Postgres replays WAL on start.
  • 252. ARIES recovery algorithm — the classic paper behind most of this.
  • 253. fsync, synchronous_commit, and honest durability trade-offs.
  • 254. Logical decoding — turning physical WAL into logical change events; output plugins, replication slots and the disk they can eat.
  • 255. Two-phase commit (PREPARE TRANSACTION) — and why it is rarely used in practice.

database/legend/query-planner-and-optimi.title: W. Query planner & optimizer internals
database/legend/query-planner-and-optimi.html:
Checklist

  • 256. Parse → analyze → rewrite → plan → execute — the five stages of a query.
  • 257. Relational algebra — selection, projection, join, and why the planner is allowed to reorder your query at all.
  • 258. Cost model — how seq_page_cost, random_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost combine into a number.
  • 259. Cardinality estimation — the hardest problem in query optimization; errors compound multiplicatively up the plan tree.
  • 260. Statistics internals — histograms, most-common-values lists, n_distinct, correlation, and default_statistics_target.
  • 261. Join order search — dynamic programming, and GEQO (the genetic optimizer) for many-table joins.
  • 262. Subquery flattening and predicate pushdown.
  • 263. Executor internals — the volcano/iterator model, ExecProcNode.
  • 264. Parallel query execution — gather nodes, workers, what can and cannot be parallelized.
  • 265. JIT compilation — when it helps, and when it makes short queries slower.
  • 266. Plan caching, prepared statements, generic vs custom plans — the "it got slow after the 6th execution" mystery.
  • 267. Hint-free philosophy — why Postgres refuses query hints, and the tools you use instead (pg_hint_plan, statistics, rewriting).

database/legend/concurrency-control-theo.title: X. Concurrency control theory
database/legend/concurrency-control-theo.html:
Checklist

  • 268. Serializability — conflict serializable vs view serializable.
  • 269. Two-phase locking (2PL) and strict 2PL.
  • 270. Timestamp ordering and optimistic concurrency control.
  • 271. Snapshot isolation and write skew — the anomaly that snapshot isolation does not prevent.
  • 272. Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — Postgres's true SERIALIZABLE, predicate locks, and serialization failures your app must retry.
  • 273. Lock manager internals — lock modes, the lock table, lightweight locks, spinlocks, LWLock contention.
  • 274. Deadlock detection algorithms — wait-for graphs.
  • 275. Latch vs lock — protecting memory structures versus protecting data.

database/legend/distributed-data.title: Y. Distributed data
database/legend/distributed-data.html:
Checklist

  • 276. CAP theorem — and its correct, narrow meaning. Most "CAP" arguments online are wrong.
  • 277. PACELC — the more useful refinement.
  • 278. Consistency models — linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual.
  • 279. Consensus: Raft and Paxos — the basis of every serious distributed database.
  • 280. Quorum reads and writes.
  • 281. Distributed transactions — 2PC, 3PC, and their failure modes.
  • 282. Sagas and compensating transactions.
  • 283. Clock problems — clock skew, logical clocks, vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks, Google TrueTime.
  • 284. Distributed SQL systems — CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, Citus, Spanner: how each splits and replicates data.
  • 285. Conflict resolution and CRDTs.
  • 286. Partitioning and rebalancing algorithms — consistent hashing, range splits.

database/legend/storage-engines-and-syst.title: Z. Storage engines & systems research
database/legend/storage-engines-and-syst.html:
Checklist

  • 287. B-tree vs LSM-tree — read/write amplification trade-offs; Postgres/InnoDB versus RocksDB/Cassandra.
  • 288. Write, read and space amplification — the three-way trade nobody escapes.
  • 289. Compaction strategies — leveled versus size-tiered.
  • 290. Row store vs column store — compression, vectorized execution, why analytics is 100x faster in columnar form.
  • 291. In-memory databases and their durability tricks.
  • 292. Modern hardware effects — NVMe, io_uring, NUMA, CPU cache lines and false sharing.
  • 293. Compression algorithms in databases — LZ4, ZSTD, dictionary encoding, run-length encoding.

database/legend/extending-postgres.title: AA. Extending Postgres

next.title: AB. Practice that actually earns the title

database/legend/extending-postgres.html:
Checklist

  • 294. Writing extensions in C — PG_MODULE_MAGIC, control and SQL files, PGXS builds.
  • 295. Hooks — planner, executor, and utility hooks used by extensions like pg_stat_statements.
  • 296. Background workers.
  • 297. Custom types, operators and operator classes.
  • 298. Custom index access methods — building your own index type.
  • 299. Custom aggregates and window functions.
  • 300. Writing a logical decoding output plugin.

database/legend/practice-that-actually-e.title: AB. Practice that actually earns the title
database/legend/practice-that-actually-e.html:
Checklist

  • 301. Read the Postgres source — start with nbtree (B-tree) or heapam; the code comments are excellent documentation.
  • 302. Benchmarking properly — pgbench, TPC-C/TPC-H, controlling for cache, warm-up, and variance.
  • 303. Read the foundational papers — System R, ARIES, the Google Spanner paper, "The Log-Structured Merge-Tree", "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels".
  • 304. Read a serious book end to end — Designing Data-Intensive Applications, The Internals of PostgreSQL, Database Internals, PostgreSQL 14 Internals.
  • 305. Build a toy database — a heap file, a B-tree, a WAL, a simple planner. [Certain] One weekend of this teaches more than 100 blog posts.

database/postgresql-cheat-sheet.title: PostgreSQL Cheat Sheet
database/postgresql-cheat-sheet.html:
Two different things live here. Keep them separate in your head:

  • psql meta-commands start with a backslash (\dt). They are features of the psql program only. No semicolon needed.
  • SQL is the real language (SELECT ...). It always ends with a semicolon ;.

1. Connecting (in your terminal, not in psql)

Command-line helper tools (wrappers around SQL):

2. psql meta-commands (the ones you actually use)

Command What it does
\? help for psql commands
\h SELECT help for SQL syntax
\l list databases
\c dbname connect to another database
\dt list tables
\d tablename describe a table (columns, types, indexes)
\d+ tablename same, with more detail
\dn list schemas
\du list roles/users
\di list indexes
\df list functions
\dv list views
\x toggle expanded output (great for wide rows)
\timing show how long each query takes
\i file.sql run a SQL file
\o out.txt send output to a file
\e open the last query in an editor
\conninfo who am I, where am I connected
\q quit

3. Databases and schemas

4. Roles and permissions

In Postgres a "user" is just a role that has LOGIN. There is no separate user object.

5. Tables (DDL)

Common data types

Six mistakes that will cost you an hour each

  1. Forgetting the ; — psql just waits and shows shop-#. Type ; and Enter.
  2. NULL = NULL is not true. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
  3. Double quotes "Name" mean an identifier. Single quotes 'Name' mean a string. Never mix them.
  4. Unquoted names are folded to lowercase. CREATE TABLE Users makes a table called users.
  5. DELETE FROM customers with no WHERE deletes everything. There is no undo outside a transaction.
  6. \dt shows nothing? You are probably in the wrong database (\c dbname) or wrong schema (\dn, SET search_path).

spring-boot/concept-map/version-and-plat.html:
Checklist

  • 271. Spring Framework vs Spring Boot vs Spring Cloud version lines Core — three different version numbers. Boot 3.x ships Framework 6.x. Tutorials that mix them will not compile.
  • 272. The javax → jakarta namespace break Core — Boot 3 moved every javax.persistence / javax.servlet import to jakarta.*. This single change makes most pre-2023 tutorials wrong.
  • 273. Java baseline per version Core — Boot 2 runs on Java 8+, Boot 3 needs Java 17+. Check before copying anything.
  • 274. Removed / deprecated APIs you will still see in tutorials Core — WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter, antMatchers, @MockBean, RestTemplate as default choice. Know the replacements.
  • 275. Release train & support windows Important — OSS support ends fast; commercial support extends it. Affects which version you start a project on.
  • 276. How to read the migration guide Important — the wiki migration notes are the fastest way to upgrade a real project.
  • 277. Spring's relation to Jakarta EE / CDI Optional — Spring is not an EE server; it borrows the annotations, not the runtime.
  • 278. The Spring reference documentation structure Core — core → web → data → boot. [Certain] It is better written than 95% of tutorials. Learn to navigate it.

  • 279. Bean naming rules and BeanNameGenerator Important — the default bean name is the decapitalized class name; matters for @Qualifier and for overriding.
  • 280. Bean overriding (and why Boot disables it by default) Important — two beans with the same name used to silently replace each other. Now it fails at startup, on purpose.
  • 281. @Order, Ordered, @Priority Important — controls the order of filters, aspects, interceptors, and injected lists.
  • 282. @ConfigurationPropertiesScan Important — register config classes without @EnableConfigurationProperties.
  • 283. Configuration metadata & IDE autocomplete Important — the annotation processor that makes your own properties autocomplete in application.yml.

spring-boot/concept-map/web-layer-what-t.html:
Checklist

  • 287. HandlerMethodArgumentResolver Important — inject your own custom object as a controller parameter (for example the current user). Very commonly needed, rarely taught.
  • 288. HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler Optional — the mirror image for return types.
  • 289. RequestBodyAdvice / ResponseBodyAdvice Important — modify every request or response body globally (envelopes, masking, encryption).
  • 290. Custom HttpMessageConverter Optional — support a format Jackson does not handle.
  • 291. Customizing the ObjectMapper Core — date formats, naming strategy, unknown-property behaviour, null handling. You will need this in every real project.
  • 292. Date, time and time zones Core — LocalDate vs Instant vs ZonedDateTime, storing UTC, @JsonFormat. [Certain] A top-3 source of real bugs.
  • 293. BigDecimal for money Core — never double. Scale and rounding mode matter.
  • 294. ErrorController and the whitelabel error page Important — what Boot does when nothing handles the exception.
  • 295. HTTP caching: ETag, Cache-Control, Last-Modified Important — plus ShallowEtagHeaderFilter.
  • 296. Response compression and HTTP/2 Important — a two-line config change with real impact.
  • 297. Request size limits & multipart config Important — upload limits, temp file location.
  • 298. Reading the request body twice Important — why it fails, and ContentCachingRequestWrapper.
  • 299. Rate limiting / brute-force protection Important — filter-level or gateway-level; Bucket4j or Resilience4j.
  • 300. Idempotency keys for POST Important — how clients retry safely.
  • 301. Spring Session Optional — sessions stored in Redis so multiple instances share them.
  • 302. Sending email (JavaMailSender) + templated emails Important.

spring-boot/concept-map/jpa-and-hibernat.html:
Checklist

  • 303. equals() and hashCode() on entities Core — [Certain] the most damaging quiet bug in Spring apps. Never use Lombok @Data/@EqualsAndHashCode on an entity; a generated ID is null before persist, so the object breaks inside HashSet and the persistence context.
  • 304. Lombok on entities in general Core — @ToString triggers lazy loading and can print your whole database. @Data generates setters you did not want.
  • 305. Inheritance strategies Important — SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, TABLE_PER_CLASS, and @MappedSuperclass. Different performance and schema shape.
  • 306. Composite keys Important — @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass.
  • 307. @ElementCollection Important — collections of value objects without a full entity.
  • 308. AttributeConverter Important — map a custom type (or an encrypted column) to a database column.
  • 309. Enum mapping Core — EnumType.STRING, always. ORDINAL breaks the moment someone reorders the enum.
  • 310. getReferenceById vs findById Important — a lazy proxy versus a real select; useful for setting a foreign key without loading the row.
  • 311. save() on an existing entity Important — it is a merge, and often an extra select you did not need. Dirty checking usually makes save() unnecessary.
  • 312. Batch inserts and saveAll performance Important — needs hibernate.jdbc.batch_size and an ID strategy that does not force a select per row.
  • 313. ID generation strategies Core — IDENTITY disables batching, SEQUENCE allows it, UUIDs cost index locality.
  • 314. Second-level cache & query cache Optional — powerful and easy to misuse.
  • 315. Soft deletes Important — @SQLDelete, @SQLRestriction, and why a deleted flag complicates every query.
  • 316. Flush modes and when Hibernate writes Important — before a query, before commit; explains surprising SQL ordering.
  • 317. open-in-view Core — Boot enables it by default; it hides LazyInitializationException and holds connections during view rendering. [Likely] you should turn it off and fix the real cause.
  • 318. Reading the generated SQL Core — show-sql, formatted SQL, statistics, or a tool like p6spy. You cannot tune what you cannot see.
  • 319. Connection pool sizing Core — bigger is not better; pool size interacts with DB max connections and thread count.
  • 320. Read replicas & routing datasources Optional — sending reads elsewhere.
  • 321. Multi-tenancy Optional — schema-per-tenant, discriminator column, database-per-tenant.
  • 322. Testing SQL against the real database Core — H2 accepts SQL that Postgres rejects. This is why Testcontainers exists.

  • 351. Reading a Spring stack trace Core — find the last line that belongs to your code; ignore the 60 framework frames above it.

spring-boot/concept-map/the-trap-list-bu.title: I. The Trap List — bugs that compile, pass tests, and break in production

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/the-trap-list-bu.html:
Checklist

Read this section twice. [Likely] you will meet at least six of these personally.

  • 357. Self-invocation kills @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize — calling this.method() bypasses the proxy. Silent, no error.
  • 358. Checked exceptions do not roll back by default.
  • 359. Mutable state in a singleton bean — works locally with one user, corrupts data under load.
  • 360. Field injection hides missing dependencies and makes plain unit tests impossible.
  • 361. @Transactional on a method that calls an external HTTP API — you hold a DB connection while waiting on the network.
  • 362. No timeout on an HTTP client — one slow dependency exhausts your threads and takes the whole service down.
  • 363. N+1 queries — fine with 10 rows in dev, fatal with 100,000 in prod.
  • 364. EAGER fetching everywhere — one query pulls half the database.
  • 365. ddl-auto=update in production — silent schema drift, no rollback, eventual data loss.
  • 366. Exposing entities directly as API responses — leaks fields, breaks the API on every schema change, causes lazy-loading errors during serialization.
  • 367. Lombok @Data on JPA entities — see item 303.
  • 368. @Scheduled job running on every instance — the job executes N times when you scale out.
  • 369. Cache without an eviction strategy — memory leak, or stale data forever.
  • 370. Retrying a non-idempotent call — duplicate charges, duplicate orders.
  • 371. Storing local time instead of UTC — breaks at the daylight-saving boundary.
  • 372. Secrets in application.properties committed to git.
  • 373. permitAll() placed after a broader rule — order in the security chain matters; you can open or lock everything by accident.
  • 374. CSRF disabled "to make it work" without understanding whether you are cookie-based or token-based.
  • 375. Blocking call inside a reactive chain — destroys the event loop and the whole point of WebFlux.
  • 376. Default thread pool used for @Async — unbounded queue, hidden memory growth.
  • 377. Catching Exception and logging it without rethrowing — the transaction commits a half-finished state.
  • 378. open-in-view masking a design problem — see item 317.
  • 379. Testing with H2 while running Postgres — different SQL dialect, different behaviour, false confidence.
  • 380. Connection pool too small (or far too large) — queueing at the pool looks exactly like a slow database.

spring-boot/concept-map/beliefs-to-unlea.title: J. Beliefs to unlearn

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

prev.title: I. The Trap List — bugs that compile, pass tests, and break in production

next.title: L. Appendix — everything I deliberately left out (and why)

spring-boot/concept-map/beliefs-to-unlea.html:
Checklist

  • 381. "Spring Boot replaced Spring." — No. Boot is configuration and packaging on top of the same Spring container. [Certain]
  • 382. "@Service, @Component and @Repository do different things." — Almost nothing differs technically; only @Repository adds exception translation. The rest is intent. [Certain]
  • 383. "Singleton scope means the Singleton pattern." — It means one instance per container, not per JVM. [Certain]
  • 384. "Annotations are magic." — They are metadata. A BeanPostProcessor or proxy does the actual work. Once you accept this, the framework stops being mysterious. [Certain]
  • 385. "Reactive is faster." — It gives higher concurrency per thread, not lower latency, and it costs you debuggability. With virtual threads, most apps do not need it. [Likely]
  • 386. "Microservices are the professional choice." — They trade code complexity for operational and distributed-systems complexity. Most teams under ~30 engineers are better off with a modular monolith. [Likely]
  • 387. "Spring Data JPA means I do not need SQL." — The opposite. It generates SQL you are responsible for. [Certain]
  • 388. "If it works locally it works in production." — Concurrency, data volume, network failure and time zones are the four things your laptop hides from you. [Certain]

spring-boot/concept-map/appendix-everyth.html:
Checklist

These are real, but they are edge modules. Do not open any of them until a project forces you to. Listed for completeness so you stop wondering what is missing.

  • 389. Spring Data JDBC Important — the one genuine omission. A simpler alternative to JPA: no persistence context, no lazy loading, no dirty checking. Aggregate-based. Worth knowing that it exists as the "JPA is too much magic" option.
  • 390. Spring Retry Optional — @Retryable, @Recover. Older and simpler than Resilience4j.
  • 391. Spring Cloud Stream Optional — a binder abstraction so your code does not know if it is Kafka or Rabbit.
  • 392. Spring Cloud Function Optional — write a Function<T,R> and deploy it as an HTTP endpoint or a serverless function.
  • 393. Spring Cloud Task Optional — short-lived jobs.
  • 394. Spring Cloud Kubernetes Optional — config maps as property sources, discovery via the K8s API.
  • 395. Spring Web Services Optional — SOAP. Only if you touch enterprise or government systems.
  • 396. Spring Statemachine Optional — formal state machines as beans.
  • 397. JMX support Optional — exposing beans as managed MBeans. Mostly replaced by Actuator.
  • 398. JNDI lookup Optional — legacy app-server integration.
  • 399. Spring Boot Loader internals Optional — how a nested jar actually boots.
  • 400. CDS / AppCDS Optional — class data sharing to cut startup time without going native.
  • 401. Project CRaC (checkpoint & restore) Optional — snapshot a warmed-up JVM and restore it in milliseconds.
  • 402. Spring's TaskScheduler / TaskDecorator Optional — lower-level scheduling and context propagation onto worker threads.
  • 403. @ConfigurationPropertiesBinding and custom converters for config Optional.
  • 404. @ServletComponentScan Optional — registering plain servlet-API filters and servlets.
  • 405. Groovy / Spring Boot CLI Optional — rarely used today.

This list is now closed. Anything beyond item 405 is a specific library's documentation, not a Spring concept.
