spring-boot/concept-map/phase-00-prerequ.html:
Checklist

  • 1. JVM, JDK, JRE, classpath Core — what runs your code, and how Java finds classes at runtime.
  • 2. Build tools (Maven / Gradle) Core — dependencies, build lifecycle, pom.xml / build.gradle, transitive dependencies.
  • 3. Java annotations Core — what @Something actually is: metadata on code, readable at runtime.
  • 4. Reflection & classloading (basic idea) Core — how a framework can create objects and call methods it never saw at compile time. This is the engine under Spring.
  • 5. Interfaces & "program to an interface" Core — why depending on an interface instead of a concrete class makes swapping and testing possible.
  • 6. Core design patterns Core — Singleton, Factory, Proxy, Template Method, Strategy, Observer, Decorator. Spring is these patterns wearing annotations.
  • 7. Servlet, Servlet container, filter chain Core — the layer Spring MVC sits on top of.
  • 8. HTTP fundamentals Core — methods, status codes, headers, body, content types, statelessness.
  • 9. JSON & serialization Core — object ⇄ text, and why field names matter.
  • 10. SQL & relational basics Core — tables, joins, indexes, transactions. Needed long before JPA.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-01-the-ioc.title: Phase 1 — The IoC Container (the true core of Spring)

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

prev.title: Phase 0 — Prerequisites (Spring will feel like magic without these)

next.title: Phase 2 — Bean Lifecycle, Scope, Extension Points

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-01-the-ioc.html:
Checklist

  • 11. IoC (Inversion of Control) Core — you stop calling new; the framework creates and connects objects for you. Control is inverted from your code to the container.
  • 12. DI (Dependency Injection) Core — the concrete technique that implements IoC: dependencies are handed to an object from outside.
  • 13. Why IoC exists Core — loose coupling, easier testing, replaceable implementations, central configuration.
  • 14. Bean Core — any object created and managed by the Spring container.
  • 15. IoC container Core — the thing that reads config, builds beans, wires them, manages their life.
  • 16. BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext Core — BeanFactory = minimal container; ApplicationContext = BeanFactory + events, i18n, resource loading, auto post-processing.
  • 17. BeanDefinition Important — the recipe of a bean (class, scope, dependencies) before the object exists. Spring reads definitions first, creates objects later.
  • 18. Configuration metadata: annotations vs Java config vs XML Core — three ways to tell the container what beans exist. Modern default: annotations + Java config.
  • 19. Component scanning (@ComponentScan) Core — Spring walks your packages and registers annotated classes as beans.
  • 20. Stereotype annotations Core — @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller. Technically almost the same; they express intent (and @Repository adds exception translation).
  • 21. @Configuration + @Bean Core — define beans by writing a factory method. Needed for third-party classes you cannot annotate.
  • 22. Full vs lite @Configuration (proxyBeanMethods) Important — with full mode, calling one @Bean method from another returns the same singleton, not a new object.
  • 23. @Autowired Core — "give me a bean of this type".
  • 24. Constructor vs setter vs field injection Core — constructor is the recommended one: immutable, no hidden nulls, testable without Spring. Field injection is convenient and bad.
  • 25. Injection resolution rules Core — by type first, then by name/qualifier when several candidates match.
  • 26. @Qualifier Core — pick a specific bean when many of the same type exist.
  • 27. @Primary Core — mark the default winner among candidates.
  • 28. Injecting collections and maps of beans Important — List<Validator> gives you every implementation; a powerful plugin pattern.
  • 29. @Resource, @Inject, JSR-330 Optional — alternative standard annotations and how they differ from @Autowired.
  • 30. Optional, ObjectProvider, @Autowired(required=false) Important — handling a dependency that may not exist.
  • 31. Circular dependencies Core — A needs B, B needs A. Why constructor injection makes this fail loudly, and why that failure is a design signal.
  • 32. @Lazy Important — create the bean on first use instead of at startup.
  • 33. @DependsOn Optional — force creation order when there is a hidden dependency.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-02-bean-li.title: Phase 2 — Bean Lifecycle, Scope, Extension Points

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

prev.title: Phase 1 — The IoC Container (the true core of Spring)

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-02-bean-li.html:
Checklist

  • 34. Bean lifecycle overview Core — instantiate → populate dependencies → aware callbacks → post-process before init → init → post-process after init → in use → destroy.
  • 35. @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy Core — run code after wiring, and before shutdown.
  • 36. InitializingBean / DisposableBean Important — the interface-based version (couples you to Spring, so prefer the annotations).
  • 37. @Bean(initMethod, destroyMethod) Important — lifecycle hooks for classes you don't own.
  • 38. *Aware interfaces Important — ApplicationContextAware, BeanNameAware, EnvironmentAware: ask the container about itself.
  • 39. BeanPostProcessor Important — intercept every bean after creation. This is how AOP, @Autowired, @Async etc. are actually implemented.
  • 40. BeanFactoryPostProcessor Important — change bean definitions before any object is created.
  • 41. BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor Optional — register brand-new bean definitions programmatically.
  • 42. Scope: singleton Core — one instance per container (the default). Not the Singleton pattern; it is per-container.
  • 43. Scope: prototype Core — new instance on every request; Spring does not manage its destruction.
  • 44. Web scopes Important — request, session, application, websocket.
  • 45. Scoped proxies Important — how a short-lived bean can be injected into a singleton without breaking.
  • 46. Singleton + mutable state = bug Core — the single most common beginner mistake. Beans must be stateless or thread-safe.
  • 47. FactoryBean<T> Optional — a bean whose job is producing another bean; used heavily inside Spring itself.
  • 48. ApplicationContext refresh sequence Important — the ordered startup steps of the container. Read it once; it explains a lot of "why does X happen before Y".
  • 49. Application events (ApplicationEvent, @EventListener) Important — in-process publish/subscribe for decoupling components.
  • 50. Built-in events Important — ApplicationReadyEvent, ContextRefreshedEvent, ContextClosedEvent.
  • 51. Async events & @TransactionalEventListener Optional — fire after commit, or on another thread.
  • 52. Lifecycle / SmartLifecycle Optional — start/stop components in a controlled order.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-03-configu.title: Phase 3 — Configuration & Environment

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

prev.title: Phase 2 — Bean Lifecycle, Scope, Extension Points

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-03-configu.html:
Checklist

  • 53. Externalized configuration Core — never hardcode values that change between environments.
  • 54. Environment abstraction Core — the unified view over all sources of properties.
  • 55. PropertySource Important — one source of properties (file, env vars, command line, system properties).
  • 56. Property precedence order Core — command line > env vars > profile files > application file > defaults. Know this or you will lose hours.
  • 57. @Value Core — inject a single property into a field or parameter.
  • 58. SpEL (Spring Expression Language) Important — small expression language usable inside annotations: #{...}, ${...}, operators, bean references.
  • 59. @ConfigurationProperties Core — bind a whole group of properties into a typed object. Better than scattering @Value everywhere.
  • 60. Relaxed binding Important — my-prop, myProp, MY_PROP all bind to the same field.
  • 61. Validating configuration Important — @Validated on config classes so bad config fails at startup, not at 3am.
  • 62. Profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active) Core — different beans and config per environment (dev, test, prod).
  • 63. application.properties vs application.yml Core — same power, different syntax; yaml handles nesting and lists better.
  • 64. Profile-specific files & config groups Important — application-dev.yml, spring.config.import, config trees.
  • 65. @Conditional and @ConditionalOnX Core — create a bean only if some condition holds. This is the mechanism auto-configuration is built on.
  • 66. @Import, ImportSelector, ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar Optional — pull configuration classes in programmatically; how @EnableX annotations work.
  • 67. Resource abstraction (Resource, ResourceLoader) Important — read classpath files, filesystem files and URLs the same way.
  • 68. XML configuration Optional — legacy, but you will meet it in old codebases.
  • 69. Secrets handling Important — env vars, vaults, config server; never in git.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-04-aop.title: Phase 4 — AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming)

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-04-aop.html:
Checklist

  • 70. Cross-cutting concern Core — logging, security, transactions, caching: logic that repeats everywhere and belongs to no single class.
  • 71. AOP core idea Core — extract that repeated logic and weave it in around your methods automatically.
  • 72. Vocabulary Core — aspect, join point, pointcut, advice, target, proxy, weaving. Learn these six words properly.
  • 73. @Aspect + @EnableAspectJAutoProxy Important — declaring an aspect.
  • 74. Advice types Important — @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Around.
  • 75. Pointcut expressions Important — execution(), within(), @annotation(), and combining them.
  • 76. Proxies: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB Core — interface-based vs subclass-based. Explains why final and private methods are not advised.
  • 77. Self-invocation problem Core — calling this.method() skips the proxy, so @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async silently do nothing. Extremely common bug.
  • 78. Aspect ordering (@Order) Important — which aspect wraps which.
  • 79. Spring AOP vs full AspectJ Optional — proxy-based (method calls only) vs bytecode weaving (everything).
  • 80. Where Spring itself uses AOP Core — transactions, security, caching, retry, async, validation. Understanding this de-mystifies half the framework.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-05-spring-.title: Phase 5 — Spring Boot Fundamentals

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

next.title: Phase 6 — Spring MVC & Building REST APIs

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-05-spring-.html:
Checklist

  • 81. What Boot adds to Spring Core — opinionated defaults, auto-configuration, starters, embedded server, production tooling. Boot is not a different framework.
  • 82. @SpringBootApplication Core — it is three annotations in one: @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.
  • 83. SpringApplication.run() Core — what actually happens at startup, step by step.
  • 84. Auto-configuration Core — Boot guesses your setup from the classpath and existing beans, and configures beans conditionally. Backs off the moment you define your own.
  • 85. AutoConfiguration.imports Important — the registry file listing all auto-config classes (older versions used spring.factories).
  • 86. Excluding auto-configuration Important — when Boot's guess is wrong.
  • 87. Starters Core — curated dependency bundles (spring-boot-starter-web, -data-jpa, -security...).
  • 88. Dependency management / BOM Core — the parent POM pins compatible versions so you don't play version roulette.
  • 89. Embedded server Core — Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow inside your jar; no external app server needed.
  • 90. Executable fat jar & layered jars Important — how packaging works and why layering helps Docker caching.
  • 91. CommandLineRunner / ApplicationRunner Important — run code once after startup.
  • 92. The auto-configuration report Core — --debug shows which configs matched and which did not. Your best debugging tool.
  • 93. Failure analyzers Important — why Boot's startup errors are readable.
  • 94. DevTools Important — restart on change, live reload, dev-only property defaults.
  • 95. Spring Initializr Important — project generation; know what each checkbox pulls in.
  • 96. Writing your own auto-configuration / starter Optional — the real test of whether you understood phases 1–5.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-06-spring-.title: Phase 6 — Spring MVC & Building REST APIs

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-06-spring-.html:
Checklist

  • 97. DispatcherServlet (front controller) Core — one entry point that routes every request.
  • 98. Full request lifecycle Core — filter → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → HandlerAdapter → interceptors → controller → return value handler → message converter → response. Memorize this shape.
  • 99. HandlerMapping / HandlerAdapter Important — how a URL finds its method and how that method is invoked.
  • 100. @Controller vs @RestController Core — view names vs response bodies.
  • 101. @RequestMapping and shortcuts Core — @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @PatchMapping, @DeleteMapping.
  • 102. Reading input Core — @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue, @RequestBody, @ModelAttribute.
  • 103. @ResponseBody and ResponseEntity Core — controlling body, status and headers.
  • 104. HttpMessageConverter + Jackson Core — how a Java object becomes JSON. Learn @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonFormat, custom serializers.
  • 105. Content negotiation Important — Accept header decides the representation.
  • 106. DTOs vs entities Core — never expose your database entities directly through the API. Mapping layer (manual or MapStruct).
  • 107. Bean Validation Core — @Valid, @NotNull, @Size, @Email, groups, @Validated on services.
  • 108. Custom validators / custom constraint annotations Important.
  • 109. Exception handling Core — @ExceptionHandler, @ControllerAdvice, global error shape, ResponseStatusException.
  • 110. ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) Important — the standard error body format.
  • 111. Filters vs Interceptors vs Aspects Core — three levels to hook in; know which one to pick.
  • 112. HandlerInterceptor Important — pre/post handle hooks.
  • 113. CORS Core — why the browser blocks your frontend and how @CrossOrigin / global config fix it.
  • 114. File upload / download Important — MultipartFile, streaming responses.
  • 115. Static resources & resource handlers Important.
  • 116. Server-side views Optional — Thymeleaf, Model, ModelAndView, ViewResolver. Skip if you build APIs only.
  • 117. Async MVC Important — Callable, DeferredResult, StreamingResponseBody, SSE.
  • 118. WebMvcConfigurer Important — the customization hook for converters, interceptors, CORS, formatters.
  • 119. REST design Core — resource naming, correct status codes, idempotency, pagination, filtering.
  • 120. API versioning Important — URL, header or media-type strategies and their trade-offs.
  • 121. OpenAPI / Swagger (springdoc) Important — generated, always-current API documentation.
  • 122. HATEOAS Optional — hypermedia links; rarely used in practice, good to recognise.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-07-calling.title: Phase 7 — Calling Other Services (HTTP clients)

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

prev.title: Phase 6 — Spring MVC & Building REST APIs

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-07-calling.html:
Checklist

  • 123. RestTemplate Important — the classic blocking client; maintenance mode but everywhere in existing code.
  • 124. RestClient Core — the modern, fluent, blocking client. Default choice today.
  • 125. WebClient Important — non-blocking/reactive client; also usable in blocking apps.
  • 126. Declarative HTTP interfaces (@HttpExchange) Important — define a Java interface, Spring implements the calls.
  • 127. Timeouts, connection pools, error decoding Core — the parts everyone forgets until production.
  • 128. OpenFeign Optional — declarative client from Spring Cloud.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-08-data-ac.title: Phase 8 — Data Access & Transactions

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

next.title: Phase 9 — Testing (learn this earlier than you want to)

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-08-data-ac.html:
Checklist

  • 129. DataSource and connection pooling (HikariCP) Core — connections are expensive; pool size is a real tuning parameter.
  • 130. JdbcTemplate Core — plain SQL without boilerplate.
  • 131. JdbcClient Important — the modern fluent replacement for JdbcTemplate.
  • 132. RowMapper / ResultSetExtractor Important — result set → object.
  • 133. NamedParameterJdbcTemplate Important — named placeholders instead of ?.
  • 134. DataAccessException hierarchy & @Repository Important — vendor SQL exceptions translated into one consistent hierarchy.
  • 135. Transaction fundamentals Core — ACID, commit, rollback; what a transaction actually guarantees.
  • 136. @Transactional Core — declarative transaction boundaries.
  • 137. Propagation Core — REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, NESTED, SUPPORTS, MANDATORY, NEVER, NOT_SUPPORTED.
  • 138. Isolation levels Important — read uncommitted → serializable; dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read.
  • 139. Rollback rules Core — by default only unchecked exceptions roll back. Checked exceptions do not. Surprising and important.
  • 140. readOnly = true Important — hints and real optimizations.
  • 141. @Transactional pitfalls Core — self-invocation, private methods, wrong layer, transaction spanning HTTP calls, lazy loading after commit.
  • 142. PlatformTransactionManager / TransactionTemplate Important — the programmatic API under the annotation.
  • 143. ORM & JPA vs Hibernate Core — JPA is the specification, Hibernate is the implementation, Spring Data JPA is the convenience layer on top.
  • 144. Entity mapping Core — @Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue, @Column, @Enumerated, @Embeddable.
  • 145. EntityManager & the persistence context Core — the first-level cache; the single biggest source of "why did my object change by itself".
  • 146. Entity states Core — transient, managed, detached, removed.
  • 147. Dirty checking & flush Core — changing a managed entity writes to the DB without any save().
  • 148. Relationships Core — @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @OneToOne, owning side, mappedBy, cascade, orphan removal.
  • 149. Fetch types: LAZY vs EAGER Core — default to LAZY, always.
  • 150. N+1 select problem Core — the classic performance killer; fix with fetch joins, @EntityGraph, or batch size.
  • 151. LazyInitializationException Core — accessing a lazy field outside the session; and why "open session in view" is a bad fix.
  • 152. Spring Data JPA repositories Core — Repository, CrudRepository, JpaRepository; how an interface with no code gets an implementation.
  • 153. Derived query methods Core — findByEmailAndActiveTrue(...) parsed from the method name.
  • 154. @Query, JPQL and native SQL Core.
  • 155. @Modifying + queries that write Important — and why they need a transaction and can desync the persistence context.
  • 156. Pagination & sorting Core — Pageable, Page, Slice, and why Page costs an extra count query.
  • 157. Projections & DTO queries Core — select only what you need, interface or constructor projections.
  • 158. Specification / Criteria API / QueryDSL Important — dynamic queries built at runtime.
  • 159. Auditing Important — @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedBy, @EnableJpaAuditing.
  • 160. Locking Important — optimistic (@Version) vs pessimistic; how to avoid lost updates.
  • 161. Schema migration (Flyway / Liquibase) Core — versioned SQL migrations. ddl-auto=update is not a production strategy.
  • 162. Multiple data sources Optional — separate config, transaction managers, and the pain that follows.
  • 163. Spring Data for NoSQL Optional — MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Cassandra; same repository idea, different store.
  • 164. Redis as cache and as store Important.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-09-testing.title: Phase 9 — Testing (learn this earlier than you want to)

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-09-testing.html:
Checklist

  • 165. Unit vs integration vs end-to-end Core — what each one buys you and costs you.
  • 166. JUnit 5 + AssertJ Core — lifecycle annotations, parameterized tests, readable assertions.
  • 167. Mockito Core — mock, when/thenReturn, verify, argument captors.
  • 168. Testing without Spring Core — with constructor injection most service tests need no container at all. Fastest tests you will ever write.
  • 169. @SpringBootTest Core — full context test; web environments (MOCK, RANDOM_PORT).
  • 170. Test slices Core — @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest, @JdbcTest. Load only the part you test.
  • 171. MockMvc Core — call controllers without a real server.
  • 172. @MockitoBean / @MockBean Core — replace a bean in the context with a mock.
  • 173. TestRestTemplate / WebTestClient Important — real HTTP against a running test server.
  • 174. @TestConfiguration Important — test-only beans.
  • 175. Test context caching & @DirtiesContext Important — why your suite is slow and how to keep it fast.
  • 176. @ActiveProfiles, test properties, @TestPropertySource Important.
  • 177. Testcontainers Core — real Postgres/Kafka/Redis in Docker for tests. H2 lies to you about SQL behaviour.
  • 178. Spring Security test support Important — @WithMockUser, security-aware MockMvc.
  • 179. WireMock / MockWebServer Important — faking external HTTP services.
  • 180. Test data strategy Important — builders, fixtures, cleanup, transactional rollback in tests.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-10-spring-.title: Phase 10 — Spring Security

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

prev.title: Phase 9 — Testing (learn this earlier than you want to)

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-10-spring-.html:
Checklist

  • 181. Authentication vs authorization Core — who you are vs what you may do.
  • 182. The security filter chain Core — security is a chain of servlet filters running before your controller. Everything else follows from this.
  • 183. SecurityFilterChain bean configuration Core — the modern lambda DSL config style (WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is gone).
  • 184. SecurityContext & Authentication Core — where the current user lives and how to read it.
  • 185. UserDetails / UserDetailsService Core — loading users from your own store.
  • 186. PasswordEncoder / BCrypt Core — never store plain or simply hashed passwords.
  • 187. AuthenticationManager / AuthenticationProvider Important — the pluggable authentication engine.
  • 188. HTTP Basic and form login Important.
  • 189. Sessions vs stateless (token) authentication Core — and why REST APIs usually go stateless.
  • 190. CSRF Core — what the attack is, why it matters for cookies, why it is disabled for token APIs.
  • 191. Authorization rules by URL Core — requestMatchers().hasRole(), order matters.
  • 192. Method security Core — @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured, SpEL in expressions.
  • 193. Roles vs authorities Core — the ROLE_ prefix trap.
  • 194. JWT Core — structure, signature, expiry, refresh tokens, and why you cannot revoke a plain JWT easily.
  • 195. OAuth2 & OpenID Connect concepts Important — grant types, tokens, the four roles.
  • 196. OAuth2 client (login with Google/GitHub) Important.
  • 197. Resource server (validating tokens) Important.
  • 198. Authorization server Optional — issuing tokens yourself.
  • 199. CORS + security interaction Important — the order of filters explains most "it works with curl but not the browser" bugs.
  • 200. Security headers & common attacks Important — XSS, clickjacking, HSTS, injection, mass assignment.
  • 201. Custom filters and entry points Important — where to insert your own logic in the chain.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-11-product.title: Phase 11 — Production: Observability & Operations

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-11-product.html:
Checklist

  • 202. Spring Boot Actuator Core — health, info, metrics, env, mappings, loggers endpoints.
  • 203. Securing and exposing actuator endpoints Core — do not open /actuator/env to the world.
  • 204. Health indicators, liveness & readiness Core — what Kubernetes actually probes.
  • 205. Micrometer & metrics Important — counters, gauges, timers, @Timed.
  • 206. Prometheus + Grafana Important — scraping and dashboards.
  • 207. Distributed tracing Important — Micrometer Tracing / OpenTelemetry, trace and span IDs across services.
  • 208. Logging Core — SLF4J + Logback, levels, patterns, MDC, correlation IDs, structured JSON logs.
  • 209. Graceful shutdown Important — finish in-flight requests before dying.
  • 210. Startup performance Important — lazy initialization, class data sharing, what actually costs time.
  • 211. AOT processing & GraalVM native images Optional — near-instant startup, at the cost of reflection restrictions.
  • 212. Virtual threads (Loom) Important — high concurrency without going reactive.
  • 213. Containerizing Spring Boot Core — Dockerfile, layered jars, buildpacks, JVM memory flags in containers.
  • 214. Twelve-factor app principles Important — config, logs, stateless processes, disposability.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-12-async-s.title: Phase 12 — Async, Scheduling, Caching, Resilience

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-12-async-s.html:
Checklist

  • 215. @Async and TaskExecutor Core — run a method on another thread; needs @EnableAsync and a properly sized pool.
  • 216. CompletableFuture in Spring Important — returning async results.
  • 217. Thread pool sizing & exhaustion Important — the default pool is rarely what you want.
  • 218. @Scheduled Core — fixed rate, fixed delay, cron expressions.
  • 219. Scheduling in multiple instances Important — the job runs N times unless you add locking (ShedLock, DB lock, leader election).

  • 222. Resilience4j Important — retry, circuit breaker, rate limiter, bulkhead, time limiter.

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-13-messagi.title: Phase 13 — Messaging, Batch, Integration

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-13-messagi.html:
Checklist

crumbs.title: Spring & Spring Boot — Complete Concept Map

spring-boot/concept-map/phase-14-reactiv.html:
Checklist

spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.title: 4.1 The full bean lifecycle, in exact order
spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.html:
Checklist

  • 4.1.1 Instantiation — the constructor runs
  • 4.1.2 Populate properties — dependency injection happens (setter/field injection specifically; constructor injection happened during instantiation itself)
  • 4.1.3 BeanNameAware.setBeanName() — if implemented, the bean learns its own name
  • 4.1.4 BeanFactoryAware.setBeanFactory() / ApplicationContextAware.setApplicationContext() — if implemented, the bean gets a handle back to the container
  • 4.1.5 BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization() — runs for every bean, before init callbacks (this is where @PostConstruct processing and many proxy-wrapping mechanisms hook in)
  • 4.1.6 @PostConstruct — the standard (JSR-250) annotation for post-injection initialization logic
  • 4.1.7 InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() — the Spring-specific interface equivalent of @PostConstruct
  • 4.1.8 Custom init-method (XML) / @Bean(initMethod = "...") — a third way to hook initialization, useful for third-party classes you can't annotate
  • 4.1.9 Why @PostConstruct is generally preferred over InitializingBean in modern code — no Spring-specific interface coupling
  • 4.1.10 BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization() — runs after init callbacks; this is exactly where AOP proxies get created and returned in place of the raw bean (the single most important line connecting Stage 4 to Stage 5)
  • 4.1.11 Bean is now fully ready and in use
  • 4.1.12 DisposableBean.destroy() / @PreDestroy / custom destroy-method — shutdown callbacks, mirroring the init callbacks, fired during container shutdown (for singleton-scoped beans only — see 4.2)

spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.title: 4.2 Bean scopes

prev.title: 4.1 The full bean lifecycle, in exact order

spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.html:
Checklist

  • 4.2.1 singleton (default) — exactly one instance per Spring container
  • 4.2.2 Why "singleton" here means "one per container," not "one per JVM" — a genuinely important distinction in multi-context applications
  • 4.2.3 prototype — a new instance every time the bean is requested
  • 4.2.4 Critical gotcha: Spring does not manage the full lifecycle of prototype beans — no automatic destruction callback, the container "hands it off" and forgets it, cleanup is the caller's responsibility
  • 4.2.5 request — one instance per HTTP request (web-aware contexts only)
  • 4.2.6 session — one instance per HTTP session
  • 4.2.7 application — one instance per ServletContext
  • 4.2.8 websocket — one instance per WebSocket session
  • 4.2.9 Custom scopes — implementing Scope yourself for a niche lifecycle need (rare, know it's possible)

spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.title: 4.3 The singleton-injecting-prototype problem
spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.html:
Checklist

  • 4.3.1 The core problem: a singleton bean injects a prototype dependency once, at singleton construction time — so it effectively becomes a singleton too, defeating the point of prototype scope
  • 4.3.2 Fix 1 — ObjectProvider<T> / Provider<T> injected into the singleton, calling .getObject() each time a fresh prototype instance is actually needed
  • 4.3.3 Fix 2 — @Lookup method injection: an abstract method Spring overrides at runtime to return a fresh prototype bean on each call
  • 4.3.4 Fix 3 — scoped proxy (proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) on the prototype bean definition, so the singleton holds a proxy that resolves to a fresh instance per invocation
  • 4.3.5 Why this exact same "singleton holding a stale reference" shape reappears with request/session scoped beans injected into singletons — and why scoped proxies are the standard fix there too

spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.title: 4.4 `Aware` interfaces (the full family, beyond 4.1.4)
spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.html:

  • 4.4.3 ApplicationEventPublisherAware
  • 4.4.4 MessageSourceAware
  • 4.4.5 The general pattern: implementing an *Aware interface is how a bean opts into receiving a container-provided capability during initialization, without needing full DI for it
  • 4.4.6 Why reaching for *Aware interfaces directly in application code is rare and usually a sign you actually just wanted a normal injected dependency instead — these exist mostly for framework-level code

  • 4.5.2 ContextRefreshedEvent — the container has finished initializing, all singletons are ready
  • 4.5.3 ContextStartedEvent / ContextStoppedEvent / ContextClosedEvent

  • 4.5.5 @EventListener annotation — the modern, method-level alternative to implementing ApplicationListener<T>
  • 4.5.6 Publishing your own custom application events with ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent()
  • 4.5.7 Synchronous by default — an event listener runs in the same thread as the publisher, blocking it, unless made @Async

spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.title: 4.6 Circular dependency resolution mechanics (the deeper cut)
spring-boot/bean-configuration-and-lifec.html:
Checklist

  • 4.6.1 How Spring resolves setter/field-based circular dependencies via early bean references exposed through a three-tier cache (singleton cache, early singleton cache, singleton factory cache) — the actual mechanism behind the "it just works for setter injection" behavior
  • 4.6.2 Why constructor injection cannot be resolved this way — the object literally doesn't exist yet to hand out an early reference, hence the fail-fast BeanCurrentlyInCreationException

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-1-why-aop-exist.title: 5.1 Why AOP exists
spring-boot/spring-aop/5-1-why-aop-exist.html:
Checklist

  • 5.1.1 Cross-cutting concerns — logic that applies across many unrelated classes (logging, transactions, security, caching) and doesn't belong inside any single one of them
  • 5.1.2 The problem without AOP: the same boilerplate (try/catch logging, transaction begin/commit, permission checks) copy-pasted into every method that needs it
  • 5.1.3 AOP's answer: define the cross-cutting logic once, declare where it applies, let the framework weave it in
  • 5.1.4 AOP terminology, precisely:
    • Aspect — the module containing the cross-cutting logic
    • Advice — the actual action taken (the code that runs)
    • Join point — a point during program execution where advice could apply (in Spring AOP, always a method execution)
    • Pointcut — an expression that selects which join points get the advice
    • Weaving — the process of linking aspects with target objects to create the advised object
    • Target object — the object being advised
    • AOP proxy — the object actually created to implement the aspect's behavior

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-2-spring-aop-vs.title: 5.2 Spring AOP vs full AspectJ

next.title: 5.3 How the proxy is actually built

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-2-spring-aop-vs.html:
Checklist

  • 5.2.1 Spring AOP is proxy-based and runtime-woven — no special compiler, no bytecode manipulation at build time
  • 5.2.2 Full AspectJ supports compile-time weaving, load-time weaving, and field/constructor join points — a strictly more powerful but heavier tool
  • 5.2.3 The critical limitation of Spring AOP: it can only advise method executions on Spring-managed beans, called from outside the bean — not field access, not constructors, not internal calls
  • 5.2.4 This single limitation is the direct root cause of the self-invocation bug you already met twice (Security's @PreAuthorize, JPA's @Transactional) — now you know exactly why: an internal this.method() call never passes through the proxy at all
  • 5.2.5 When you'd actually reach for full AspectJ instead of Spring AOP: needing to advise object construction, static methods, or non-Spring-managed objects — rare in typical application code

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-3-how-the-proxy.title: 5.3 How the proxy is actually built
spring-boot/spring-aop/5-3-how-the-proxy.html:
Checklist

  • 5.3.1 JDK dynamic proxies — used when the target implements at least one interface; the proxy implements the same interface(s)
  • 5.3.2 CGLIB proxies — used when the target has no interface (or when explicitly forced); generates a runtime subclass of the target class
  • 5.3.3 spring.aop.proxy-target-class — forcing CGLIB proxying even when an interface exists (Spring Boot's default is true, meaning CGLIB is actually the more common case in Boot apps than people assume)
  • 5.3.4 Why CGLIB proxies require a non-final class and non-final methods — the subclassing mechanism can't override what's final
  • 5.3.5 Why CGLIB proxies need a default/no-arg constructor accessible in older versions (objenesis in modern Spring works around this, but it's worth knowing the historical constraint)
  • 5.3.6 ProxyFactory — the lower-level API that actually creates these proxies under the hood
  • 5.3.7 AopProxy interface and its two implementations (JdkDynamicAopProxy, CglibAopProxy)
  • 5.3.8 The proxy sits in front of the real bean in the container — every external caller talks to the proxy, which delegates to the real target after running advice

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-4-advice-types.title: 5.4 Advice types

prev.title: 5.3 How the proxy is actually built

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-4-advice-types.html:
Checklist

  • 5.4.1 @Before — runs before the join point, cannot prevent execution (unless it throws)
  • 5.4.2 @AfterReturning — runs after successful completion, can access the return value
  • 5.4.3 @AfterThrowing — runs if the method throws, can access the exception
  • 5.4.4 @After — runs regardless of outcome (the AOP equivalent of finally)
  • 5.4.5 @Around — wraps the entire join point; the only advice type that can control whether the method even runs, modify arguments, modify the return value, or suppress/replace an exception
  • 5.4.6 ProceedingJoinPoint.proceed() — the call inside @Around advice that actually invokes the target method (or the next advice in the chain)
  • 5.4.7 Why forgetting to call proceed() inside @Around advice silently skips the real method entirely — a very easy mistake when you're new to this
  • 5.4.8 JoinPoint — available to all advice types except @Around (which uses the more capable ProceedingJoinPoint), gives access to method signature, arguments, target

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-5-pointcut-expr.title: 5.5 Pointcut expressions
spring-boot/spring-aop/5-5-pointcut-expr.html:
Checklist

  • 5.5.1 @Pointcut — defining a reusable, named pointcut expression separately from advice
  • 5.5.2 execution(...) — the most common designator, matching method execution by signature pattern
  • 5.5.3 Reading an execution expression: execution(modifiers? return-type declaring-type? method-name(params) throws?)
  • 5.5.4 Wildcards: * for any single element, .. for any number of arguments or any package depth
  • 5.5.5 within(...) — matching all join points within a certain type or package, coarser than execution
  • 5.5.6 @annotation(...) — matching methods that carry a specific annotation, the mechanism behind building your own @LogExecutionTime-style custom annotations
  • 5.5.7 @within(...) / @target(...) — matching based on annotations present on the declaring class/target object
  • 5.5.8 args(...) — matching based on argument types at runtime
  • 5.5.9 bean(...) — matching by Spring bean name pattern
  • 5.5.10 Combining pointcuts with &&, ||, !
  • 5.5.11 Binding method arguments into advice parameters by name, so advice logic can inspect specific argument values directly

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-6-declaring-asp.html:

  • 5.6.1 @Aspect — marking a class as an aspect
  • 5.6.2 @Aspect classes must also be registered as Spring beans (@Component or a @Bean method) — being @Aspect alone doesn't register it
  • 5.6.3 @EnableAspectJAutoProxy — turning on annotation-driven AOP proxy creation (Spring Boot enables this automatically when spring-boot-starter-aop — or anything pulling it transitively — is present)
  • 5.6.4 XML-based aspect declaration — legacy, recognize it, don't write new code this way

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-7-where-this-co.title: 5.7 Where this connects to everything you've already learned

next.title: 5.8 Writing your own aspect (the exercise that cements this)

spring-boot/spring-aop/5-7-where-this-co.html:
Checklist

  • 5.7.1 @Transactional (JPA roadmap Stage 15) — implemented as @Around-style advice via TransactionInterceptor, itself just a specialized MethodInterceptor
  • 5.7.2 @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize (Security roadmap Stage 15) — implemented via AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor/AfterMethodInterceptor, the exact same underlying proxy machinery with different advice logic
  • 5.7.3 @Cacheable/@CacheEvict (Spring Cache abstraction) — same pattern again, caching-specific advice
  • 5.7.4 @Retryable (Spring Retry) — same pattern, retry-specific advice
  • 5.7.5 @Async — same pattern, delegates execution to a different thread instead of running inline
  • 5.7.6 The single unifying insight worth internalizing: Spring's declarative annotations are almost all just pre-built AOP aspects — once you understand this stage, none of them are magic anymore, they're all "some advice wrapped around a proxy"

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-1.html:
Checklist

  • 6.1.1 Front controller pattern — one entry point receiving all requests, delegating to the right handler, instead of many separate servlets
  • 6.1.2 DispatcherServlet — Spring MVC's implementation of the front controller pattern, itself just a HttpServlet
  • 6.1.3 How DispatcherServlet gets registered: web.xml in the old world, DispatcherServletAutoConfiguration registering it automatically in Spring Boot
  • 6.1.4 The relationship to Stage 4 of the Security roadmap restated precisely: servlet Filters run before the request ever reaches DispatcherServlet; everything in this stage happens after that filter chain
  • 6.1.5 DispatcherServlet's own internal ApplicationContext (the "web application context") vs the root context — a legacy multi-context distinction largely irrelevant in modern Spring Boot's single-context model, but worth recognizing in older tutorials

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-1.title: 6.10 Reactive web (bridge, not a repeat)
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-1.html:
Checklist

  • 6.10.1 @RestController methods returning Mono<T>/Flux<T> — Spring MVC can host reactive return types even in a non-WebFlux (servlet) app, though the servlet thread model doesn't gain true non-blocking behavior from this alone
  • 6.10.2 Full WebFlux (@EnableWebFluxSecurity-style reactive stack) is out of scope here — cross-reference the Security roadmap's Stage 16 for the reactive security angle specifically; this roadmap stays servlet-based

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-2.title: 6.2 The full request lifecycle, in exact order
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-2.html:
Checklist

  • 6.2.1 Request arrives at DispatcherServlet
  • 6.2.2 HandlerMapping — determines which handler method should process this request based on the URL/method/headers
  • 6.2.3 RequestMappingHandlerMapping — the concrete implementation that reads your @RequestMapping-family annotations to build this mapping
  • 6.2.4 HandlerAdapter — knows how to actually invoke the handler found above (different adapters exist for different handler types, though @Controller methods are by far the dominant case today)
  • 6.2.5 HandlerInterceptor — Spring MVC's own pre/post/after-completion hooks around handler invocation, distinct from and running after servlet Filters (compare directly against the Security roadmap's Filter vs Interceptor note in its Stage 4.6)
  • 6.2.6 Argument resolution — binding path variables, query params, request body, headers into your handler method's parameters (HandlerMethodArgumentResolver)
  • 6.2.7 The handler method executes, returns a value
  • 6.2.8 HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler — turns that return value into an actual response (this is where @ResponseBody and ResponseEntity handling live)
  • 6.2.9 ViewResolver — for traditional server-rendered apps, resolves a returned view name (e.g. "login") to an actual view (a Thymeleaf template, JSP, etc.)
  • 6.2.10 Response rendered and sent
  • 6.2.11 Exception handling short-circuits this normal flow at any point — covered fully in 6.6

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-3.title: 6.3 Controllers and request mapping

prev.title: 6.2 The full request lifecycle, in exact order

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-3.html:
Checklist

  • 6.3.1 @Controller (returns view names by default) vs @RestController (@Controller + @ResponseBody combined — every method's return value is written directly to the response body)
  • 6.3.2 @RequestMapping — the general-purpose base annotation
  • 6.3.3 @GetMapping/@PostMapping/@PutMapping/@PatchMapping/@DeleteMapping — HTTP-method-specific shorthand
  • 6.3.4 Class-level @RequestMapping("/api/users") combined with method-level paths
  • 6.3.5 Path variables: @PathVariable, including optional path variables and type conversion
  • 6.3.6 Query parameters: @RequestParam, required vs optional, default values
  • 6.3.7 Request headers: @RequestHeader
  • 6.3.8 Cookies: @CookieValue
  • 6.3.9 Request body: @RequestBody — deserializing JSON into a Java object via HttpMessageConverter (usually Jackson)
  • 6.3.10 @ResponseBody — the mirror of @RequestBody, serializing the return value
  • 6.3.11 ResponseEntity<T> — full control over status code, headers, and body together, vs a bare return type that only controls the body
  • 6.3.12 Content negotiation — how Spring MVC decides JSON vs XML vs other formats based on Accept headers and configured converters
  • 6.3.13 Matrix variables and less common binding annotations — know they exist, rarely needed in typical REST APIs

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-4.title: 6.4 `HttpMessageConverter`
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-4.html:
Checklist

  • 6.4.1 The interface responsible for turning HTTP request/response bodies into/from Java objects
  • 6.4.2 MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter — the default JSON converter, backed by Jackson
  • 6.4.3 How Spring Boot auto-configures the ObjectMapper and how to customize it (naming strategy, date formatting, null handling) without losing the auto-configured defaults
  • 6.4.4 StringHttpMessageConverter, ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter, FormHttpMessageConverter and other built-ins
  • 6.4.5 Registering a custom HttpMessageConverter for a non-standard format

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-5.title: 6.5 Validation
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-5.html:
Checklist

  • 6.5.1 Bean Validation (JSR-380/Jakarta Validation) — @NotNull, @Size, @Min/@Max, @Email, @Pattern, and the rest of the standard annotation set
  • 6.5.2 @Valid / @Validated on a @RequestBody parameter — triggering validation before the handler body runs
  • 6.5.3 The difference between @Valid (standard Bean Validation) and @Validated (Spring's variant, adds validation groups support)
  • 6.5.4 BindingResult — capturing validation errors instead of throwing immediately, when you want to handle them manually inside the method
  • 6.5.5 What happens without a BindingResult parameter present: a MethodArgumentNotValidException is thrown automatically (bridges into 6.6)
  • 6.5.6 Validation groups — applying different validation rules to the same class in different contexts (e.g., create vs update)
  • 6.5.7 Custom validator: implementing ConstraintValidator<Annotation, Type> for domain-specific rules the standard annotations can't express
  • 6.5.8 Method-level validation on service-layer beans (@Validated at the class level) — validation isn't only a web-layer concern

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-6.title: 6.6 Exception handling
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-6.html:
Checklist

  • 6.6.1 @ExceptionHandler — handling a specific exception type within one controller
  • 6.6.2 @ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice — applying exception handling globally across all controllers, instead of duplicating @ExceptionHandler methods everywhere
  • 6.6.3 Ordering multiple @ExceptionHandler methods for related exception types — most specific match wins
  • 6.6.4 Building a consistent error response body (cross-reference the Security roadmap's RFC 7807 application/problem+json recommendation)
  • 6.6.5 ResponseEntityExceptionHandler — Spring's own base class handling many built-in MVC exceptions consistently, extendable for your own global handler
  • 6.6.6 ProblemDetail (Spring 6+) — built-in RFC 7807 support, replacing a lot of hand-rolled error DTO boilerplate
  • 6.6.7 The critical scope limitation restated from the Security roadmap (8.6.7): @ControllerAdvice only catches exceptions thrown from within the DispatcherServlet's handler-invocation flow — it cannot catch exceptions thrown inside a servlet Filter, which runs entirely outside this mechanism
  • 6.6.8 Default Spring Boot error handling: BasicErrorController and the /error fallback endpoint when nothing else handles an exception
  • 6.6.9 Customizing the default error page/response (ErrorAttributes, custom ErrorController)

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-7.title: 6.7 Cross-cutting web concerns
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-7.html:
Checklist

  • 6.7.1 WebMvcConfigurer — the interface for customizing Spring MVC without writing raw XML/@Configuration boilerplate: interceptors, formatters, CORS, resource handlers, view resolvers
  • 6.7.2 Registering a HandlerInterceptor via WebMvcConfigurer.addInterceptors()
  • 6.7.3 addCorsMappings() — and the exact reason this alone doesn't work once Spring Security is on the classpath (cross-reference Security roadmap 11.2.10) — Security's own CORS config takes precedence
  • 6.7.4 Static resource handling — default locations (/static, /public, /resources, /META-INF/resources) and addResourceHandlers() for custom mappings
  • 6.7.5 Converter/Formatter registration — custom type conversion for @RequestParam/@PathVariable binding (e.g., a custom String → LocalDate format)
  • 6.7.6 Content negotiation configuration beyond the defaults

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-8.title: 6.8 File uploads and multipart handling
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-8.html:
Checklist

  • 6.8.1 MultipartFile — receiving an uploaded file in a controller method
  • 6.8.2 multipart/form-data request structure at a glance
  • 6.8.3 spring.servlet.multipart.* properties — max file size, max request size, and the exception thrown when exceeded
  • 6.8.4 Streaming large uploads vs loading the whole file into memory — awareness of the trade-off for very large files

spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-9.title: 6.9 WebClient and RestClient (calling other services)
spring-boot/spring-mvc-and-web-layer/6-9.html:
Checklist

  • 6.9.1 RestTemplate — the traditional, now feature-frozen synchronous HTTP client
  • 6.9.2 WebClient — the reactive, non-blocking HTTP client (usable in non-reactive apps too, just without the non-blocking benefit unless the whole call chain is reactive)
  • 6.9.3 RestClient (Spring 6.1+) — the modern synchronous replacement for RestTemplate, fluent API similar to WebClient but blocking
  • 6.9.4 Which to reach for in new code: RestClient for synchronous apps, WebClient for reactive/WebFlux apps, RestTemplate only in legacy maintenance
  • 6.9.5 Error handling, timeouts, and retries when calling downstream services (cross-reference the Security roadmap's @RegisteredOAuth2AuthorizedClient + WebClient combination from Stage 14.3.23)

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: Auto-Configuration Internals
spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Stage 7: Spring Boot auto-configuration internals. Everything before this stage was "how Spring works." This stage is specifically "how Spring Boot decides what to configure for you without being asked" — the exact mechanism your Security roadmap kept gesturing at (spring-boot-starter-security "does auto-configuration") without opening it up.

Stage 7 — Spring Boot auto-configuration internals

  1. 7.1 @SpringBootApplication unpacked0/5
  2. 7.2 How @EnableAutoConfiguration actually finds configuration classes0/5
  3. 7.3 Conditional evaluation in practice0/7
  4. 7.4 Starters vs auto-configuration — the distinction people conflate0/4
  5. 7.5 Configuration properties feeding auto-configuration0/2
  6. 7.6 Embedded server auto-configuration as a concrete worked example0/3
  7. 7.7 Writing your own starter/auto-configuration (the exercise that cements this stage)0/5
  8. 7.8 Failure analysis and startup diagnostics0/3

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.1 `@SpringBootApplication` unpacked
spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.1.1 @SpringBootApplication is a meta-annotation — it's actually three annotations combined
  • 7.1.2 @SpringBootConfiguration — a specialized @Configuration, marks this as the primary config source
  • 7.1.3 @ComponentScan — scans the package of the annotated class and everything below it (why your main class's package placement matters — putting it in the wrong package silently misses beans, the same trap from Stage 2.2.4, now at the application root level)
  • 7.1.4 @EnableAutoConfiguration — the actual auto-configuration trigger, the piece that does the interesting work
  • 7.1.5 SpringApplication.run() — what actually happens when your main() method calls this: creating the ApplicationContext, refreshing it, publishing lifecycle events, starting the embedded server

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.2 How `@EnableAutoConfiguration` actually finds configuration classes
spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.2.1 AutoConfigurationImportSelector — the ImportSelector implementation (cross-reference Stage 3.6.3, where you first met this interface) that @EnableAutoConfiguration triggers
  • 7.2.2 META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports — the file (Spring Boot 2.7+) listing every candidate auto-configuration class, one per line, bundled inside each starter's jar
  • 7.2.3 The older mechanism you'll still see referenced in tutorials/older Boot versions: META-INF/spring.factories under the EnableAutoConfiguration key — functionally the same idea, different file format
  • 7.2.4 Why this means auto-configuration classes are discovered via a file on the classpath, not reflection-based scanning of arbitrary packages — a deliberate, fast, explicit mechanism
  • 7.2.5 The candidate list can be huge (100+ classes) — most get excluded immediately by their own conditions, not because they were never considered

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.3 Conditional evaluation in practice

next.title: 7.4 Starters vs auto-configuration — the distinction people conflate

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.3.1 Every auto-configuration class is essentially a @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) class wrapped in layers of @Conditional* annotations (cross-reference Stage 3.3 — nothing new here, just applied at framework scale)
  • 7.3.2 A concrete worked example: reading through DataSourceAutoConfiguration's actual conditions (@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class), @ConditionalOnMissingBean, etc.) to see the pattern for real
  • 7.3.3 Why adding a dependency to your pom.xml/build.gradle is often the entire trigger for a new feature turning on — the jar shows up on the classpath, @ConditionalOnClass flips from false to true, the auto-configuration activates
  • 7.3.4 This is the precise mechanism behind the Security roadmap's opening claim that adding spring-boot-starter-security "does auto-configuration automatically" — now traceable to an exact annotation on an exact class
  • 7.3.5 @AutoConfigureOrder / @AutoConfigureBefore / @AutoConfigureAfter — controlling evaluation order between auto-configuration classes, needed because some configs depend on beans another config would create
  • 7.3.6 spring.autoconfigure.exclude (property) or @SpringBootApplication(exclude = ...) — explicitly turning off an auto-configuration class you don't want, even if its conditions would otherwise pass
  • 7.3.7 --debug flag / debug=true property — printing the full auto-configuration report at startup: positive matches, negative matches, and why each one was excluded (the single best debugging tool for "why isn't my feature auto-configuring")

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.4 Starters vs auto-configuration — the distinction people conflate
spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.4.1 A starter (spring-boot-starter-*) is just a Maven/Gradle dependency descriptor — a curated bundle of transitive dependencies, containing no code of its own in most cases
  • 7.4.2 Auto-configuration is the actual @Configuration classes that run — usually living in a separate spring-boot-autoconfigure module (or a library's own autoconfigure jar), pulled in because the starter brought the right jars onto the classpath
  • 7.4.3 A starter's real job: get the right jars present so the right @ConditionalOnClass checks pass — it doesn't "activate" anything directly
  • 7.4.4 Third-party libraries can ship their own auto-configuration the exact same way (their own .imports file) — auto-configuration isn't an Anthropic-of-Spring-only mechanism, any library can plug into it

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.5 Configuration properties feeding auto-configuration

prev.title: 7.4 Starters vs auto-configuration — the distinction people conflate

next.title: 7.6 Embedded server auto-configuration as a concrete worked example

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.5.1 How auto-configuration classes commonly pair with a @ConfigurationProperties-annotated class to expose tunable settings (previewed here, full depth in Stage 8) — e.g., DataSourceProperties backing DataSourceAutoConfiguration
  • 7.5.2 @EnableConfigurationProperties inside an auto-configuration class — registering the properties class as a bean so its values are actually bound and usable

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.6 Embedded server auto-configuration as a concrete worked example

next.title: 7.7 Writing your own starter/auto-configuration (the exercise that cements this stage)

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.6.1 ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration — how Tomcat (the default), Jetty, or Undertow gets selected and configured purely from what's on the classpath
  • 7.6.2 Why excluding spring-boot-starter-tomcat and adding spring-boot-starter-jetty is genuinely enough to swap servers — no code changes, just classpath changes, because that's exactly what the conditional annotations are keyed on
  • 7.6.3 ServletWebServerFactoryCustomizer — the extension point for tweaking the embedded server (port, connection timeouts, thread pool size) without replacing the whole auto-configuration

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.7 Writing your own starter/auto-configuration (the exercise that cements this stage)

prev.title: 7.6 Embedded server auto-configuration as a concrete worked example

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.7.1 Creating a minimal custom starter module: an empty starter jar (dependencies only) + a separate autoconfigure jar (the actual @Configuration class)
  • 7.7.2 Writing the AutoConfiguration.imports file by hand and confirming your config class gets picked up in a separate test application
  • 7.7.3 Adding a @ConditionalOnClass and a @ConditionalOnMissingBean to your custom auto-configuration, then proving both branches (present vs absent) actually change behavior
  • 7.7.4 Pairing it with a @ConfigurationProperties class so your starter is externally configurable, closing the loop into Stage 8
  • 7.7.5 Running with --debug against your own custom starter and reading your own class's entry in the auto-configuration report

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.title: 7.8 Failure analysis and startup diagnostics

prev.title: 7.7 Writing your own starter/auto-configuration (the exercise that cements this stage)

spring-boot/auto-configuration-internals.html:
Checklist

  • 7.8.1 FailureAnalyzer — Spring Boot's mechanism for turning a raw, ugly startup exception into the friendly, actionable error message you're used to seeing in the console
  • 7.8.2 A concrete example: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException for a DataSource becoming a clear "no database configured" message instead of a bare stack trace
  • 7.8.3 Why understanding this exists helps you read startup failures faster — the friendly message is itself pointing you toward a specific missing condition/property, not an arbitrary error

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: Configuration & Properties
spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:
Stage 8: Spring Boot configuration & properties. This stage takes @Value (Stage 3.4) and profiles (Stage 3.5) further — into the structured, type-safe, environment-driven configuration model Boot actually expects you to use at scale.

Stage 8 — Spring Boot configuration & properties

  1. 8.1 Property file formats and structure0/6
  2. 8.2 @ConfigurationProperties in full depth0/9
  3. 8.3 Property source precedence0/7
  4. 8.4 Profiles at the Boot application level (building on Stage 3.5)0/5

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: 8.1 Property file formats and structure
spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:
Checklist

  • 8.1.1 application.properties — flat key-value format
  • 8.1.2 application.yml — hierarchical format, indentation-sensitive, and the classic "YAML is not a superset of properties" surprises (no ${} inside YAML the same way, list syntax differences)
  • 8.1.3 Why mixing both formats in the same project is legal but confusing — pick one and stay consistent
  • 8.1.4 List/array binding in properties (app.servers[0]=...) vs YAML (- item sequences)
  • 8.1.5 Map binding in both formats
  • 8.1.6 Relaxed binding rules — my-property, myProperty, MY_PROPERTY, and my.property all bind to the same underlying property; this is why environment variables (which can't contain dots) still work for configuration

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: 8.2 `@ConfigurationProperties` in full depth
spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:
Checklist

  • 8.2.1 The structural difference from @Value restated concretely: one class, one prefix, many related fields bound together — instead of scattering individual @Value annotations across the codebase (cross-reference Stage 3.4.6)
  • 8.2.2 @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail") on a dedicated class
  • 8.2.3 Constructor binding vs setter binding — constructor binding (with @ConstructorBinding pre-Boot 3, implicit for single-constructor classes in Boot 3+) enables immutable properties classes
  • 8.2.4 Nested properties objects — a properties class containing another properties-annotated class as a field, mapping to nested YAML structure naturally
  • 8.2.5 Java record types as configuration properties classes (Boot 3+) — concise, immutable, and now the generally recommended style for new code
  • 8.2.6 @EnableConfigurationProperties(MyProps.class) vs @ConfigurationPropertiesScan — two different ways to actually register a properties class as a bean, and why forgetting either one means your properties class silently never gets bound at all
  • 8.2.7 Validation on configuration properties: @Validated + Bean Validation annotations (@NotNull, @Min, etc.) directly on properties fields — fail-fast at startup instead of discovering a bad config value deep in production
  • 8.2.8 spring-boot-configuration-processor — the annotation processor that generates additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json, giving you IDE autocomplete and inline docs for your own custom properties
  • 8.2.9 Type-safe conversion Boot handles for free: Duration (10s, 5m), DataSize (10MB), and why using these types instead of raw long/int avoids unit-confusion bugs entirely

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: 8.3 Property source precedence

next.title: 8.4 Profiles at the Boot application level (building on Stage 3.5)

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:
Checklist

  • 8.3.1 The full precedence order, highest to lowest (the version worth memorizing, roughly): command-line arguments → SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON → servlet init params → JNDI → Java system properties → OS environment variables → profile-specific application-{profile}.yml → application.yml → @PropertySource-loaded files → default properties
  • 8.3.2 Why this ordering exists conceptually: more specific/deployment-time sources should always be able to override more general/build-time ones
  • 8.3.3 application-{profile}.yml overriding values from the base application.yml only for that active profile, not replacing the whole file
  • 8.3.4 Multi-document YAML files (--- separators) with spring.config.activate.on-profile — packing multiple profiles' overrides into a single application.yml file instead of separate files
  • 8.3.5 spring.config.import — explicitly importing additional config files, including from external locations
  • 8.3.6 Config file search locations and order (classpath:/, classpath:/config/, file:./, file:./config/) and why a ./config/application.yml next to your jar silently overrides the one bundled inside it — a genuinely common deployment surprise
  • 8.3.7 --spring.config.location= for pointing entirely at an external config location

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: 8.4 Profiles at the Boot application level (building on Stage 3.5)

next.title: 8.5 Externalizing secrets properly (bridging to production reality)

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:
Checklist

  • 8.4.1 spring.profiles.active set via application.yml, environment variable, command-line arg, or SpringApplicationBuilder
  • 8.4.2 spring.profiles.default — the fallback when no active profile is set at all
  • 8.4.3 Profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=db,cache,monitoring) — activating one named profile that expands into several, keeping deployment configs simple while keeping the underlying profile files granular
  • 8.4.4 Why profile-specific beans (@Profile) and profile-specific property files are two separate but complementary mechanisms — you'll typically use both together
  • 8.4.5 The genuine risk from the Security roadmap's own note (9.4.9) resurfacing here in concrete form: a dev profile with relaxed security/logging accidentally becoming active in production because of a misconfigured deployment pipeline — treat active-profile determination as a first-class operational concern, not an afterthought

prev.title: 8.4 Profiles at the Boot application level (building on Stage 3.5)

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:

  • 8.5.2 Environment variable overrides as the most common real-world secret-injection method, via the relaxed binding rules from 8.1.6
  • 8.5.3 spring.config.import=optional:vault://... / cloud config server integration — Boot's spring.config.import mechanism extends to more than local files
  • 8.5.4 RandomValuePropertySource — generating random values (${random.uuid}, ${random.int}) directly in property files, useful for local dev secrets/ports, not a production secret strategy

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: 8.6 `Environment` and property resolution APIs

prev.title: 8.5 Externalizing secrets properly (bridging to production reality)

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:

  • 8.6.2 Environment.getActiveProfiles() / getDefaultProfiles()

spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.title: 8.7 Custom `SpringApplication` behavior
spring-boot/configuration-and-properties.html:

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.1 What Actuator actually is
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.1.1 spring-boot-starter-actuator — a starter (cross-reference Stage 7.4) bringing in operational/monitoring endpoints via the exact same auto-configuration mechanism as everything else
  • 9.1.2 The core idea: expose insight into a running application's internals — health, metrics, environment, beans — over HTTP (or JMX) without writing that code yourself
  • 9.1.3 Endpoint — Actuator's own concept, distinct from a regular @RestController endpoint, implemented via @Endpoint/@ReadOperation/@WriteOperation
  • 9.1.4 Actuator endpoints are exposed over both HTTP and JMX by default, independently configurable

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.2 Exposure control
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.2.1 Almost every endpoint is enabled but not exposed over HTTP by default (except /health) — enabled means "the bean exists," exposed means "reachable over a channel," two separate settings often confused
  • 9.2.2 management.endpoints.web.exposure.include / .exclude — controlling which endpoints are reachable over HTTP
  • 9.2.3 Why include=* is convenient in local dev and dangerous in production (direct restatement of the Security roadmap's 19.3.2, now with the actual property mechanics behind it)
  • 9.2.4 management.endpoint.<id>.enabled=false — disabling a specific endpoint's underlying bean entirely, a stronger measure than just un-exposing it
  • 9.2.5 management.server.port — running Actuator on a separate port, enabling network-level isolation (cross-reference Security roadmap 19.3.3) independent of any Spring Security config

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.3 Built-in endpoints tour
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.3.1 /health — aggregate application health, the one endpoint exposed by default
  • 9.3.2 /info — arbitrary static/build info you configure, useful for "what version is actually deployed"
  • 9.3.3 /env — full environment properties (why this is sensitive — cross-reference Security roadmap 19.3.1/19.3.5, now you know exactly what it dumps: every resolved property from every property source in Stage 8.3)
  • 9.3.4 /configprops — every bound @ConfigurationProperties bean and its current values
  • 9.3.5 /beans — the full list of beans in the ApplicationContext — a genuine map of your entire application's internals to anyone who can reach it
  • 9.3.6 /mappings — every HandlerMapping, i.e. every URL your app responds to, mapped from Stage 6.2.3
  • 9.3.7 /loggers — viewing and changing log levels at runtime without a redeploy (a write-capable endpoint, doubly worth restricting)
  • 9.3.8 /threaddump / /heapdump — full JVM thread state / heap snapshot, the two endpoints most likely to leak substantial sensitive data or crash a small instance if pulled carelessly
  • 9.3.9 /metrics — raw metric names and values, the low-level counterpart to the Micrometer-formatted /prometheus endpoint
  • 9.3.10 /shutdown — a write-capable endpoint that terminates the application, disabled by default, and exactly why it must never be exposed unauthenticated
  • 9.3.11 /scheduledtasks, /caches, /conditions — the auto-configuration report from Stage 7.3.7, now available live over HTTP instead of only at startup with --debug

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.4 Health indicators
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.4.1 HealthIndicator interface — the contract for reporting one component's health status
  • 9.4.2 Auto-configured indicators: DataSourceHealthIndicator, DiskSpaceHealthIndicator, RedisHealthIndicator, and others — again selected by classpath presence, same conditional mechanism as Stage 7.3
  • 9.4.3 Health.up() / Health.down() / Health.outOfService() / Health.unknown() builders, plus custom detail key-value pairs
  • 9.4.4 Writing a custom HealthIndicator for an app-specific dependency (an external API, a message queue) that Boot has no built-in check for
  • 9.4.5 management.endpoint.health.show-details — never / when-authorized / always, controlling whether the aggregate /health response includes each component's detail or just a top-level status (cross-reference Security roadmap 19.3.7)
  • 9.4.6 Health groups — grouping indicators (e.g., a readiness group vs a liveness group) for different consumers
  • 9.4.7 Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes — management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled, and the distinction between "is the process alive" (liveness) vs "is it ready to receive traffic" (readiness) that Kubernetes specifically needs, not the same question

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.5 Metrics and Micrometer
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.5.1 Micrometer — the metrics facade Actuator is built on, conceptually "SLF4J for metrics" (one API, pluggable backend)
  • 9.5.2 MeterRegistry — the core object you inject to record custom metrics
  • 9.5.3 Meter types: Counter (only goes up), Gauge (current value, can go up or down), Timer (duration + count), DistributionSummary
  • 9.5.4 Auto-instrumented metrics Boot gives you for free: HTTP request timings, JVM memory/GC, thread pool stats, DataSource pool stats (direct payoff of the HikariCP metrics mentioned in the JPA roadmap's Stage 19.5.1/14.6.2)
  • 9.5.5 @Timed annotation — declarative timing of a method, another entry in the "it's just AOP advice" family from Stage 5.7
  • 9.5.6 Tags/dimensions on metrics — attaching labels (e.g., method, status, endpoint) for later filtering/grouping in your monitoring backend
  • 9.5.7 Registry implementations: SimpleMeterRegistry (in-memory, default, not for real monitoring), PrometheusMeterRegistry, and others for Datadog/New Relic/CloudWatch etc.
  • 9.5.8 /actuator/prometheus endpoint — the scrape target format Prometheus expects, once micrometer-registry-prometheus is on the classpath
  • 9.5.9 MeterFilter — controlling which metrics get recorded/renamed/denied at the registry level, useful for cardinality control (too many unique tag combinations can blow up a metrics backend)

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.6 Distributed tracing

next.title: 9.7 Securing Actuator (tying back to the Security roadmap)

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.6.1 Micrometer Tracing (the modern replacement for the older Spring Cloud Sleuth) — propagating trace/span IDs across a request's lifecycle and across service boundaries
  • 9.6.2 Trace ID vs span ID — one request, one trace ID, many spans (one per hop/operation)
  • 9.6.3 Automatic propagation through RestClient/WebClient calls and messaging, so a trace ID survives a call from Service A to Service B
  • 9.6.4 Exporters: Zipkin, OpenTelemetry — where the collected trace data actually goes
  • 9.6.5 Connecting log lines to a trace via MDC (direct callback to the JPA roadmap's Stage 19.4.4 — this is the concrete mechanism behind "correlation IDs" mentioned there)

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.7 Securing Actuator (tying back to the Security roadmap)
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.7.1 Actuator endpoints are just more URLs — Spring Security's authorizeHttpRequests() applies to them exactly like any other endpoint once both are on the classpath together
  • 9.7.2 EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint() — a Spring Security matcher specifically built to target "anything under /actuator/**" without hardcoding the path (full context: Security roadmap Stage 8.3.16 and 9.4.6)
  • 9.7.3 EndpointRequest.to("health", "info") — targeting a specific subset of endpoints with different rules than the rest
  • 9.7.4 The layered recommendation restated concretely, now that you know each piece: separate management port (network isolation) + exposure include-list (don't publish what you don't need) + Spring Security authorization (authenticate/authorize what remains exposed) — three independent layers, not one

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.8 Custom Actuator endpoints

prev.title: 9.7 Securing Actuator (tying back to the Security roadmap)

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.8.1 @Endpoint(id = "...") — defining your own custom Actuator endpoint from scratch
  • 9.8.2 @ReadOperation / @WriteOperation / @DeleteOperation — mapping to GET/POST/DELETE semantics for your custom endpoint
  • 9.8.3 @Selector — path-variable-style arguments on a custom endpoint operation
  • 9.8.4 When a custom Actuator endpoint is the right tool vs just building a normal @RestController admin endpoint — Actuator endpoints get exposure control, JMX support, and consistent conventions for free; a plain controller doesn't

spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.title: 9.9 Info contributors
spring-boot/actuator-and-production-read.html:
Checklist

  • 9.9.1 InfoContributor interface — feeding custom data into /info
  • 9.9.2 Build info: spring.info.build.* properties + the Maven/Gradle plugin generating build-info.properties automatically, so /info can report the actual deployed version/commit
  • 9.9.3 Git info: git.properties generation via a build plugin, surfaced automatically if present on the classpath

spring-boot/testing.title: Testing
spring-boot/testing.html:
Stage 10: Testing Spring & Spring Boot applications. You already met @DataJpaTest and @WithMockUser/@SpringBootTest in the other two roadmaps without their full context. This stage is that missing context — the general testing infrastructure they're both built on top of.

Stage 10 — Testing Spring & Spring Boot applications

  1. 10.1 The testing pyramid, applied to Spring apps specifically0/5
  2. 10.2 spring-boot-starter-test — what's actually bundled0/5
  3. 10.3 @SpringBootTest in depth0/6
  4. 10.4 Slice test annotations tour0/7
  5. 10.5 Mocking dependencies inside the Spring context0/5
  6. 10.6 Testing web layer specifics0/5
  7. 10.7 Context caching — why test suite speed depends on this0/4
  8. 10.8 @ActiveProfiles and test-specific configuration0/4
  9. 10.9 Testing configuration and conditional logic itself0/3
