spring-boot/testing/10-1-the-testing-pyr.title: 10.1 The testing pyramid, applied to Spring apps specifically
spring-boot/testing/10-1-the-testing-pyr.html:
Checklist

  • 10.1.1 Pure unit tests — no Spring container at all, just plain JUnit + Mockito against a class in isolation
  • 10.1.2 Slice tests — a partial ApplicationContext loading only the beans relevant to one layer (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, etc.)
  • 10.1.3 Full integration tests — @SpringBootTest, the entire application context, closest to production behavior, slowest to run
  • 10.1.4 The trade-off underlying all three: speed and isolation vs realism, restated from the JPA roadmap's 17.1.6 but now as a general principle across every layer, not just persistence
  • 10.1.5 A healthy test suite shape: many unit tests, a moderate number of slice tests, few but meaningful full integration tests — not inverted

spring-boot/testing/10-10-testcontainers.title: 10.10 Testcontainers as general Spring Boot test infrastructure (not just JPA)

prev.title: 10.9 Testing configuration and conditional logic itself

next.title: 10.11 What to test at this layer generally

spring-boot/testing/10-10-testcontainers.html:
Checklist

  • 10.10.1 @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+, first met in the JPA roadmap's 17.3.3) generalized: it works for Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, and other containerized dependencies too, not only databases
  • 10.10.2 @Testcontainers + @Container combined with @SpringBootTest for genuinely realistic integration tests against real infrastructure
  • 10.10.3 @TestConfiguration classes returning Testcontainers-backed beans as a pattern for centralizing container setup across many test classes without duplicating boilerplate

spring-boot/testing/10-11-what-to-test-a.title: 10.11 What to test at this layer generally

prev.title: 10.10 Testcontainers as general Spring Boot test infrastructure (not just JPA)

spring-boot/testing/10-11-what-to-test-a.html:
Checklist

  • 10.11.1 Controller-level: correct status codes, correct response shape, validation error handling — not business logic (that belongs in service-layer unit tests)
  • 10.11.2 @ConfigurationProperties binding — a genuinely worthwhile test given how silently a typo or wrong prefix can leave a properties bean unbound
  • 10.11.3 Custom HealthIndicator/Actuator endpoint logic — small, isolated, and easy to unit test directly without a container
  • 10.11.4 Custom AOP aspects tested against real proxies, not just the raw advice logic in isolation — the self-invocation/final-class failure modes from Stage 5.8 only surface through a real proxy
  • 10.11.5 Auto-configuration conditional logic, using 10.9's ApplicationContextRunner approach specifically

spring-boot/testing/10-2-spring-boot-sta.title: 10.2 `spring-boot-starter-test` — what's actually bundled

prev.title: 10.1 The testing pyramid, applied to Spring apps specifically

spring-boot/testing/10-2-spring-boot-sta.html:
Checklist

  • 10.2.1 JUnit 5 (Jupiter) — the test execution engine
  • 10.2.2 Mockito — mocking framework
  • 10.2.3 AssertJ — fluent assertions (cross-reference JPA roadmap 17.6.1)
  • 10.2.4 spring-test — the actual Spring testing support module underneath everything else in this stage
  • 10.2.5 JSONPath, XMLUnit, and other content-assertion libraries bundled for convenience

spring-boot/testing/10-3-springboottest-.title: 10.3 `@SpringBootTest` in depth
spring-boot/testing/10-3-springboottest-.html:
Checklist

  • 10.3.1 What it actually does: finds your @SpringBootApplication class (via @SpringBootConfiguration detection walking up the package tree) and boots the full context exactly like production startup
  • 10.3.2 webEnvironment options: MOCK (default, no real server), RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT, NONE
  • 10.3.3 RANDOM_PORT + TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient — genuine end-to-end HTTP tests against a real running embedded server (cross-reference JPA roadmap's 17.6.3)
  • 10.3.4 Why @SpringBootTest is the slowest common test type — full context startup cost paid per test class (mitigated by context caching, see 10.7)
  • 10.3.5 @SpringBootTest(properties = {"key=value"}) — overriding specific properties just for this test class
  • 10.3.6 @TestPropertySource — an alternative/complementary way to layer test-specific properties on top of the normal precedence chain from Stage 8.3

spring-boot/testing/10-4-slice-test-anno.title: 10.4 Slice test annotations tour

next.title: 10.5 Mocking dependencies inside the Spring context

spring-boot/testing/10-4-slice-test-anno.html:
Checklist

  • 10.4.1 @WebMvcTest — loads only the web layer (controllers, @ControllerAdvice, converters, filters) — no service/repository beans unless explicitly provided as mocks
  • 10.4.2 @WebMvcTest(UserController.class) — narrowing to one specific controller
  • 10.4.3 @DataJpaTest (JPA roadmap 17.1.2 revisited) — now understood as one instance of this same general slicing pattern, not a special JPA-only trick
  • 10.4.4 @JsonTest — loads only Jackson-related infrastructure, for testing serialization/deserialization of a DTO in isolation
  • 10.4.5 @RestClientTest — for testing code that uses RestClient/RestTemplate/WebClient against a mocked server response
  • 10.4.6 @WebFluxTest — the reactive counterpart to @WebMvcTest (cross-reference Security roadmap 17.5.3)
  • 10.4.7 The general pattern worth internalizing: each @*Test slice annotation is really just a curated @SpringBootTest-adjacent context with a specific, narrow auto-configuration subset activated — not a fundamentally different mechanism

spring-boot/testing/10-5-mocking-depende.title: 10.5 Mocking dependencies inside the Spring context
spring-boot/testing/10-5-mocking-depende.html:
Checklist

  • 10.5.1 @MockBean (pre-Boot 3.4) — replaces a real bean in the context with a Mockito mock, for the duration of the test
  • 10.5.2 @MockitoBean / @MockitoSpyBean (Boot 3.4+) — the renamed, generalized replacement for @MockBean/@SpyBean, decoupled from Spring Boot Test specifically
  • 10.5.3 Why @MockBean-style annotations cause a new context to be created if the combination of mocked beans differs from a previously cached context — a direct, concrete cause of slow test suites (bridges into 10.7)
  • 10.5.4 @SpyBean/@MockitoSpyBean — wrapping a real bean instead of fully replacing it, so real logic runs but calls can still be verified/stubbed selectively
  • 10.5.5 Plain Mockito (@Mock, @InjectMocks, MockitoExtension) for pure unit tests that don't need a Spring context at all — the right default when you don't need the container

spring-boot/testing/10-6-testing-web-lay.title: 10.6 Testing web layer specifics

prev.title: 10.5 Mocking dependencies inside the Spring context

next.title: 10.7 Context caching — why test suite speed depends on this

spring-boot/testing/10-6-testing-web-lay.html:
Checklist

  • 10.6.1 MockMvc — simulating HTTP requests against controllers without a real running server (already used extensively in the Security roadmap's Stage 17)
  • 10.6.2 @AutoConfigureMockMvc — adding MockMvc support to a full @SpringBootTest instead of only via @WebMvcTest
  • 10.6.3 WebTestClient — the reactive-friendly test client, usable against both WebFlux apps and, in non-reactive mode, against a real running server started by @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
  • 10.6.4 Asserting JSON response bodies with JSONPath expressions (jsonPath("$.field").value(...))
  • 10.6.5 Testing @ControllerAdvice exception handling explicitly — triggering the exception path and asserting the resulting error response shape

spring-boot/testing/10-7-context-caching.title: 10.7 Context caching — why test suite speed depends on this
spring-boot/testing/10-7-context-caching.html:
Checklist

  • 10.7.1 Spring's TestContext framework caches an ApplicationContext keyed by its exact configuration (active profiles, property overrides, mocked beans, imported configs) — identical configuration across test classes reuses the same context instead of rebuilding it
  • 10.7.2 Why seemingly small differences between test classes (a different @MockitoBean, a different @ActiveProfiles set) silently create a new cache entry and a full context rebuild
  • 10.7.3 @DirtiesContext — explicitly telling Spring a test has mutated shared context state in a way that makes it unsafe to reuse for subsequent tests, forcing a rebuild afterward
  • 10.7.4 Practical suite-speed strategy: minimize the number of distinct context configurations across your test suite — a large test suite with many slightly-different @SpringBootTest setups is often slower for this reason alone, not because any single test is slow

spring-boot/testing/10-8-activeprofiles-.title: 10.8 `@ActiveProfiles` and test-specific configuration

prev.title: 10.7 Context caching — why test suite speed depends on this

next.title: 10.9 Testing configuration and conditional logic itself

spring-boot/testing/10-8-activeprofiles-.html:
Checklist

  • 10.8.1 @ActiveProfiles("test") — the test-level counterpart to spring.profiles.active (Stage 8.4.1), the standard way to swap in test-specific beans/properties
  • 10.8.2 A conventional application-test.yml — pointing at a test database, disabling certain scheduled jobs, relaxing certain settings, precisely for test runs
  • 10.8.3 @TestConfiguration — a @Configuration class meant only for test contexts, either nested inside a test class or as a separate class, providing test-only bean overrides without polluting production configuration
  • 10.8.4 The difference between @TestConfiguration (additive, combined with the main config) and fully replacing @SpringBootApplication's component scan with @ContextConfiguration (rare, more manual)

spring-boot/testing/10-9-testing-configu.title: 10.9 Testing configuration and conditional logic itself

next.title: 10.10 Testcontainers as general Spring Boot test infrastructure (not just JPA)

spring-boot/testing/10-9-testing-configu.html:
Checklist

  • 10.9.1 ApplicationContextRunner — a lightweight way to test auto-configuration classes and conditional bean logic in isolation, without a full @SpringBootTest (directly useful for the custom starter exercise from Stage 7.7)
  • 10.9.2 Asserting a bean is/isn't present under specific simulated conditions (withPropertyValues(), withClassLoader(new FilteredClassLoader(...))) — testing your @ConditionalOnClass/@ConditionalOnProperty logic actually behaves as intended
  • 10.9.3 @ConfigurationPropertiesTest / testing @ConfigurationProperties binding directly with ApplicationContextRunner plus withUserConfiguration()

spring-boot/project-ladder.title: Project Ladder
spring-boot/project-ladder.html:
Stage 11: Project ladder. Same principle as your other two roadmaps — these force the muscle memory the first 10 stages only gave you vocabulary for. Do them in order.

Stage 11 — Project ladder

  1. 11.1 Project 1 — Plain Spring, no Boot at all (Stages 1–4 applied)0/8
  2. 11.2 Project 2 — AOP from scratch (Stage 5 applied)0/7
  3. 11.3 Project 3 — Full Spring MVC REST API (Stage 6 applied)0/7
  4. 11.4 Project 4 — Auto-configuration and properties from scratch (Stages 7–8 applied)0/7
  5. 11.5 Project 5 — Production-instrumented capstone (Stages 9–10 applied, everything integrated)0/9
  6. You are done when...0/4

spring-boot/project-ladder/you-are-done-.title: You are done when...

next.title: 11.1 Project 1 — Plain Spring, no Boot at all (Stages 1–4 applied)

spring-boot/project-ladder/you-are-done-.html:
Checklist

  • You can explain, without notes, exactly what happens between SpringApplication.run() being called and your first request being handled
  • You can look at any @Transactional, @PreAuthorize, @Cacheable, or custom annotation and immediately recognize "this is AOP advice around a proxy" instead of treating it as separate magic per-feature
  • You can explain why a bean is missing, wrongly scoped, or not receiving a property value by reasoning through the exact mechanism, not by trial-and-error guessing
  • You've broken your own auto-configuration, your own AOP aspect, and your own bean wiring at least once each on purpose, and fixed each one

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-1-project-.title: 11.1 Project 1 — Plain Spring, no Boot at all (Stages 1–4 applied)
spring-boot/project-ladder/11-1-project-.html:
Checklist

  • 11.1.1 A bare Java app using spring-context only — no Spring Boot, no auto-configuration, no embedded server
  • 11.1.2 Manually create an AnnotationConfigApplicationContext from a @Configuration class in main()
  • 11.1.3 Wire 4–5 beans by hand across @Component scanning and explicit @Bean methods, mixing constructor and setter injection deliberately to feel the difference
  • 11.1.4 Implement @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy on one bean and print the lifecycle order to confirm it matches Stage 4.1 exactly
  • 11.1.5 Create a genuine circular dependency with constructor injection, watch it fail fast, then fix it by switching one side to setter injection and watch it succeed via the early-reference cache (Stage 4.6)
  • 11.1.6 Build the singleton-injecting-prototype problem on purpose (Stage 4.3), confirm the prototype is effectively "stuck," then fix it with ObjectProvider
  • 11.1.7 Write your own BeanPostProcessor that logs every bean's class name as it initializes — proof that this isn't a black box
  • 11.1.8 Break it on purpose: register two beans of the same type with no @Primary/@Qualifier, inject by type, watch NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, then fix it both ways (once with @Primary, once with @Qualifier)

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-2-project-.title: 11.2 Project 2 — AOP from scratch (Stage 5 applied)

prev.title: 11.1 Project 1 — Plain Spring, no Boot at all (Stages 1–4 applied)

next.title: 11.3 Project 3 — Full Spring MVC REST API (Stage 6 applied)

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-2-project-.html:
Checklist

  • 11.2.1 Add spring-boot-starter-aop to a small Boot app
  • 11.2.2 Build @LogExecutionTime + an @Around aspect measuring and logging duration on any annotated method
  • 11.2.3 Build @Retry(times = n) + an @Around aspect that retries on any thrown exception up to n times before propagating
  • 11.2.4 Build a pointcut using execution(...) targeting all public methods in your service package, and a separate one using @annotation(...) targeting only annotated methods — compare the two approaches on the same target
  • 11.2.5 Apply your @Retry aspect to a method, then call it from another method in the same class — confirm the self-invocation bug happens exactly as predicted, then fix it by moving the caller into a different bean
  • 11.2.6 Force CGLIB proxying deliberately (a class with no interface) and confirm AopUtils.isCglibProxy() returns true; then implement an interface and confirm it switches to a JDK dynamic proxy
  • 11.2.7 Break it on purpose: write @Around advice that forgets to call proceed(), confirm the real method never runs, then fix it

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-3-project-.title: 11.3 Project 3 — Full Spring MVC REST API (Stage 6 applied)

next.title: 11.4 Project 4 — Auto-configuration and properties from scratch (Stages 7–8 applied)

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-3-project-.html:
Checklist

  • 11.3.1 A @RestController-based CRUD API with path variables, query params, and @RequestBody/ResponseEntity used correctly and deliberately (not just copy-pasted from a tutorial)
  • 11.3.2 Bean Validation on request DTOs (@Valid), including at least one custom ConstraintValidator
  • 11.3.3 A global @RestControllerAdvice handling validation errors, a custom business exception, and a fallback handler — returning ProblemDetail-shaped responses consistently
  • 11.3.4 A custom HandlerInterceptor logging request duration, registered via WebMvcConfigurer
  • 11.3.5 A custom Converter<String, YourType> registered for a non-trivial @RequestParam binding
  • 11.3.6 A downstream call to another API using RestClient, with explicit timeout and error handling
  • 11.3.7 Break it on purpose: throw an exception from inside your custom HandlerInterceptor and confirm your @RestControllerAdvice does not catch it (mirroring the filter-exception gap from 6.6.7) — then fix the interceptor's own error handling directly

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-4-project-.title: 11.4 Project 4 — Auto-configuration and properties from scratch (Stages 7–8 applied)

prev.title: 11.3 Project 3 — Full Spring MVC REST API (Stage 6 applied)

next.title: 11.5 Project 5 — Production-instrumented capstone (Stages 9–10 applied, everything integrated)

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-4-project-.html:
Checklist

  • 11.4.1 Build your own two-module custom starter: an empty my-feature-spring-boot-starter and a my-feature-spring-boot-autoconfigure module with real logic (e.g., a simple rate limiter, or a request-signing client)
  • 11.4.2 Write the AutoConfiguration.imports file by hand and confirm it's picked up in a separate consumer application with zero manual @Import
  • 11.4.3 Add @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and @ConditionalOnProperty to your auto-configuration, and prove each one changes behavior with a targeted test
  • 11.4.4 Pair it with a @ConfigurationProperties record class, validated with Bean Validation, and confirm IDE autocomplete works after adding spring-boot-configuration-processor
  • 11.4.5 Run the consumer app with --debug and find your own auto-configuration class's entry in the positive-match report
  • 11.4.6 Set up profile-specific YAML files (application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml) with genuinely different values for at least 3 properties, and confirm switching spring.profiles.active actually changes runtime behavior
  • 11.4.7 Break it on purpose: deliberately place your @ConfigurationProperties class without @EnableConfigurationProperties/@ConfigurationPropertiesScan, confirm the values silently stay null/default despite correct YAML, then fix it

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-5-project-.title: 11.5 Project 5 — Production-instrumented capstone (Stages 9–10 applied, everything integrated)

prev.title: 11.4 Project 4 — Auto-configuration and properties from scratch (Stages 7–8 applied)

spring-boot/project-ladder/11-5-project-.html:
Checklist

  • 11.5.1 Take Project 3 or 4 and add Actuator with /health, /info, /metrics, /prometheus explicitly exposed, everything else excluded
  • 11.5.2 A custom HealthIndicator for a real external dependency (or a simulated one) reporting DOWN under a forced failure condition
  • 11.5.3 A custom business metric (Counter or Timer) recorded via MeterRegistry on a real code path, visible in /actuator/prometheus
  • 11.5.4 A custom @Endpoint exposing something app-specific (e.g., current feature-flag state) via @ReadOperation
  • 11.5.5 Wire Micrometer Tracing with an exporter (Zipkin locally is easiest) and confirm a trace ID appears consistently across a multi-hop call (even a self-call through RestClient to your own second endpoint counts)
  • 11.5.6 Full test suite: unit tests, at least one @WebMvcTest, at least one @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) end-to-end test, and an ApplicationContextRunner test proving your custom auto-configuration's conditionals
  • 11.5.7 Measure your test suite's context-cache behavior directly — count distinct context startups across the suite, then deliberately reduce that count by unifying @ActiveProfiles/@MockitoBean combinations, and confirm suite runtime drops
  • 11.5.8 Lock Actuator down behind Spring Security if you have it available (or a simple Basic Auth config if not) on a separate management port
  • 11.5.9 Final exercise: have someone else (or a fresh AI session) try to find a bean they can't explain the lifecycle of, a property that silently doesn't bind, or an AOP aspect that silently doesn't fire — fix everything they find

spring-data-jpa/database-theory-sql-and-.title: 2.1 DDL (Data Definition Language)
spring-data-jpa/database-theory-sql-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 2.1.1 CREATE TABLE — columns, types, constraints inline
  • 2.1.2 ALTER TABLE — add/drop column, add/drop constraint
  • 2.1.3 DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE — the difference, and why truncate is not transactional in most engines

  • 8.2.4 The jakarta.persistence vs javax.persistence package split (Jakarta EE rename) and which Spring Boot version uses which

  • 8.2.6 The three-layer stack to keep straight: Spring Data JPA → JPA spec → Hibernate → JDBC → database

spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.html:
Checklist

  • 8.3.2 EntityManager — the actual work-horse, cheap, one per unit of work (typically one per request/transaction)

spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.title: 8.4 Entity lifecycle states
spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.html:
Checklist

  • 8.4.1 Transient — a plain Java object, not yet known to JPA
  • 8.4.2 Managed (persistent) — attached to a persistence context, changes tracked
  • 8.4.3 Detached — was managed, persistence context closed or entity explicitly detached
  • 8.4.4 Removed — marked for deletion, still in the persistence context until flush/commit
  • 8.4.5 State transition diagram — draw it from memory: new → persist() → managed; find() → managed; detach()/close → detached; merge() on detached → managed copy; remove() → removed → deleted
  • 8.4.6 EntityManager.persist() — transient → managed
  • 8.4.7 EntityManager.merge() — detached → new managed copy (returns a different object reference, a very common source of bugs)
  • 8.4.8 EntityManager.remove() — managed → removed
  • 8.4.9 EntityManager.detach() / clear() — managed → detached
  • 8.4.10 EntityManager.find() vs getReference() — eager load vs lazy proxy, and when getReference() throws EntityNotFoundException (only on access, not on call)
  • 8.4.11 EntityManager.contains() — checking managed status

spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.title: 8.5 The persistence context in depth
spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.html:
Checklist

  • 8.5.1 First-level cache — the persistence context itself acts as a cache within one EntityManager
  • 8.5.2 Identity map pattern — same row, same Java object instance, within one persistence context
  • 8.5.3 Dirty checking — Hibernate compares current state to a snapshot to decide what SQL to generate, without you calling "update"
  • 8.5.4 How dirty checking actually works internally: snapshot taken at load time, compared at flush time
  • 8.5.5 flush() — synchronizing pending changes to the database without committing
  • 8.5.6 FlushModeType.AUTO vs COMMIT — when Hibernate decides to flush automatically
  • 8.5.7 Why a query can trigger an automatic flush first (to see your own uncommitted changes)
  • 8.5.8 clear() vs close() — evicting everything vs ending the context entirely
  • 8.5.9 Memory growth risk: a long-lived persistence context holding thousands of managed entities (classic batch-job bug)

spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.title: 8.6 Persistence context scope patterns
spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.html:
Checklist

  • 8.6.1 Transaction-scoped persistence context — the Spring/JTA default, one per transaction
  • 8.6.2 Extended persistence context — spans multiple transactions (stateful, mostly EJB-world, rare in Spring)
  • 8.6.3 Open Session in View (OSIV) — what it is, spring.jpa.open-in-view default (true), and why it's controversial
  • 8.6.4 The trade-off OSIV makes: convenience (lazy loading works in the view/controller) vs holding a DB connection open for the entire request

  • 8.6.6 The correct fix when disabling OSIV: fetch what you need inside the service/transaction boundary, not in the view layer

spring-data-jpa/orm-theory-and-hibernate.title: 9.3 Schema generation and validation

spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-1-decl.title: 10.1 Declaring an entity
spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-1-decl.html:
Checklist

  • 10.1.1 @Entity — the annotation that makes a class persistable
  • 10.1.2 The requirement for a no-arg constructor (protected is fine, Hibernate needs it for proxying/reflection)
  • 10.1.3 Why entity classes should not be final — CGLIB/bytecode proxies can't subclass a final class
  • 10.1.4 @Table(name = ..., schema = ..., uniqueConstraints = ...)
  • 10.1.5 Why the Java class name and table name diverging is fine and common (naming strategy handles it)
  • 10.1.6 Default naming strategy: ImplicitNamingStrategy and PhysicalNamingStrategy — how firstName becomes first_name
  • 10.1.7 SpringPhysicalNamingStrategy — Spring Boot's default (snake_case conversion)
  • 10.1.8 Overriding naming strategy globally vs annotating every column manually

spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-2-prim.title: 10.2 Primary keys
spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-2-prim.html:
Checklist

  • 10.2.1 @Id — marking the primary key field
  • 10.2.2 @GeneratedValue and the four strategies: AUTO, IDENTITY, SEQUENCE, TABLE
  • 10.2.3 IDENTITY — relies on DB auto-increment; disables JDBC batching for inserts (a real, common performance surprise)
  • 10.2.4 SEQUENCE — Hibernate can pre-allocate IDs client-side, enabling batching; the generally preferred strategy on Postgres/Oracle
  • 10.2.5 @SequenceGenerator — name, allocationSize, and why allocationSize mismatched with the actual DB sequence increment causes ID gaps or collisions
  • 10.2.6 TABLE strategy — a table simulating a sequence; portable but slow, rarely the right choice
  • 10.2.7 AUTO — Hibernate picks based on dialect; fine for prototyping, be explicit in real projects
  • 10.2.8 UUID primary keys: @GeneratedValue with a UUID generator vs assigning in application code
  • 10.2.9 Composite primary keys: @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass — two different approaches, pick one style per project
  • 10.2.10 @EmbeddedId with an @Embeddable key class — the more object-oriented approach
  • 10.2.11 @IdClass — a separate class mirroring the ID fields, no embedding required
  • 10.2.12 Natural ID (@NaturalId) — a business-meaningful unique key distinct from the surrogate PK, with its own Hibernate caching support

spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-3-basi.title: 10.3 Basic column mapping
spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-3-basi.html:
Checklist

  • 10.3.1 @Column(name, nullable, unique, length, precision, scale, columnDefinition)
  • 10.3.2 nullable = false at the JPA level vs NOT NULL at the DB level — both matter, for different reasons (validation timing)
  • 10.3.3 insertable/updatable flags — read-only or write-only columns
  • 10.3.4 @Transient — a field Hibernate must ignore entirely
  • 10.3.5 transient Java keyword vs @Transient annotation — they are not the same thing, and both can matter
  • 10.3.6 columnDefinition — dropping to raw DDL for a column when the abstraction isn't enough, and its portability cost

spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-4-enti.title: 10.4 Entity equality and identity
spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-4-enti.html:
Checklist

  • 10.4.1 Why default Object.equals()/hashCode() (reference equality) usually breaks once entities cross persistence-context boundaries
  • 10.4.2 Business-key equality — implementing equals()/hashCode() on a stable natural key
  • 10.4.3 Why using the generated @Id in equals()/hashCode() is risky before the entity is persisted (ID is null, breaks Set semantics)
  • 10.4.4 The "use a constant hashCode + business key equals" pattern as a common, defensible solution
  • 10.4.5 Why Lombok's @Data/@EqualsAndHashCode on entities is a well-known footgun (includes all fields including lazy collections, triggers unwanted loads, breaks proxies)
  • 10.4.6 Recommended Lombok usage on entities: @Getter/@Setter only, hand-write equals/hashCode, or use @EqualsAndHashCode(onlyExplicitlyIncluded = true)
  • 10.4.7 toString() on entities and the lazy-loading trap (auto-generated toString() touching a lazy collection triggers an unwanted query or a LazyInitializationException)

spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-5-inhe.title: 10.5 Inheritance mapping strategies
spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-5-inhe.html:
Checklist

  • 10.5.1 Why you'd model inheritance in JPA at all (Vehicle → Car, Truck)
  • 10.5.2 @Inheritance(strategy = SINGLE_TABLE) — one table, a discriminator column, nullable columns for subclass-specific fields
  • 10.5.3 @DiscriminatorColumn / @DiscriminatorValue
  • 10.5.4 SINGLE_TABLE trade-off: fastest queries (no joins), but a wide table full of nullable columns
  • 10.5.5 @Inheritance(strategy = JOINED) — a table per class, joined by shared PK
  • 10.5.6 JOINED trade-off: normalized and clean, but every subclass query pays a join cost
  • 10.5.7 @Inheritance(strategy = TABLE_PER_CLASS) — a complete table per concrete class, UNION needed for polymorphic queries
  • 10.5.8 TABLE_PER_CLASS trade-off: rarely the right choice — poor polymorphic query performance, ID generation complications
  • 10.5.9 @MappedSuperclass — sharing fields across entities without an inheritance relationship in the DB at all (the most commonly used option in practice, e.g. shared audit fields)
  • 10.5.10 Decision guide: MappedSuperclass for pure code reuse, SINGLE_TABLE for performance-critical polymorphic queries, JOINED for normalized correctness, TABLE_PER_CLASS almost never

spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-6-embe.title: 10.6 Embeddable / value types
spring-data-jpa/entity-mapping/10-6-embe.html:
Checklist

  • 10.6.1 @Embeddable — a class with no identity of its own, embedded into an owning entity's table

  • 10.6.3 @AttributeOverride / @AttributeOverrides — renaming embedded columns when reused in multiple entities
  • 10.6.4 Modeling value objects (Address, Money, DateRange) as embeddables instead of primitive obsession
  • 10.6.5 Nested embeddables — an @Embeddable containing another @Embeddable
  • 10.6.6 Collections of embeddables: @ElementCollection with an @Embeddable element type

  • 10.7.3 Collection of basic types (List<String>, Set<Integer>)
  • 10.7.4 @OrderColumn — preserving list order via an extra index column
  • 10.7.5 @MapKeyColumn — using Map<String, String> with a key column
  • 10.7.6 Why @ElementCollection entries have no independent identity — you replace the whole collection, you don't "update one element" the way you would an entity
  • 10.7.7 Performance reality: element collections are convenient but often the wrong choice at scale — a full entity with @OneToMany gives you more control

Stage 11 — Relationships & associations

  2. 11.2 @ManyToOne0/6
  3. 11.3 @OneToMany0/7
  4. 11.4 @OneToOne0/5
  5. 11.5 @ManyToMany0/6
  6. 11.6 Cascade types0/10

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.1 Foundational concepts before any annotation
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.1.1 Owning side vs inverse (mapped-by) side — the relationship exists once in the DB (one FK column), but is described from both Java classes
  • 11.1.2 mappedBy — always placed on the inverse side, points to the field name (not column name) on the owning side
  • 11.1.3 Unidirectional vs bidirectional associations — start unidirectional by default, add the inverse side only when you actually need to navigate that direction
  • 11.1.4 Why bidirectional associations require manual synchronization in application code (setting both sides) — Hibernate does not do this for you
  • 11.1.5 The standard fix: helper methods (addItem()/removeItem()) on the parent that update both sides consistently
  • 11.1.6 Fetch type default per association type — memorize this table:
    • @ManyToOne → EAGER by default
    • @OneToOne → EAGER by default
    • @OneToMany → LAZY by default
    • @ManyToMany → LAZY by default
  • 11.1.7 Why the @ManyToOne/@OneToOne EAGER defaults are widely considered a design mistake in the JPA spec — and why almost every experienced team overrides them to LAZY explicitly

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.2 `@ManyToOne`
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.2.1 The most common association — always the owning side, always holds the FK column
  • 11.2.2 @JoinColumn(name = ...) — naming the FK column explicitly instead of relying on the default
  • 11.2.3 @JoinColumn(nullable = false) — required relationship, generates NOT NULL on the FK
  • 11.2.4 optional = false on @ManyToOne itself — a JPA-level hint that also affects fetch join generation
  • 11.2.5 Explicitly setting fetch = FetchType.LAZY — the near-universal recommendation
  • 11.2.6 Why lazy @ManyToOne requires bytecode enhancement or proxy generation, and what a proxy object actually is at runtime

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.3 `@OneToMany`
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.3.1 Unidirectional @OneToMany — Hibernate creates a hidden join table by default unless you specify @JoinColumn (a very common surprise for beginners)
  • 11.3.2 Fixing the hidden-join-table surprise with @JoinColumn on a unidirectional @OneToMany to use a direct FK instead
  • 11.3.3 Bidirectional @OneToMany/@ManyToOne pair — the standard, recommended pattern for one-to-many in practice
  • 11.3.4 mappedBy on the @OneToMany side referencing the @ManyToOne field name
  • 11.3.5 Collection type choice: List (ordered, allows duplicates) vs Set (no duplicates, needs correct equals/hashCode) vs Map
  • 11.3.6 Why List with @OrderColumn can cause expensive reshuffling updates on removal from the middle
  • 11.3.7 Set and the equals/hashCode dependency from Stage 10.4 becoming critical here — a broken equals() silently corrupts Set behavior

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.4 `@OneToOne`
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.4.1 Owning side (holds the FK, typically with a @JoinColumn + unique constraint) vs inverse side (mappedBy)
  • 11.4.2 Shared primary key strategy — @MapsId, where the child's PK is also its FK to the parent
  • 11.4.3 Why @OneToOne EAGER-by-default is especially easy to forget about since it "looks like" a simple association
  • 11.4.4 The lazy @OneToOne complication: on the inverse side, Hibernate cannot build a lazy proxy without an extra query anyway (because it doesn't know if a row exists without checking) — bytecode enhancement is required for true laziness here
  • 11.4.5 When to just use @ManyToOne with a unique constraint instead of true @OneToOne — often simpler and gets you real laziness

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.5 `@ManyToMany`
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.5.1 The join table requirement — @JoinTable(name, joinColumns, inverseJoinColumns)
  • 11.5.2 Owning side vs mappedBy inverse side for @ManyToMany
  • 11.5.3 Why plain @ManyToMany is often the wrong modeling choice once the join table needs its own attributes (a timestamp, a status, a quantity)
  • 11.5.4 The standard fix: break the @ManyToMany into two @ManyToOne relationships pointing at an explicit join entity (e.g. Enrollment between Student and Course)
  • 11.5.5 @ManyToMany collection mutation pitfalls: removing and re-adding instead of relying on cascade to manage join rows
  • 11.5.6 Performance reality: @ManyToMany fetches the entire other side's collection unless carefully paged — rarely appropriate for large collections

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.6 Cascade types
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.6.1 What cascading means: propagating an operation from parent to child entities automatically
  • 11.6.2 CascadeType.PERSIST — saving the parent also saves new children
  • 11.6.3 CascadeType.MERGE — merging the parent also merges children
  • 11.6.4 CascadeType.REMOVE — deleting the parent also deletes children (dangerous if the child could be shared)
  • 11.6.5 CascadeType.REFRESH, CascadeType.DETACH
  • 11.6.6 CascadeType.ALL — all of the above, and why blanket use of ALL is a common source of accidental cascading deletes
  • 11.6.7 orphanRemoval = true — distinct from CascadeType.REMOVE; removes a child when it's taken out of the collection, not only when the parent is deleted
  • 11.6.8 The specific difference: CascadeType.REMOVE cascades only on explicit parent deletion; orphanRemoval cascades on collection disassociation too
  • 11.6.9 Choosing cascade rules by ownership semantics: true parent-owns-child (Order→OrderLine) gets aggressive cascade; shared/independent entities (Student``Course) get none
  • 11.6.10 Cascade and the persistence context — cascading operations happen within the same EntityManager, not as separate transactions

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.7 Fetch strategies in depth
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.7.1 FetchType.EAGER — loaded immediately with the parent, always, no matter what the query needs
  • 11.7.2 FetchType.LAZY — loaded only on first access, via a proxy
  • 11.7.3 Why LAZY is a hint, not a guarantee — Hibernate may still eager-load under certain query forms
  • 11.7.4 The proxy mechanism: Hibernate returns a subclass proxy for @ManyToOne/@OneToOne, and a lazy-initializing collection wrapper (PersistentBag/PersistentSet/PersistentList) for collections
  • 11.7.5 LazyInitializationException — accessing a lazy association after the persistence context/session is closed, the single most common JPA runtime error
  • 11.7.6 The wrong fix: making everything EAGER "to make the error go away" (masks N+1 problems, discussed fully in Stage 14)
  • 11.7.7 The right fixes: fetch joins, entity graphs, DTO projections, or restructuring the transaction boundary (previewed here, detailed in Stage 14)
  • 11.7.8 Bytecode enhancement (hibernate-enhance-maven-plugin / Gradle equivalent) for lazy loading of basic attributes and true @OneToOne laziness — an advanced, often-skipped feature

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.8 Bidirectional relationship management pitfalls
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.8.1 Forgetting to set both sides — the parent's collection shows the child, but the child's FK is never persisted (or vice versa)
  • 11.8.2 toString() and Lombok on bidirectional entities causing infinite recursion (parent → child → parent → …)
  • 11.8.3 JSON serialization infinite recursion on bidirectional associations — @JsonManagedReference/@JsonBackReference or (better) DTOs instead of serializing entities directly
  • 11.8.4 Why serializing JPA entities directly as API responses is broadly discouraged — lazy proxies, recursion, and leaking DB structure into the API contract

spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.title: 11.9 Modeling decisions and trade-offs
spring-data-jpa/relationships-and-associ.html:
Checklist

  • 11.9.1 When to use a direct entity association vs just storing a foreign key ID and querying separately (sometimes simpler and avoids proxy/laziness complexity entirely)
  • 11.9.2 Aggregate boundaries (a DDD concept) as a guide for where cascade/ownership should stop
  • 11.9.3 Avoiding "God object" entity graphs where everything cascades into everything, making any single save touch half the database
  • 11.9.4 Rule of thumb: model the relationship you actually query, not every relationship that theoretically exists

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.1 The repository abstraction
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.1.1 What problem Spring Data JPA solves: eliminating boilerplate DAO implementation code
  • 12.1.2 Repository<T, ID> — the root marker interface, no methods
  • 12.1.3 CrudRepository<T, ID> — basic CRUD: save, findById, findAll, delete, count, existsById
  • 12.1.4 PagingAndSortingRepository<T, ID> — adds findAll(Pageable) and findAll(Sort)
  • 12.1.5 JpaRepository<T, ID> — the one you actually use; adds batch operations, flush(), saveAndFlush(), deleteAllInBatch()
  • 12.1.6 How Spring generates an implementation at runtime — no code you write, a dynamic proxy backed by SimpleJpaRepository
  • 12.1.7 SimpleJpaRepository — the default implementation class, worth reading the source of at least once
  • 12.1.8 @Repository annotation — exception translation into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy (cross-reference Stage 6.5.2)
  • 12.1.9 @EnableJpaRepositories — what it scans, and why Spring Boot usually makes this invisible via auto-configuration
  • 12.1.10 Repository interfaces require no implementation class — a common early point of confusion for beginners

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.2 `save()` semantics — the most misunderstood method
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.2.1 save() is not always an INSERT — it calls persist() for new entities and merge() for detached ones
  • 12.2.2 How Spring Data decides new vs existing: checks if the @Id field is null (default strategy)
  • 12.2.3 Persistable<ID> interface — overriding the new-vs-existing check yourself (needed when you assign IDs manually, e.g. UUIDs set before persist)
  • 12.2.4 Why calling save() on an entity with a manually-assigned, non-null ID triggers a merge() (an extra SELECT) even though you intended an INSERT — and how Persistable fixes it
  • 12.2.5 saveAndFlush() — forcing immediate synchronization, useful right before a native query that needs to see the change
  • 12.2.6 saveAll() — batching behavior and its interaction with hibernate.jdbc.batch_size (cross-reference 9.2.5)

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.3 Query derivation from method names
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.3.1 The naming convention: findBy, readBy, queryBy, getBy, countBy, existsBy, deleteBy/removeBy
  • 12.3.2 Property expressions: findByLastName, findByAddressCity (traverses nested objects/embeddables)
  • 12.3.3 The nested-property ambiguity problem (AddressCity could mean address.city or an addressCity field) and how to disambiguate with underscores (findByAddress_City)
  • 12.3.4 Logical operators: And, Or
  • 12.3.5 Comparison keywords: Between, LessThan, GreaterThan, LessThanEqual, GreaterThanEqual, After, Before
  • 12.3.6 IsNull / IsNotNull
  • 12.3.7 Like, NotLike, StartingWith, EndingWith, Containing — and how Spring Data wraps the value with % for you
  • 12.3.8 In / NotIn — accepting a Collection parameter
  • 12.3.9 True / False for boolean properties
  • 12.3.10 IgnoreCase / AllIgnoreCase
  • 12.3.11 OrderBy embedded directly in the method name, with Asc/Desc
  • 12.3.12 First/Top + a number — limiting results (findTop5ByOrderByCreatedAtDesc)
  • 12.3.13 Distinct
  • 12.3.14 Why derived query methods become unreadable past 3–4 conditions — the practical signal to switch to @Query (Stage 12.4)
  • 12.3.15 What happens at startup if a method name doesn't parse correctly — a PropertyReferenceException at application boot, not at call time (a genuine safety benefit worth understanding)

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.4 `@Query` — explicit queries
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.4.1 @Query("JPQL here") — writing JPQL directly on a repository method
  • 12.4.2 Named parameters: :paramName + @Param("paramName")
  • 12.4.3 Positional parameters: ?1, ?2 — and why named parameters are generally preferred for readability/refactor-safety
  • 12.4.4 @Query(nativeQuery = true) — dropping to raw SQL when JPQL can't express what you need
  • 12.4.5 Native query limitations: no automatic entity graph mapping by default, pagination requires a countQuery
  • 12.4.6 @Query with Pageable and Sort parameters injected automatically
  • 12.4.7 @Modifying — required for UPDATE/DELETE queries, since @Query defaults to expecting a SELECT
  • 12.4.8 @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) — clearing the persistence context after a bulk update so stale in-memory entities aren't served afterward
  • 12.4.9 @Modifying(flushAutomatically = true)
  • 12.4.10 Bulk UPDATE/DELETE via JPQL bypasses the persistence context and lifecycle callbacks entirely — a critical, frequently-missed gotcha (no @PreUpdate, no dirty checking, no cascade)
  • 12.4.11 SpEL in @Query: #{#entityName} for entity-name-agnostic queries

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.5 Query by Example (QBE)
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.5.1 Example.of(probe) — building a query from a partially-populated entity instance
  • 12.5.2 ExampleMatcher — customizing string matching (contains, startsWith), case sensitivity, ignored fields
  • 12.5.3 QueryByExampleExecutor<T> interface
  • 12.5.4 Genuine use case: simple dynamic search forms with a handful of optional filters
  • 12.5.5 Real limitation: no support for nested/complex conditions, OR logic, or ranges — where Specifications (12.6) take over

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.6 JPA Criteria API and Specifications
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.6.1 The problem Criteria/Specifications solve: building queries with a variable, runtime-determined set of conditions
  • 12.6.2 CriteriaBuilder, CriteriaQuery, Root<T> — the raw JPA Criteria API building blocks
  • 12.6.3 Why raw Criteria API is verbose, and why Spring Data's Specification<T> wraps it more usably
  • 12.6.4 JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> — adding findAll(Specification) to a repository
  • 12.6.5 Writing a Specification<T> — implementing toPredicate(root, query, criteriaBuilder)
  • 12.6.6 Composing specifications: .and(), .or(), .not()
  • 12.6.7 Building a dynamic filter service that composes specifications conditionally based on which search parameters were actually supplied
  • 12.6.8 Type-safe attribute access with the JPA Metamodel (Order_.customer, generated by an annotation processor) vs plain string field names — trade-off between compile-time safety and setup overhead
  • 12.6.9 The metamodel generator (hibernate-jpamodelgen) as an annotation processor dependency
  • 12.6.10 When Specifications are still the wrong tool: highly complex reporting queries are often clearer as native SQL or a dedicated query object (Stage 13)

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.7 Custom repository implementations
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.7.1 When derived methods, @Query, and Specifications all fall short — custom logic time
  • 12.7.2 The fragment interface pattern: MyRepositoryCustom interface + MyRepositoryCustomImpl implementation class
  • 12.7.3 Naming convention requirement: implementation class must be named <RepositoryName>Impl for Spring Data to auto-detect it
  • 12.7.4 Extending the main repository interface with the custom fragment interface
  • 12.7.5 Injecting EntityManager directly inside the custom implementation for raw Criteria API or native queries
  • 12.7.6 Composing multiple fragment interfaces on one repository
  • 12.7.7 When to just write a plain @Service-layer query class instead of forcing everything through the repository abstraction — it's fine, and sometimes clearer

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 12.8 Repository configuration details
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 12.8.1 @Query vs derived methods — a performance non-issue (both compile to the same underlying plan), a readability issue instead
  • 12.8.2 Repository base class customization (repositoryBaseClass on @EnableJpaRepositories) for adding cross-cutting behavior to every repository
  • 12.8.3 Null handling: Optional<T> return types vs raw T vs @NonNull/@Nullable (Spring's null-safety annotations)
  • 12.8.4 Streamable<T> and Stream<T> return types — and the requirement to close the stream (try-with-resources) since it holds a DB cursor open
  • 12.8.5 Asynchronous repository methods (@Async + CompletableFuture<T>) and why this is rarely the right tool compared to reactive repositories for real async workloads
  • 12.8.6 @Lock — pessimistic locking directly on a repository method (LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE, connects to Stage 3.12)

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 13.1 JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language)
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 13.1.1 JPQL operates on entities and their fields, not tables and columns — the core distinction from SQL
  • 13.1.2 Basic SELECT e FROM Entity e WHERE ... syntax
  • 13.1.3 JPQL joins: JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and the requirement to name the joined association explicitly
  • 13.1.4 JOIN FETCH — eagerly fetching an association for this query only, overriding the mapping's default fetch type, the single most important tool for fixing N+1 (full treatment in Stage 14)
  • 13.1.5 Why JOIN FETCH with a collection can produce duplicate parent rows, and DISTINCT (JPQL-level, deduplicating in-memory) as the fix
  • 13.1.6 Aggregate functions and GROUP BY/HAVING in JPQL — same concepts as SQL, applied to entity properties
  • 13.1.7 Constructor expressions: SELECT new com.example.dto.UserSummary(u.id, u.name) FROM User u — projecting directly into a DTO
  • 13.1.8 Subqueries in JPQL
  • 13.1.9 CASE WHEN in JPQL
  • 13.1.10 Named queries: @NamedQuery on the entity — static, validated at startup, rarely used over @Query in modern Spring Data projects but you'll see it in legacy code
  • 13.1.11 Bulk UPDATE/DELETE JPQL statements (cross-reference 12.4.10's caveat)
  • 13.1.12 Parameter binding — always bind, never string-concatenate a value into JPQL (SQL-injection-equivalent risk exists in JPQL too)

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 13.2 Native SQL queries

next.title: 13.3 Projections (fetching less than the full entity)

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 13.2.1 When JPQL genuinely can't express what you need: vendor-specific functions, window functions, CTEs, complex UNIONs
  • 13.2.2 @Query(value = "...", nativeQuery = true)
  • 13.2.3 Mapping native query results to an entity automatically (works when column names/aliases match)
  • 13.2.4 @SqlResultSetMapping — explicit mapping for complex or multi-entity native result sets
  • 13.2.5 @NamedNativeQuery
  • 13.2.6 Native queries and pagination — must supply an explicit countQuery since Hibernate can't derive one from raw SQL
  • 13.2.7 Portability cost: native queries tie you to one database vendor — an explicit, deliberate trade-off, not a default choice
  • 13.2.8 Calling stored procedures: @Procedure on a repository method, or @NamedStoredProcedureQuery on the entity

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 13.3 Projections (fetching less than the full entity)
spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 13.3.1 Why projections matter: fetching only needed columns reduces I/O and avoids full entity/proxy overhead
  • 13.3.2 Interface-based projections — declare an interface with getter methods matching property names, Spring Data implements it with a proxy
  • 13.3.3 Closed projections — only the declared properties are selected in the generated SQL (the efficient case)
  • 13.3.4 Open projections — using @Value("#{target.firstname} #{target.lastname}") SpEL, which still fetches the whole entity first (a common performance misunderstanding — open projections do not save a query)
  • 13.3.5 Nested/dynamic projections — projecting into related entities' fields
  • 13.3.6 Class-based (DTO) projections — a plain Java/record class with a matching constructor, Spring Data instantiates it directly
  • 13.3.7 DTO projections via constructor expression in @Query (cross-reference 13.1.7) as the most explicit, most efficient option
  • 13.3.8 Dynamic projection types — a generic repository method parameterized by the return type (<T> List<T> findByLastName(String name, Class<T> type))
  • 13.3.9 Java record types as projection targets (modern, concise DTOs)
  • 13.3.10 Choosing between interface, open, and DTO projections — DTO/closed-interface for performance-critical paths, open interface only for convenience where it doesn't matter

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.title: 13.4 Pagination and sorting

spring-data-jpa/repositories-and-queries.html:
Checklist

  • 13.4.1 Pageable — encapsulates page number, page size, and sort
  • 13.4.2 PageRequest.of(page, size) / PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)
  • 13.4.3 Page<T> — includes total count and total pages (executes a second COUNT query automatically — a real performance cost on large tables)
  • 13.4.4 Slice<T> — avoids the count query, only knows if there's a next page; the better choice when you don't need a total, e.g. infinite scroll
  • 13.4.5 Sort — standalone sort specification, Sort.by(...).ascending()/.descending(), combinable with multiple properties
  • 13.4.6 Offset pagination's cost at large offsets (cross-reference Stage 5.4.7) — Spring Data's default Pageable is offset-based
  • 13.4.7 Keyset/cursor-based pagination — manually implemented with @Query using WHERE id > :lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT :size, the fix for deep-pagination performance
  • 13.4.8 Spring Data 3.1+'s ScrollPosition / Window<T> API — built-in keyset scrolling support, worth checking your version for
  • 13.4.9 Exposing Pageable directly from a @RestController method parameter (PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver) and the security/DoS consideration of an unbounded page size from client input
