spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 14.1 The N+1 select problem
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 14.1.1 What N+1 actually is: 1 query to fetch parents, then N additional queries — one per parent — to lazily fetch each one's association
  • 14.1.2 Why it's invisible in development (small datasets, fast local DB) and catastrophic in production (network latency × N)
  • 14.1.3 How to actually see it: enable SQL logging (cross-reference 9.2.2) and count the queries for a single request
  • 14.1.4 hibernate.generate_statistics + Statistics API — programmatically counting query executions in tests
  • 14.1.5 A dedicated tool: datasource-proxy or p6spy to log and count real query counts in integration tests
  • 14.1.6 The classic trigger: iterating a list of parent entities and accessing a lazy @ManyToOne or @OneToMany on each one inside a loop

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 14.2 Fixing N+1 — the main techniques
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 14.2.1 JOIN FETCH in JPQL/@Query — the most direct fix, pulls the association in the same SQL query (cross-reference 13.1.4)
  • 14.2.2 The JOIN FETCH + collection + pagination conflict — Hibernate cannot paginate correctly in SQL when fetch-joining a collection (it paginates in memory instead, a well-known trap that silently loads the whole table)
  • 14.2.3 @EntityGraph — declarative alternative to JOIN FETCH, defined once and reused across queries
  • 14.2.4 @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"association1", "association2"}) on a repository method
  • 14.2.5 @NamedEntityGraph defined on the entity itself, referenced by name
  • 14.2.6 EntityGraph.EntityGraphType.FETCH vs LOAD — FETCH treats listed attributes as eager and everything else as lazy regardless of mapping; LOAD only upgrades the listed attributes, leaving the rest at their mapped default
  • 14.2.7 Batch fetching — @BatchSize(size = N) on an entity or collection, turning N individual queries into ⌈N/batchSize⌉ WHERE id IN (...) queries
  • 14.2.8 hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size — applying batch fetching globally instead of per-entity (cross-reference 9.2.7)
  • 14.2.9 Subselect fetching — @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT), replacing N queries with a single query using the original query's WHERE as a subquery
  • 14.2.10 DTO projections as a structural fix — if you only need 3 fields, don't fetch the entity graph at all (cross-reference 13.3)
  • 14.2.11 Comparing the fixes: JOIN FETCH/EntityGraph (single query, but collection+pagination limits) vs batch fetching (multiple small queries, but pagination-safe) vs DTO projection (avoids the problem structurally) — knowing which to reach for in which situation
  • 14.2.12 The inverse trap: "fixing" N+1 by making everything EAGER — this doesn't fix it, it just moves the N+1 to every query that touches the entity, including ones that never needed the association

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 14.3 Fetch mode details
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 14.3.1 FetchMode.SELECT (Hibernate default for lazy) — one query per association access
  • 14.3.2 FetchMode.JOIN — always join at the SQL level, effectively forcing eager-like behavior for that specific fetch mode regardless of FetchType
  • 14.3.3 FetchMode.SUBSELECT — detailed in 14.2.9
  • 14.3.4 The distinction between FetchType (JPA standard, lazy vs eager when) and FetchMode (Hibernate-specific, how the SQL is generated) — a genuinely confusing pair of similarly-named concepts worth being precise about

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 14.4 Second-level cache
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 14.4.1 First-level cache recap (Stage 8.5.1) — scoped to one persistence context/request, always on
  • 14.4.2 Second-level cache — shared across persistence contexts/sessions, opt-in, application-wide
  • 14.4.3 When it helps: read-heavy, rarely-changing reference data (lookup tables, configuration)
  • 14.4.4 When it actively hurts: frequently-updated entities (stale reads, cache invalidation overhead exceeding the benefit)
  • 14.4.5 Cache providers: Ehcache, Caffeine, Infinispan, Hazelcast — Hibernate needs a RegionFactory implementation
  • 14.4.6 @Cacheable (JPA) / @org.hibernate.annotations.Cache (Hibernate-specific, more control) on an entity
  • 14.4.7 CacheConcurrencyStrategy: READ_ONLY, READ_WRITE, NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, TRANSACTIONAL — trade-offs between consistency and performance
  • 14.4.8 Query cache — caching the result of a query (a list of IDs), separate from and dependent on the entity second-level cache being populated
  • 14.4.9 hibernate.cache.use_query_cache and the query cache's own invalidation behavior (invalidated whenever any row in a table used by the query changes — coarser than it sounds)
  • 14.4.10 Collection caching — caching @OneToMany/@ManyToMany collections separately from the entities themselves
  • 14.4.11 Cache region configuration and per-entity/per-collection region naming
  • 14.4.12 The distributed-cache-invalidation problem in a multi-instance deployment — why second-level cache needs a cluster-aware provider (Hazelcast, Infinispan) once you run more than one app instance, or you'll serve stale data from instances that didn't see the write
  • 14.4.13 The pragmatic default: don't reach for second-level cache first — fix N+1 and indexing before considering it; it solves a narrower problem than people assume and adds real operational complexity

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 14.5 Batch processing at scale
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 14.5.1 The persistence-context memory growth problem when processing large datasets in one transaction (cross-reference 8.5.9)
  • 14.5.2 Periodic flush() + clear() pattern inside a batch loop to bound memory usage
  • 14.5.3 hibernate.jdbc.batch_size tuning for the actual batch write throughput (cross-reference 9.2.5)
  • 14.5.4 Spring Batch as a dedicated framework for large-scale chunked processing, when hand-rolled batching isn't enough
  • 14.5.5 Stateless sessions (StatelessSession) — a Hibernate-native escape hatch that skips the persistence context entirely (no dirty checking, no cascade, no first-level cache) for pure bulk-throughput scenarios
  • 14.5.6 When StatelessSession trades away too much (no cascade, no lifecycle callbacks) vs when that's exactly what you want

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 14.6 Monitoring performance continuously
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 14.6.1 Wiring datasource-proxy/p6spy query counting into integration tests as an automated N+1 regression guard
  • 14.6.2 Micrometer + Hibernate statistics integration for production dashboards (query count, cache hit ratio, flush count)
  • 14.6.3 Setting a "max queries per request" assertion in tests for critical endpoints — turning a performance concern into a CI-enforced contract

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.1 `@Transactional` fundamentals
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.1.1 @Transactional on a Spring-managed bean method — how it maps down to the JDBC-level transaction calls from Stage 6.2
  • 15.1.2 PlatformTransactionManager — the abstraction; JpaTransactionManager — the JPA implementation Spring Boot auto-configures
  • 15.1.3 Declarative (@Transactional) vs programmatic (TransactionTemplate) transaction management
  • 15.1.4 Why @Transactional is implemented via a Spring AOP proxy — the exact same proxy mechanism as method security (cross-reference Spring Security Stage 15.1.4)
  • 15.1.5 Self-invocation bypasses @Transactional — same root cause, same fix (extract to another bean) as the security self-invocation trap
  • 15.1.6 @Transactional must be on a public method to be proxied by default (CGLIB can technically handle non-public, but it's not the safe assumption to build on)
  • 15.1.7 Class-level vs method-level @Transactional — method-level always overrides class-level

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.2 Propagation
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.2.1 What propagation controls: what happens when a @Transactional method is called from inside another transaction
  • 15.2.2 REQUIRED (default) — join the existing transaction, or create one if none exists
  • 15.2.3 REQUIRES_NEW — always suspend any existing transaction and start a fresh, independent one
  • 15.2.4 NESTED — a savepoint within the existing transaction (cross-reference Stage 3.7), rollback only to that savepoint
  • 15.2.5 MANDATORY — must be called within an existing transaction, throws if none exists
  • 15.2.6 SUPPORTS — joins if a transaction exists, runs non-transactionally otherwise
  • 15.2.7 NOT_SUPPORTED — suspends any existing transaction, runs without one
  • 15.2.8 NEVER — throws if called within an existing transaction
  • 15.2.9 Practical use case for REQUIRES_NEW: writing an audit log entry that must persist even if the outer business transaction rolls back
  • 15.2.10 The real risk of REQUIRES_NEW: two separate DB transactions means two separate connections held simultaneously, and no atomicity between them (the audit log can commit while the main operation still fails)

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.3 Isolation at the Spring level
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.3.1 @Transactional(isolation = ...) — overriding the DB default per-method (cross-reference Stage 3.8–3.10)
  • 15.3.2 Why overriding isolation per-method is rare in practice — usually a database-wide/connection-pool-wide decision, not a per-call one
  • 15.3.3 readOnly = true — a hint, not an enforcement; lets Hibernate skip dirty-checking overhead and allows some drivers/DBs to optimize (e.g., routing to a read replica)

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.4 Rollback rules
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.4.1 The default rule: unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) trigger rollback; checked exceptions do not — a genuinely surprising default for developers coming from other ecosystems
  • 15.4.2 rollbackFor = SomeCheckedException.class — forcing rollback on a checked exception
  • 15.4.3 noRollbackFor = SomeException.class — excluding a specific exception from triggering rollback
  • 15.4.4 Why catching an exception inside the @Transactional method and swallowing it silently prevents rollback entirely — even if the exception "should have" caused one
  • 15.4.5 UnexpectedRollbackException — thrown when an inner REQUIRED transaction marks the whole (outer, shared) transaction as rollback-only, but the outer code tries to commit anyway
  • 15.4.6 setRollbackOnly() — programmatically forcing a rollback without throwing

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.5 Timing and boundary pitfalls
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.5.1 The @Transactional self-call trap restated concretely: this.saveOrder() called from another method in the same class silently runs with no transaction
  • 15.5.2 @Transactional on a private method — silently ignored, no error, no warning (know this explicitly, it will bite you once)
  • 15.5.3 @Transactional combined with @Async — the transaction context does not automatically propagate to the async thread; needs deliberate handling
  • 15.5.4 Where exactly the transaction begins and ends relative to the AOP proxy boundary — draw the call stack: controller → proxy → @Transactional method → persistence code
  • 15.5.5 The transaction commits after the method returns, meaning the flush (and any constraint violations) can surface outside your own try/catch inside the method
  • 15.5.6 TransactionSynchronizationManager and TransactionSynchronization — hooking into commit/rollback events (e.g., publishing a domain event only after successful commit)
  • 15.5.7 @TransactionalEventListener — Spring's built-in way to run code after a transaction commits (or rolls back), the standard tool instead of hand-rolling TransactionSynchronization
  • 15.5.8 TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT as the default and most common choice — avoiding "acted on data that then got rolled back" bugs

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.6 Long transactions and their costs
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.6.1 A transaction held open for a slow external call (HTTP request, email send) holds a pooled DB connection the entire time (cross-reference Stage 7.3.4 — this is the same bug from a different angle)
  • 15.6.2 The fix pattern: do the DB work in a short transaction, do the slow external call outside any transaction, and reconcile afterward if needed
  • 15.6.3 Long transactions increasing lock contention and deadlock likelihood (cross-reference Stage 3.14)
  • 15.6.4 Long transactions bloating MVCC-based databases (Postgres) by preventing old row versions from being vacuumed

spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.title: 15.7 Testing transactional code
spring-data-jpa/performance-and-transact.html:
Checklist

  • 15.7.1 @Transactional on a @SpringBootTest — automatically rolls back after each test, a convenient default for test isolation
  • 15.7.2 Why this convenience can hide real bugs: code that relies on AFTER_COMMIT events, or on data actually being visible to a separate connection, won't behave the same in a test that never truly commits
  • 15.7.3 @Rollback(false) / TestTransaction.flagForCommit() when you specifically need to test post-commit behavior
  • 15.7.4 Testing propagation and rollback rules directly with TestTransaction utilities or a real integration test hitting a Testcontainers database

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: Auditing, Migrations & Testing
spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Stages 16–17: Auditing, migrations, multi-tenancy, and testing. Prerequisite: Stages 14–15. This part is about running real, evolving, shared databases safely — not just querying a static schema.

Stage 16 — Auditing, schema migrations, and multi-tenancy

  1. 16.1 Spring Data JPA auditing0/9
  2. 16.2 Full history auditing (beyond just "last modified")0/8
  3. 16.3 Schema migration tools0/9
  4. 16.4 Writing safe migrations0/6
  5. 16.5 Multi-tenancy with Spring Data JPA0/10

Stage 17 — Testing Spring Data JPA

  1. 17.1 Test types and what each actually verifies0/6
  2. 17.2 Why in-memory databases (H2) are a testing trap0/5
  3. 17.3 Testcontainers — testing against the real database engine0/8
  4. 17.4 What to actually test at the repository/persistence layer0/9
  5. 17.5 Test data setup patterns0/5
  6. 17.6 Assertions and tooling0/3

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 16.1 Spring Data JPA auditing
spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 16.1.1 @EnableJpaAuditing — turning on the auditing infrastructure
  • 16.1.2 @CreatedDate / @LastModifiedDate — automatic timestamp population
  • 16.1.3 @CreatedBy / @LastModifiedBy — automatic current-user population
  • 16.1.4 AuditingEntityListener — the @EntityListeners class that actually does the work (connects to Stage 10.9)
  • 16.1.5 @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class) required on each audited entity, or applied via a shared @MappedSuperclass
  • 16.1.6 AuditorAware<T> — the interface you implement to tell Spring who the "current user" is
  • 16.1.7 Wiring AuditorAware to Spring Security's SecurityContextHolder (cross-reference the Spring Security roadmap, Stage 5.23) — the standard real-world implementation
  • 16.1.8 What happens when there's no authenticated user (system/batch processes) — returning Optional.empty() or a sentinel "system" value deliberately
  • 16.1.9 Base Auditable @MappedSuperclass pattern — one shared class with all four audit fields, extended by every auditable entity

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 16.2 Full history auditing (beyond just "last modified")
spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 16.2.1 The difference between auditing (who/when for the current row) and history tracking (every past version of the row)
  • 16.2.2 Hibernate Envers — automatic revision history via a shadow _AUD table per entity
  • 16.2.3 @Audited annotation and what it generates
  • 16.2.4 AuditReader — querying historical revisions programmatically
  • 16.2.5 Revision entities — attaching metadata (who, when, why) to each revision
  • 16.2.6 Storage cost of Envers at scale — every update doubles into a history-table write, and this compounds over years of data
  • 16.2.7 When to reach for Envers vs a simpler hand-rolled audit log table vs an external event log — matching the tool to how much history detail you actually need
  • 16.2.8 Application-level event sourcing as an alternative philosophy entirely (know it exists, out of scope for a CRUD-first roadmap)

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 16.3 Schema migration tools
spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 16.3.1 Why ddl-auto=update is unacceptable for production (cross-reference Stage 9.3.1) — migrations are the actual answer
  • 16.3.2 The core idea: versioned, ordered, repeatable SQL/scripted changes checked into source control alongside the code that needs them
  • 16.3.3 Flyway — naming convention (V1__description.sql), the flyway_schema_history tracking table, baseline, repair
  • 16.3.4 Flyway's default philosophy: plain versioned SQL files, minimal magic
  • 16.3.5 Liquibase — changelogs in XML/YAML/JSON/SQL, databaseChangeLog, changeSet with unique id+author
  • 16.3.6 Liquibase's extra capabilities over Flyway: rollback scripts defined per changeset, database-agnostic change types (abstracted DDL)
  • 16.3.7 Choosing between them: Flyway for simplicity and raw SQL control, Liquibase when you need vendor-agnostic changelogs or built-in rollback definitions
  • 16.3.8 Spring Boot auto-configuration for either (spring.flyway.* / spring.liquibase.*) and automatic run-on-startup behavior
  • 16.3.9 Migrations run before Hibernate's own schema validation (ddl-auto=validate) — the correct production pairing: migrations own the schema, Hibernate only checks it matches

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 16.4 Writing safe migrations
spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 16.4.1 Never editing a migration that has already run in any shared environment — always add a new one
  • 16.4.2 Backward-compatible migration ordering for zero-downtime deploys: add nullable column → deploy code that writes to it → backfill → make it non-null → deploy code that requires it → drop old column, each as a separate migration/deploy step
  • 16.4.3 Why a single migration that adds a NOT NULL column with no default locks/breaks existing rows and existing running application instances
  • 16.4.4 Long-running migrations (adding an index, backfilling a large table) and locking implications — CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres) as the non-blocking alternative
  • 16.4.5 Testing migrations against a realistic data volume before running them in production, not just an empty test database
  • 16.4.6 Migration rollback strategy — most tools favor "roll forward with a fix" over true rollback, and why that's usually the safer real-world default anyway

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 16.5 Multi-tenancy with Spring Data JPA

next.title: 17.1 Test types and what each actually verifies

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 16.5.1 The three standard models restated in JPA terms: separate database per tenant, separate schema per tenant, shared schema with a discriminator column
  • 16.5.2 Separate-database: AbstractRoutingDataSource (cross-reference Stage 7.4.4) routing to a different DataSource per tenant, resolved from TenantContext
  • 16.5.3 Separate-schema: Hibernate's built-in multi-tenancy support (MultiTenancyStrategy.SCHEMA) and CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver
  • 16.5.4 Shared-schema-with-discriminator: @TenantId (Hibernate 6.4+) automatically appending a tenant filter to every query for annotated entities — the lowest-ceremony option
  • 16.5.5 Hibernate @Filter / @FilterDef as the pre-6.4 way to achieve the same shared-schema row-filtering, applied/enabled per session
  • 16.5.6 The danger of relying on @Filter alone: a forgotten session.enableFilter() call silently returns all tenants' data — no error, just a data leak
  • 16.5.7 Why @TenantId is safer than a manually-enabled @Filter — it's applied automatically, not opt-in per query
  • 16.5.8 Combining this with Spring Security's per-tenant resolution (cross-reference the Spring Security roadmap, Stage 18.2) — tenant resolution happens once, early, and both auth and data access read from the same resolved context
  • 16.5.9 Connection pool sizing implications for separate-database-per-tenant at scale — pool-per-tenant doesn't scale past a modest tenant count, know the ceiling
  • 16.5.10 Testing tenant isolation explicitly as its own test category, same principle as the Spring Security roadmap's 18.2.10 — this is the single highest-value test in a multi-tenant system

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 17.1 Test types and what each actually verifies

next.title: 17.2 Why in-memory databases (H2) are a testing trap

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 17.1.1 Unit tests with mocked repositories — verify service-layer logic, tell you nothing about actual query correctness
  • 17.1.2 @DataJpaTest — a slice test loading only JPA-related beans (repositories, EntityManager), not the full application context
  • 17.1.3 @DataJpaTest defaults to an in-memory database (H2) unless reconfigured — and why that default is a trap (see 17.2)
  • 17.1.4 @DataJpaTest is @Transactional by default, rolling back after each test — same convenience/hidden-bug trade-off as Stage 15.7
  • 17.1.5 TestEntityManager — the @DataJpaTest-provided helper for setting up test data with explicit persist()/flush() control
  • 17.1.6 Full @SpringBootTest — the whole application context, needed when you're testing interactions across service + repository + transaction boundaries together

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 17.2 Why in-memory databases (H2) are a testing trap

prev.title: 17.1 Test types and what each actually verifies

next.title: 17.3 Testcontainers — testing against the real database engine

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 17.2.1 H2's SQL dialect and behavior differences from your real production database (Postgres/MySQL/Oracle) — different date handling, different constraint enforcement, different function names
  • 17.2.2 Native queries written for Postgres often simply don't run on H2 — masking the fact that they were never really tested
  • 17.2.3 Sequence/identity generation differences between H2 and your real DB silently changing test behavior around Stage 10.2's generation strategies
  • 17.2.4 The specific failure mode: tests pass against H2, the exact same code breaks in production against the real dialect
  • 17.2.5 Why "fast but wrong" tests are worse than "slower but real" tests for a persistence layer specifically

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 17.3 Testcontainers — testing against the real database engine

prev.title: 17.2 Why in-memory databases (H2) are a testing trap

next.title: 17.4 What to actually test at the repository/persistence layer

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 17.3.1 The core idea: spin up a real, disposable Docker container of your actual production database for the test run
  • 17.3.2 @Testcontainers + @Container annotations, PostgreSQLContainer/MySQLContainer etc.
  • 17.3.3 @ServiceConnection (Spring Boot 3.1+) — automatic DataSource wiring to the container, replacing manual @DynamicPropertySource boilerplate
  • 17.3.4 Container reuse across test classes (.withReuse(true)) to avoid paying startup cost per test class
  • 17.3.5 Singleton container pattern via a shared base test class — the standard way to avoid dozens of container startups in a large suite
  • 17.3.6 Combining Testcontainers with your real Flyway/Liquibase migrations — the test database gets built exactly the way production does, closing the gap from Stage 16.4.5
  • 17.3.7 CI pipeline requirements: Docker-in-Docker or a Docker socket available to the test runner
  • 17.3.8 The trade-off honestly stated: slower test suite in exchange for tests that actually mean something for a persistence layer

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 17.4 What to actually test at the repository/persistence layer

prev.title: 17.3 Testcontainers — testing against the real database engine

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 17.4.1 Custom @Query/native query correctness — the thing most worth testing, since it's hand-written SQL/JPQL that the compiler can't verify
  • 17.4.2 Cascade behavior — saving a parent actually persists/updates/removes children as configured (cross-reference Stage 11.6)
  • 17.4.3 orphanRemoval behavior specifically — removing from a collection actually deletes the row
  • 17.4.4 Unique constraint violations surfacing as the expected exception type
  • 17.4.5 Query method count/N+1 regression tests (cross-reference Stage 14.6.1) — asserting the number of queries executed for a critical path stays bounded
  • 17.4.6 Pagination correctness — total count, page boundaries, empty-page edge cases
  • 17.4.7 Specification composition — combining several optional filters produces the right WHERE clause and right results
  • 17.4.8 Auditing fields actually populate on create/update (cross-reference Stage 16.1)
  • 17.4.9 Multi-tenant isolation — the test from Stage 16.5.10, made concrete: tenant A's repository call never returns tenant B's row

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 17.5 Test data setup patterns

prev.title: 17.4 What to actually test at the repository/persistence layer

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 17.5.1 Object Mother / Test Data Builder pattern for constructing valid entity graphs without repeating setup boilerplate in every test
  • 17.5.2 @Sql annotation — running a SQL script before/after a test method for fixture setup
  • 17.5.3 Programmatic setup via TestEntityManager/repository calls vs SQL fixture scripts — trade-off between readability and realism
  • 17.5.4 Avoiding shared mutable fixture data across tests — each test should set up (and via rollback, tear down) its own state
  • 17.5.5 Faker libraries (java-faker, datafaker) for generating realistic bulk test data, especially useful for pagination/performance tests

spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.title: 17.6 Assertions and tooling
spring-data-jpa/auditing-migrations-and-.html:
Checklist

  • 17.6.1 AssertJ for fluent, readable assertions over plain JUnit assertions, especially for entity graphs and collections
  • 17.6.2 Asserting on the actual database state (a second query, or the TestEntityManager) rather than just the in-memory object, since dirty checking can lie about what was actually persisted if you never flush
  • 17.6.3 entityManager.flush() + entityManager.clear() inside a test specifically to force a real round-trip and catch mapping bugs that in-memory state would hide

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder.title: Project Ladder
spring-data-jpa/project-ladder.html:
Stage 18: Project ladder. Same principle as the Security roadmap — reading 17 stages gives you vocabulary, these 5 projects force actual muscle memory. Do them in order.

Stage 18 — Project ladder

  1. 18.1 Project 1 — Schema design + raw SQL mastery (Stages 1–3 applied, no JPA yet)0/7
  2. 18.2 Project 2 — First real Spring Data JPA CRUD app (Stages 8–13 applied)0/9
  3. 18.3 Project 3 — Performance-hardened API (Stages 14–15 applied)0/9
  4. 18.4 Project 4 — Multi-tenant, audited, migration-driven system (Stages 16 applied)0/6
  5. 18.5 Project 5 — Production-grade capstone (Stage 17 + everything integrated)0/8
  6. You are done when...0/4

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/you-are-d.title: You are done when...

next.title: 18.1 Project 1 — Schema design + raw SQL mastery (Stages 1–3 applied, no JPA yet)

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/you-are-d.html:
Checklist

  • You can explain, without notes, exactly what SQL a given JPQL query or @OneToMany access will generate before running it
  • You can look at an entity mapping and immediately spot missing LAZY, missing equals()/hashCode(), or a dangerous CascadeType.ALL
  • You've caused and fixed N+1, a deadlock, and a lost update at least once each on purpose
  • You instinctively reach for a migration tool and never for ddl-auto=update, even in a throwaway prototype

That's the complete roadmap — 10 parts, 18 stages, raw SQL to production-grade Spring Data JPA. Good luck building through it.

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-1-proj.title: 18.1 Project 1 — Schema design + raw SQL mastery (Stages 1–3 applied, no JPA yet)

next.title: 18.2 Project 2 — First real Spring Data JPA CRUD app (Stages 8–13 applied)

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-1-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 18.1.1 Design a normalized schema by hand for a real domain (e.g., library system: books, authors, members, loans) — 3NF, correct PKs/FKs
  • 18.1.2 Write the DDL yourself, no ORM, no generator
  • 18.1.3 Populate it with realistic seed data (hundreds to thousands of rows via a faker script)
  • 18.1.4 Write 15+ queries by hand covering: joins, subqueries, GROUP BY/HAVING, window functions (top N per group), a recursive CTE (e.g., a category tree)
  • 18.1.5 Wrap 3–4 of those queries in explicit transactions, deliberately trigger a rollback, verify state afterward
  • 18.1.6 Deliberately create a slow query (missing index, function-wrapped WHERE), run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, then fix it and re-run to see the plan change
  • 18.1.7 Break it on purpose: run two concurrent transactions that both update the same row — observe the lock wait, then a deadlock with two transactions updating two rows in opposite order

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-2-proj.title: 18.2 Project 2 — First real Spring Data JPA CRUD app (Stages 8–13 applied)

prev.title: 18.1 Project 1 — Schema design + raw SQL mastery (Stages 1–3 applied, no JPA yet)

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-2-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 18.2.1 Model the same schema from Project 1 as JPA entities — every relationship type at least once (@ManyToOne, @OneToMany, @OneToOne, @ManyToMany via a join entity)
  • 18.2.2 Explicit FetchType.LAZY everywhere, overriding both EAGER defaults
  • 18.2.3 Hand-write equals()/hashCode() correctly on at least one entity used in a Set
  • 18.2.4 A full repository layer: derived query methods, at least 3 @Query JPQL methods, one native query, one Specification-based dynamic filter
  • 18.2.5 DTO/record-based projections for every read-only endpoint — no entity ever serialized directly to JSON
  • 18.2.6 Pagination with Page<T> on one endpoint and Slice<T> on another — justify the choice for each
  • 18.2.7 spring.jpa.open-in-view=false set deliberately, and every lazy-loading need resolved inside the service layer, not the controller
  • 18.2.8 Schema owned entirely by Flyway/Liquibase from day one — ddl-auto=validate, never update
  • 18.2.9 Break it on purpose: remove a JOIN FETCH from a list endpoint, watch the request logs light up with N+1 queries, then fix it and confirm the count drops to 1–2 queries

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-3-proj.title: 18.3 Project 3 — Performance-hardened API (Stages 14–15 applied)

prev.title: 18.2 Project 2 — First real Spring Data JPA CRUD app (Stages 8–13 applied)

next.title: 18.4 Project 4 — Multi-tenant, audited, migration-driven system (Stages 16 applied)

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-3-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 18.3.1 Take Project 2's dataset and scale it up (10k–100k+ rows) to make performance problems actually visible
  • 18.3.2 Wire in datasource-proxy/p6spy and add a query-count assertion test on your busiest endpoint
  • 18.3.3 Deliberately compare three N+1 fixes on the same query — JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, and batch fetching — and measure query count and latency for each
  • 18.3.4 Implement keyset/cursor pagination on the largest table and compare its latency to offset pagination at a deep page number
  • 18.3.5 Build one REQUIRES_NEW audit-logging use case and prove it survives a rollback of the outer transaction
  • 18.3.6 Build one @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) use case (e.g., send a notification only after a successful save)
  • 18.3.7 Deliberately introduce a long-running external call inside a @Transactional method, observe connection pool pressure under concurrent load, then fix it by moving the call outside the transaction
  • 18.3.8 Tune HikariCP pool size and JDBC batch size against a load test, and record before/after numbers
  • 18.3.9 Break it on purpose: swallow an exception inside a @Transactional method with a bare catch block, confirm the transaction commits anyway with corrupted state, then fix it

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-4-proj.title: 18.4 Project 4 — Multi-tenant, audited, migration-driven system (Stages 16 applied)
spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-4-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 18.4.1 Convert Project 3 into a shared-schema multi-tenant app using @TenantId (or @Filter if targeting an older Hibernate version, deliberately, to feel the difference in safety)
  • 18.4.2 Full auditing: @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate/@CreatedBy/@LastModifiedBy wired to a security context (real or stubbed)
  • 18.4.3 Add Hibernate Envers to one high-value entity and query its revision history through AuditReader
  • 18.4.4 Write a zero-downtime-style migration sequence for a real schema change: add nullable column → backfill migration → make non-null — as three separate, ordered migration files
  • 18.4.5 If integrating with the Spring Security roadmap's Project 4: share the same tenant_id claim/context resolution between auth and data access
  • 18.4.6 Break it on purpose: temporarily disable the tenant filter/@TenantId on one entity, confirm cross-tenant data leaks in a test, then restore it and add a permanent isolation test guarding against regression

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-5-proj.title: 18.5 Project 5 — Production-grade capstone (Stage 17 + everything integrated)

prev.title: 18.4 Project 4 — Multi-tenant, audited, migration-driven system (Stages 16 applied)

spring-data-jpa/project-ladder/18-5-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 18.5.1 Full Testcontainers-based integration test suite running against the real production database engine, migrations included, in CI
  • 18.5.2 N+1 regression tests and query-count budgets enforced as CI-failing assertions on your top 3 endpoints
  • 18.5.3 Cascade/orphan-removal/unique-constraint tests for every entity relationship that matters
  • 18.5.4 Multi-tenant isolation test suite as its own dedicated test category
  • 18.5.5 Connection pool and query metrics wired into a real dashboard (Micrometer + Prometheus/Grafana or equivalent)
  • 18.5.6 Load test the app under realistic concurrency and watch pool exhaustion, lock contention, and P95/P99 query latency
  • 18.5.7 Document your schema evolution/migration runbook: how a new column, a new index, and a breaking column removal are each rolled out safely
  • 18.5.8 Final exercise: have someone else (or a fresh AI session) review your entity mappings and repository layer for N+1 risks, missing indexes, and cascade footguns — fix everything they find

spring-security/fundamentals-and-core-ar.html:
Checklist

  • 2.1 Encoding vs Encryption vs Hashing — three different things, never mix them
  • 2.2 Base64 is encoding, not security
  • 2.3 Symmetric encryption (one shared key) — AES
  • 2.4 Asymmetric encryption (public/private key pair) — RSA, ECDSA
  • 2.5 Which key encrypts and which key decrypts, in each direction
  • 2.6 Digital signature — sign with private key, verify with public key
  • 2.7 Cryptographic hash function properties: one-way, deterministic, collision resistant
  • 2.8 Why MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security use
  • 2.9 Why fast hashes (SHA-256) are wrong for passwords
  • 2.10 Salt — stops rainbow tables, must be unique per user

spring-security/production-hardening.title: Production Hardening
spring-security/production-hardening.html:
Stage 19: Production hardening, monitoring, and common real-world failure patterns. This is where "it works on my machine" security config gets tested by reality.

Stage 19 — Production hardening and operations

  1. 19.1 Secrets and configuration hygiene0/8
  2. 19.2 TLS and network-level hardening0/9
  3. 19.3 Actuator and operational endpoint security0/7
  4. 19.4 Logging and data protection0/7
  5. 19.5 Monitoring, alerting, and audit0/8
  6. 19.6 Dependency and platform hardening0/7
  7. 19.7 Rate limiting, abuse prevention, DoS resilience0/7
  8. 19.8 Incident response readiness0/6
  9. 19.9 Common real-world failure patterns (the "gotcha" checklist)0/15

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.1 Secrets and configuration hygiene
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.1.1 Never commit secrets: .gitignore for application-*.properties with real values, git history scrubbing if it already happened
  • 19.1.2 Environment variables vs config server vs vault — trade-offs
  • 19.1.3 HashiCorp Vault + Spring Cloud Vault integration
  • 19.1.4 AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager — Spring Cloud bindings
  • 19.1.5 Kubernetes Secrets — and why base64 is not encryption (etcd encryption at rest still required)
  • 19.1.6 Secret rotation without downtime: dual-read old and new during transition
  • 19.1.7 Separate secrets per environment — dev/staging/prod must never share a signing key or DB password
  • 19.1.8 .env files in local dev and keeping them out of source control

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.2 TLS and network-level hardening
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.2.1 TLS termination point: load balancer/ingress vs application — know where it actually happens in your stack
  • 19.2.2 server.ssl.* properties when the app terminates TLS itself
  • 19.2.3 X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Host and trusting them only from a known proxy
  • 19.2.4 server.forward-headers-strategy=native / framework and Tomcat's RemoteIpValve
  • 19.2.5 Forcing HTTPS redirect at the app or the edge, not both inconsistently
  • 19.2.6 TLS version and cipher suite minimums (TLS 1.2+ only, no weak ciphers)
  • 19.2.7 Certificate expiry monitoring and auto-renewal (Let's Encrypt / ACM / cert-manager)
  • 19.2.8 Network segmentation: DB and internal services not reachable from the public internet
  • 19.2.9 Web Application Firewall (WAF) as a complementary layer, not a replacement for app-level security

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.3 Actuator and operational endpoint security
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.3.1 Actuator endpoints exposed by default vs sensitive ones (/env, /heapdump, /beans, /configprops)
  • 19.3.2 management.endpoints.web.exposure.include — whitelist explicitly, never * in production
  • 19.3.3 Separate management port (management.server.port) bound to an internal network only
  • 19.3.4 EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint() secured behind an admin role (cross-reference 8.3.16)
  • 19.3.5 Redacting sensitive values in /env and /configprops (Sanitizer, management.endpoint.env.show-values)
  • 19.3.6 Disabling /heapdump and /threaddump in production, or locking them down hard
  • 19.3.7 /health — what detail level is safe for public vs internal consumers (management.endpoint.health.show-details)

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.4 Logging and data protection
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.4.1 Never log passwords, tokens, full card numbers, or full session IDs — decide the "never-log list" explicitly
  • 19.4.2 Masking/redaction in log patterns (Logback MaskingPatternLayout or a custom converter)
  • 19.4.3 Structured logging (JSON) and making sure structured fields go through the same redaction rules
  • 19.4.4 MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) for correlation/request IDs without leaking PII
  • 19.4.5 Log storage access control — logs are themselves sensitive data
  • 19.4.6 GDPR/CCPA-relevant fields and log retention policy
  • 19.4.7 Error responses: generic message to the client, full detail only in server-side logs

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.5 Monitoring, alerting, and audit
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.5.1 Micrometer + AuthenticationEventPublisher (cross-reference 6.7) feeding metrics: login success rate, failure rate, lockouts
  • 19.5.2 Alerting thresholds: spike in 401/403s, spike in failed logins from one IP, impossible-travel logins
  • 19.5.3 Centralized audit log for security-relevant events: login, logout, password change, permission change, admin actions
  • 19.5.4 Immutable/append-only audit storage (write-once, or a separate audit service)
  • 19.5.5 Spring Data Envers or a custom @EntityListeners audit trail for sensitive entities
  • 19.5.6 Distributed tracing (Micrometer Tracing / OpenTelemetry) through the security filter chain without leaking tokens into spans
  • 19.5.7 Dashboards: auth latency, token validation latency, active session count
  • 19.5.8 Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) integration for larger orgs — what it is, when you need it

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.6.1 Pinning Spring Security / Spring Boot versions and subscribing to security advisories
  • 19.6.2 Reading a CVE advisory: what it actually affects vs blanket panic
  • 19.6.3 Patching cadence policy — security patches on a faster track than feature upgrades
  • 19.6.4 Minimal base Docker image, non-root container user, read-only filesystem where possible
  • 19.6.5 Distroless/slim images to shrink attack surface
  • 19.6.6 SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation for compliance and incident response
  • 19.6.7 Container image scanning in CI (Trivy, Grype)

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.7 Rate limiting, abuse prevention, DoS resilience
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.7.1 Bucket4j for in-app rate limiting
  • 19.7.2 Rate limiting at the gateway/edge (nginx, API Gateway, Cloudflare) vs in-app — layered, not either/or
  • 19.7.3 Per-IP vs per-user vs per-token limits, and combining them
  • 19.7.4 Login endpoint specifically: stricter limits than general API traffic
  • 19.7.5 Distributed rate limiting with Redis when running multiple instances
  • 19.7.6 Slow-loris and connection-exhaustion awareness (usually a gateway/infra concern, but know it exists)
  • 19.7.7 CAPTCHA or proof-of-work as a step-up defense after repeated failures

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.8 Incident response readiness

prev.title: 19.7 Rate limiting, abuse prevention, DoS resilience

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.8.1 Emergency signing-key rotation runbook — practiced, not just documented
  • 19.8.2 Global "kill switch" to revoke all active sessions/tokens
  • 19.8.3 Forcing password reset for a compromised user segment
  • 19.8.4 Playbook for a leaked credential/token: revoke, rotate, audit access logs for the window of exposure
  • 19.8.5 Communicating a breach — legal/compliance obligations (know these exist; consult legal, don't wing it)
  • 19.8.6 Post-incident review focused on the control gap, not blame

spring-security/production-hardening/19-.title: 19.9 Common real-world failure patterns (the "gotcha" checklist)
spring-security/production-hardening/19-.html:
Checklist

  • 19.9.1 CSRF disabled globally "to make the API work" instead of scoping it correctly (cross-reference 11.1.12)
  • 19.9.2 permitAll() on a broad pattern that accidentally covers an admin path
  • 19.9.3 anyRequest().permitAll() left in from local debugging, shipped to prod
  • 19.9.4 Role check present, ownership check missing → IDOR (cross-reference 8.5.1)
  • 19.9.5 JWT signature not actually verified because of a misconfigured decoder
  • 19.9.6 CORS allowedOrigins("*") combined with credentials, or reflecting Origin blindly
  • 19.9.7 Security context not saved after custom login logic (missing explicit save under Spring Security 6's requireExplicitSave)
  • 19.9.8 Actuator /env or /heapdump publicly exposed, leaking secrets
  • 19.9.9 Verbose stack traces or SQL errors returned to the client
  • 19.9.10 Password reset endpoint reveals whether an email is registered
  • 19.9.11 Long-lived JWTs used as if they were sessions, with no revocation plan
  • 19.9.12 Hardcoded default admin credentials left in for "convenience," forgotten in prod
  • 19.9.13 Self-invocation silently bypassing @PreAuthorize (cross-reference 15.1.5, 15.5.7)
  • 19.9.14 Filter order mistake putting a custom filter after AuthorizationFilter, so it never gets a say
  • 19.9.15 Multi-tenant app with a role check but no tenant check (cross-reference 18.2.8)

spring-security/project-ladder.title: Project Ladder
spring-security/project-ladder.html:
Stage 20: Project ladder. Reading the first 19 stages gives you vocabulary, not skill. These 5 projects force you to actually wire it together, break it, and fix it. Do them in order — each assumes the previous one's muscle memory.

Stage 20 — Project ladder

  1. 20.1 Project 1 — Classic session-based web app (Stages 0–12 applied)0/10
  2. 20.2 Project 2 — Stateless JWT REST API (Stages 13 applied)0/8
  3. 20.3 Project 3 — Social login + first-party API (Stage 14 applied)0/7
  4. 20.4 Project 4 — Multi-service system with a real Authorization Server (Stages 14.5, 16, 18.2 applied)0/8
  5. 20.5 Project 5 — Production-hardened capstone (Stage 19 applied, everything integrated)0/10
  6. You are done when...0/4

spring-security/project-ladder/you-are-d.title: You are done when...

next.title: 20.1 Project 1 — Classic session-based web app (Stages 0–12 applied)

spring-security/project-ladder/you-are-d.html:
Checklist

  • You can draw the full filter chain from memory, including exception translation
  • You can explain, without notes, why sessions and JWT are not "session bad, JWT good" but a real trade-off
  • You've broken your own app at least 3 separate times on purpose and fixed it
  • You instinctively write the ownership/tenant check even when nobody asked for it

That's the complete roadmap — 10 parts, 20 stages, 0 to production. Good luck building through it.

spring-security/project-ladder/20-1-proj.title: 20.1 Project 1 — Classic session-based web app (Stages 0–12 applied)

next.title: 20.2 Project 2 — Stateless JWT REST API (Stages 13 applied)

spring-security/project-ladder/20-1-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 20.1.1 Spring Boot + Thymeleaf + Spring Data JPA + spring-boot-starter-security
  • 20.1.2 Custom UserDetailsService backed by a real User JPA entity with roles
  • 20.1.3 DelegatingPasswordEncoder with BCrypt, registration form that hashes on save

  • 20.1.10 Break it on purpose: try to access another user's edit page by guessing the ID — confirm it's blocked, then fix it if it isn't

spring-security/project-ladder/20-2-proj.title: 20.2 Project 2 — Stateless JWT REST API (Stages 13 applied)

next.title: 20.3 Project 3 — Social login + first-party API (Stage 14 applied)

spring-security/project-ladder/20-2-proj.html:

  • 20.2.2 Login endpoint issuing a short-lived access token + HttpOnly refresh cookie
  • 20.2.3 spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server validating your own self-issued JWTs

spring-security/project-ladder/20-3-proj.title: 20.3 Project 3 — Social login + first-party API (Stage 14 applied)

prev.title: 20.2 Project 2 — Stateless JWT REST API (Stages 13 applied)

spring-security/project-ladder/20-3-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 20.3.1 oauth2Login() with Google or GitHub as provider
  • 20.3.2 Custom OAuth2UserService creating a local User record on first login (sub as the stable key)
  • 20.3.3 After social login succeeds, issue your own JWT/session instead of relying on the provider's token for your API
  • 20.3.4 Account linking: same email arrives via two different providers — decide and implement the policy
  • 20.3.5 @RegisteredOAuth2AuthorizedClient calling a downstream Google API (e.g., fetching the user's calendar) on the user's behalf

spring-security/project-ladder/20-4-proj.title: 20.4 Project 4 — Multi-service system with a real Authorization Server (Stages 14.5, 16, 18.2 applied)

spring-security/project-ladder/20-4-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 20.4.1 Stand up your own Spring Authorization Server (or Keycloak in Docker) as the single identity source
  • 20.4.2 Two or three downstream resource servers, each validating tokens against the shared JWKS endpoint

spring-security/project-ladder/20-5-proj.title: 20.5 Project 5 — Production-hardened capstone (Stage 19 applied, everything integrated)

prev.title: 20.4 Project 4 — Multi-service system with a real Authorization Server (Stages 14.5, 16, 18.2 applied)

spring-security/project-ladder/20-5-proj.html:
Checklist

  • 20.5.2 Secrets pulled from Vault/Secrets Manager, none in source control, none in plain env files in the repo
  • 20.5.3 Actuator locked to an internal management port with an admin-only role
  • 20.5.4 Rate limiting on the login endpoint with Bucket4j + Redis, tested under concurrent load
